en: The Chronicle of the Stūpas.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In which [stūpa] the most excellent relics of the Victor lay on all sides.
Blazing with the emission of rays of five colors,
having fashioned the form of the Jina for the sake of the world’s welfare,
they bowed their heads to that most wonderful stupa.
I shall relate the history of this stupa,
which brings welfare to the entire world, which causes joy to all people,
and which is constantly honored by the best of gods, asuras, and lords of men.
Although that stupa, resplendent with jewels and well-honored,
was built long ago by the ancient community of monks for the sake of the Sinhalese people;
Even when merely composed by Vākka in his Sinhalese existence,
it does not perfectly accomplish the welfare of all people;
and because [it was also] from the Magadhi terminology of the Thūpa—
This genealogy is crowded with conflicting methods and sounds,
and since much that ought to be said has not been told,
I shall therefore speak this genealogy once again.
"Listen all, you virtuous ones,
to the complete and orderly lineage of the Teacher’s stūpa as it is being recited by me. In this context,
regarding the phrase "I shall speak the lineage of the stūpa," the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is one worthy of a stūpa.

Because of the statement, “A Paccekabuddha is worthy of a stupa; a disciple of the Tathāgata is worthy of a stupa; a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) is worthy of a stupa,” a shrine constructed by enshrining the relics of those such as the Buddha who are worthy of stupas is called a *thūpa* in the sense of being a place of elevation.
However, what is intended here is the Mahāthūpa of Kañcanamālī, which was built after enshrining the relics of whom?
If one asks, "Who is he? It is he who received the prophecy in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara;

who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, carried out all the duties of a Buddha—from the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma until the subduing of the wanderer Suhadda—and finally passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue of clinging.
Having established the relics of that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this is the summary provided here;
however, the detailed account should be understood as follows:
It is said that at the conclusion of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand additional eons from now, there was a city named Amaravatī.
There was a city. Therein dwelt a brahmin named Sumedha. Without performing any other work, he mastered the craft of a brahmin alone;
however, while he was still in his childhood, his mother and father passed away.
Then his treasurer minister brought forth the account book, opened the storehouses filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth, and [said]: "This much..."
"O youth," they said, "this much belongs to your mother, this much belongs to your father, and this much belongs to your grandfather and great-grandfather;
having thus declared what was held by the family line down to the seventh generation, they said, 'Take charge of this.
He accepted, saying, 'Very well,' and while living as a householder, one day he reflected."
3. "The grasping of rebirth-linking in a new existence is suffering; likewise, the breaking up of the body in each place where one is born is suffering.
Furthermore, I am subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to illness, and subject to death.
Since this is so, it is fitting for me to seek the blissful, cool Nibbāna—which is beyond birth, aging, illness, and death. Having thus reflected on the reason for renunciation, [he set out].
Again he thought: "When my father, grandfather, and others departed for the next world, they did not take even a single kahāpaṇa with them;
it is fitting that I should take this entire wealth and provide the means for my own departure.
Having caused a drum to be beaten in the city and given alms to the great multitude, he entered the Himālaya mountains and went forth as an ascetic.
Having gone forth, within seven days he attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), and he spent his time enjoying the bliss of those absorptions.
At that time, the Teacher named Dīpaṅkara, having attained supreme enlightenment, spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree;
then, having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at the Sunanda Garden, he taught the deathless Dhamma to seven billion gods and humans.

Having caused [the people] to drink [the Dhamma], raining down the rain of the Dhamma like a great cloud that pours over the four continents, and surrounded by four hundred thousand who had exhausted their latent tendencies (*khīṇāsava*),
he traveled by stages on his tour and, upon reaching the city of Ramma, resided at the Sudassana Great Monastery. At that time,
the inhabitants of the city of Ramma took various medicines such as clarified butter and molasses, and went forth with flowers, incense, and perfumes in their hands.
Having approached where the Buddha was, they paid homage to the Teacher, honored him with flowers and other offerings, and sat to one side.
After hearing the Dhamma, they invited the Blessed One for the following day’s meal. Rising from their seats, they circumambulated the One of Ten Powers and departed.
On the following day, having prepared an incomparable great almsgiving, they cleared the path for the arrival of the One of Ten Powers. In that...
At that time, the ascetic Sumedha, having risen from his own hermitage, was traveling through the air above those people living in the city of Ramma.
Seeing them clearing the road with joyful hearts, he wondered, "What could be the reason for this?
While everyone was looking on, he descended from the sky and stood to one side, addressing those people.
He asked, "O sirs, for whom are you clearing this road? They replied, "Venerable Sumedha, do you not know?

A Teacher named Dīpaṅkara, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, is traveling on a journey through the countryside and has, in due course, arrived at our city and is residing at the Sudassana Great Monastery."
"We have invited that Blessed One; let us clear the path for the Blessed One's arrival. Upon hearing this, the wise Sumedha reflected:
"Even the mere report of 'Buddha' is rare to hear, let alone the actual appearance of a Buddha.
Therefore, it is fitting that I too, along with these people, should clear the path for the arrival of the One Possessing the Ten Powers."
He said to those men: "Sirs, if you would clear this path for the Buddha— having first requested a single space yourselves,
and recognizing that this wise man Sumedha is of great psychic power and great majesty—
you should select one spot that is difficult to clear, mired with water, and very uneven, and clear this heap of refuse."
"Adorn it! they said, and so they did.
Having aroused joy directed toward the Buddha, the wise Sumedha thought: "I am indeed capable of making this place most beautiful by means of my psychic power (*iddhi*);
yet, having done so, it would not satisfy me. Today, however, I shall perform service with my own body."
Thinking, "It is fitting to do so," he brought earth and filled that opening;
then, having covered it with a double-layered *dupaṭṭa* robe whose color was like a *jayasumana* flower, he put it on, displaying the three circles (*timaṇḍala*).
Over that, as if scattering a cluster of flowers with a wreath of fine wool, he fastened his waistband, which was as beautiful as a streak of lightning.
It was as if they were pouring lac juice over the summit of a golden mountain peak,
as if they were encircling a golden cetiya with a net of coral, as if they were binding a golden elephant with red woolen cloth,
and as if they were shrouding the autumnal moon with crimson clouds; it was the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers soaked in lac juice.
Having put on his saffron-colored robe made of rags from a dust-heap, and emerging from the Fragrant Chamber like a lion from a golden cave,
surrounded by four hundred thousand monks whose taints were exhausted— just as the Ten-Hundred-Eyed One is surrounded by the hosts of the immortals,
or as Mahābrahmā is surrounded by the hosts of Brahmās— he appeared through the power of wholesome roots accumulated over immeasurable time.
Adorned with the peerless grace of a Buddha and surrounded by a host of stars, like the moon in the autumn sky gracing the firmament,
he set out upon the prepared road.
Sumedha the ascetic also beheld the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara approaching along that decorated and prepared path.
Beholding his own form— the pinnacle of physical beauty— adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks, embellished by the eighty minor characteristics,
majestic with a fathom-wide halo, resembling a sapphire, emitting six-colored Buddha-rays like various streaks of lightning in the sky,
he thought: "Today, I shall sacrifice my life for the One Possessed of Ten Powers."
"It is fitting for you to do this, Blessed One; do not step upon the mud as if treading upon a jeweled bridge.
Let the Blessed One walk upon my back together with the four hundred thousand whose taints are exhausted;
that shall be for my benefit and happiness for a long time. Having said this, he loosened his hair, cast off his deerskin, matted locks, and bark garments, and spread out the mud.
I lay down right there on the surface of the mud. While lying there, I thought:

"If I so desired, I could burn away all my defilements and enter the city of Ramma as a junior member of the Saṅgha; however, I have no need to burn away my defilements in secret in order to attain Nibbāna.
What if I were to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, just like the Ten-Powered One, Dīpaṅkara?"
"Having boarded the ship of the Dhamma and ferried the great multitude across the ocean of *saṃsāra*, I shall afterwards attain final *nibbāna*.
Thinking, 'This is fitting for me,' he brought together the eight qualities, made the aspiration for Buddhahood, and lay down.
Then the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara arrived, stood at the head of the wise Sumedha, and [beheld him] lying on his back in the mud."
Seeing the ascetic, and reflecting—“This ascetic has made a formal resolve for the sake of Buddhahood;

will his aspiration succeed, or will it not?”—and knowing that “In the future, one named Gotama will become a Buddha,” he gave his prediction from his very standing place in the midst of the assembly, saying: “Behold, monks, this man of lofty austerity!”
"The ascetic is lying on a bed of mud. "So it is, Bhante; this one, having made a resolution for the sake of enlightenment, will succeed.
At the end of four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons more, he will become a Buddha named Gotama"—thus he prophesied everything.
For this was said in the *Buddhavamsa*:
"Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
standing at my head, spoke these words:"
Behold this ascetic, the matted-hair ascetic of fierce penance; in an immeasurable eon from now, he will become a Buddha.

Having gone forth from the delightful city of Kapilavatthu, the Tathāgata, having exerted himself in striving and performed difficult deeds, [attained enlightenment] while some in the world were still Buddhas.
Having sat at the foot of the Ajapāla tree,
the Tathāgata took his alms-food of milk-rice there and approached the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Conqueror received the milk-rice.
"By the prepared excellent path, come indeed to the foot of the Bodhi tree";
then, having circumambulated the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to the right,
the Peerless One of great renown will awaken at the root of the Assattha tree.
Her mother, the one who gave birth to him, shall be named Māyā; his father shall be named Suddhodana—this one shall be Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated, Kolita and Upatissa shall be his chief disciples;
the attendant named Ānanda shall attend upon this Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples;
they will be free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated.
The awakening of that Blessed One is called Assattha.”
Abhinīhāra-kathā 6.
Then Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, having praised the Bodhisatta, worshipped him with eight handfuls of flowers, circumambulated him, and departed.
Those four hundred thousand arahants who had destroyed the taints likewise [honored] the Bodhisatta with flowers.
Having worshipped with perfumes and performed the prostration of the outspread hood, they departed. Gods and humans likewise worshipped and paid homage;

then the Bodhisatta, having heard the prophecy from the One of Ten Powers, considering his future Buddhahood as if it were already held in the palm of his hand, with a heart full of joy, rose from his bed after everyone had departed and placed a heap of flowers upon his head.
Sitting cross-legged, while reflecting upon the qualities that constitute a Buddha, he thought: "What indeed are the qualities that make one a Buddha?
Are they found above, below, in the cardinal directions, or in the intermediate directions?

Gradually searching through the entire realm of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), he first beheld the Perfection of Giving (*dānapāramī*), which had been practiced and cultivated by the ancient Bodhisattvas; thereupon, he made a firm resolve toward it.
Having thus performed these in succession— the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolve,
loving-kindness, and equanimity— and having seen them, he made a firm commitment to them therein; then, praised by the deities,
he ascended into the air and went directly to the snowy Himavat mountains.
The Teacher Dīpaṅkara, surrounded by four hundred thousand whose taints were exhausted, entered the city of Ramma by way of a road that had been adorned and prepared;
he was honored by the inhabitants of Ramma and greeted with acclamations by the deities. Having entered the city of Ramma, he sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.
The community of monks also sat down each upon his own assigned seat. The lay followers residing in the city of Ramma likewise [sat down].

Having given a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and having worshipped the Blessed One with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings once he had finished eating and withdrawn his hand from the bowl, they sat down desiring to hear the expression of thanksgiving for the gift.

The Blessed One, expressing his thanksgiving to them, delivered a discourse on giving, a discourse on virtue, and a discourse on heaven; and he spoke of the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and of the blessing of renunciation.
Having proclaimed the benefits, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma that culminates in the Deathless.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to that great multitude, some were established in the refuges,
some in the five precepts, some in the fruit of stream-entry, some in the fruit of once-returning, some in the fruit of non-returning, and some in all four fruits.
Having established some in the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), some in the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and some in the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha samāpatti*),
he rose from his seat, departed from the city of Ramma, and entered the Sudassana Great Monastery (*mahāvihāra*).
For this has been said:
“Then, having fed the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha,
they went for refuge to that Teacher Dīpaṅkara, who was free from all suffering.
At their taking of refuge, the Tathāgata bestowed a prediction upon one of them.”
To some he gives the five precepts, to others the supreme tenfold morality;
to some he gives the state of a recluse, to others the four highest fruits;
to some he gives the Dhamma that is free from deceit, and to others he gives the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
To some the Bull among Men grants the eight excellent attainments;
to others he bestows the three true knowledges and the six supernormal powers.
By means of this method, the Great Sage exhorts the multitude of people.
By him the teaching of the Lord of the World was made widespread:
he named Dīpaṅkara, with great jaws and the shoulders of a bull,
delivered many people and liberated them from the miserable states.
"Seeing people capable of being enlightened— even at a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas—
the Great Sage approaches them in an instant and awakens them.
Thus, that Teacher Dīpaṅkara, having remained for a hundred thousand years, brought about the release from bondage for sentient beings.
Having completed all the duties of a Buddha, he attained final Nibbāna in the Nandārāma by means of the element of Nibbāna without residue.

His relics were scattered; yet, remaining as a single solid mass like a golden statue, they formed a solid mass of thirty-six *yojanas* from the dense, gold-colored bones, for all the people dwelling throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
Some report that he offered [the gift] at the Mahāthūpa.
Therefore it was said:
“The Conqueror, the Teacher Dīpaṅkara, attained Parinibbāna in the Nandārāma.”
"Right there was his Jina-stupa, thirty-six yojanas in height";
"The bowl, robes, requisites, and the personal belongings of the Teacher—
at that time, the stupa at the foot of the Bodhi tree rose three yojanas high."
7. After the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, when one incalculable aeon had passed, a Teacher named Koṇḍañña appeared.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a universal monarch named Vijitāvī, gave a great almsgiving to a Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by a Buddha numbering one hundred thousand times ten million. The Teacher [declared], "The Bodhisatta will become a Buddha."
Having given this prediction, he taught the Dhamma. Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, [the king] handed over his kingdom and went forth.

Having mastered the Three Piṭakas and attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world without falling away from his jhāna.
That Buddha, too, having lived for a hundred thousand years and completed all the duties of a Buddha, passed away.
He attained final nibbāna in Caṇḍārāma. No fragments of that Blessed One’s relics were scattered;

instead, the people dwelling throughout the entire Jambudīpa assembled and, having performed the functions of yellow orpiment, realgar, and clay with the seven kinds of gems for a distance of seven yojanas, and having performed the functions of water with oil and ghee, they completed a stūpa.
It is said that when Koṇḍañña, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
attained final nibbāna in the delightful Caṇḍārāma, a stupa seven yojanas in height was built for him.
After his time, having passed one incalculable aeon, four Buddhas arose within a single aeon.

—Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Yohita. During the time of the Blessed One Maṅgala, however, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Suruci, approached the Teacher with the thought, "I shall invite the Teacher.
Having heard the sweetly spoken Dhamma, he invited him for the following day. Then, for seven days, he provided for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, numbering one hundred thousand crores.
The Teacher gave the gift known as the "drinking for cows"; while offering words of appreciation, he addressed the Great Man and prophesied:
"At the end of two incalculable eons and one hundred thousand kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Gotama. Upon hearing this prophecy, the Great Man thought:
"I am indeed destined to become a Buddha; what use have I for the household life? I shall go forth!"

Having reflected upon such prosperity as a mere lump of playthings, he abandoned it, went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher, mastered the word of the Buddha, and having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), was reborn in the Brahma-world at the end of his life.
When that Buddha also attained final Nibbāna, his relics did not scatter; the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, as before, constructed a stupa thirty *yojanas* in height.
Therefore it was said: "In a park, the Buddha named Maṅgala, known as Vasabha, attained Nibbāna; right there his Jina-thūpa rose up thirty yojanas high.
Subsequently, a Teacher named Sumana appeared. At that time, the Great Being was reborn as a Nāga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty.
Hearing that a Buddha had arisen, he departed from the Nāga realm surrounded by a host of kinsmen.
Having gone forth, he made offerings with divine musical instruments for that Blessed One who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand million monks;
having distributed a great almsgiving and presented pairs of cloth garments to each, he established himself in the refuges.
That Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha. When that Buddha had attained final Nibbāna, [he took] the relics...
The inhabitants of Jambudīpa did not scatter [the relics] as they had done before; they constructed a stupa four *yojanas* in height.
Therefore it is said:
"Sumana, Yasadhara—the Buddha was extinguished (passed away) in Aggārāma."
“Right there his Jina-stupa rose four yojanas high.

Later on, a Teacher named Revata appeared; at that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a brahmin named Atideva, heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, established himself in the Refuges, and raising his joined palms to his head, [honored] him.
Having spoken in praise of the Teacher’s abandonment of the defilements, he made an offering with his upper robe. The Teacher also prophesied of him, "He shall become a Buddha.
When that Buddha had attained final nibbāna, however, his relics were scattered.
Thus it was said.
“Revered Revata, the excellent Buddha, has attained Nibbāna in Mahāpura;
his relics were widespread throughout various regions.
Subsequently, after him, a teacher named Sobhita appeared; at that time, the Bodhisatta was a brahmin named Ajita.
Having made the offering and heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he established himself in the refuges and gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied of him, "You shall become a Buddha," and the relics of that Blessed One were likewise scattered.
Thus it was said.
“Sobhita, the supreme Fully Enlightened One, attained Nibbāna in Sīha Grove;
his relics were widely distributed throughout various regions.

After him, once one incalculable aeon had passed, three Buddhas appeared within a single aeon: Anomadassi, Paduma, and Nārada. During the time of the Blessed One Anomadassi, the Bodhisatta was a certain...
1. Some say that the wise Yasavara was a general of the yakkhas, possessed of great psychic power and majesty, the lord of many hundreds of thousands of millions of yakkhas.
Having heard that a Buddha had appeared, he came and offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha; the Teacher, too—
He prophesied to him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha. Furthermore, when the Blessed One Anomadassi had attained final Nibbāna, his relics did not disperse;
the inhabitants of Jambudīpa erected a stupa twenty-five yojanas in extent.
Thus it was said.
“The Conqueror Anomadassi, the Teacher, attained Nibbāna in the Dhammārāma grove;
right there stands his Conqueror’s stupa, twenty-five cubits in height.
Subsequently, after him, a Teacher named Paduma appeared, while the Bodhisatta was dwelling in remote forest retreats away from villages.
Having become a lion, he saw the Teacher absorbed in the attainment of cessation;
with a heart full of serene confidence, he paid homage, circumambulated him three times, and filled with joy and gladness, let out a lion’s roar three times.

Without abandoning the joy directed toward the Buddha for seven days, and departing from his feeding ground only while still immersed in that very joy and bliss, he remained in attendance, even at the cost of his own life.

After seven days had passed, the Teacher emerged from cessation (*nirodha*), looked at Sīha, and, having inspired confidence in the Saṅgha of monks as well, thought, "He will pay homage to the Saṅgha;
let the Saṅgha of monks come. At that very moment, the monks arrived, and Sīha inspired confidence in the Saṅgha.
The Teacher, observing his intention, [prophesied] that he would become a Buddha in the future.
He prophesied, "It shall be so," yet the relics of that Blessed One were scattered.
Therefore it was said:
"The supreme Victor, the Teacher Paduma, has attained Nibbāna in the Garden of Dhamma."
“The Dhamma was widespread throughout various regions.
Later, at that time, there was a teacher named Nārada who was the Bodhisatta.
Having gone forth as an ascetic, he attained mastery over the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and [he served] the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Having given a great gift, he made an offering with red sandalwood; he, too, prophesied that he would become a Buddha in the future.
However, the relics of the Blessed One remained as a single solid mass. Then all the gods and humans assembled and constructed a stupa four yojanas in height.
Therefore it was said:
"Nārada, the bull among Conquerors, attained Nibbāna in the city of Sudassana;
right there his excellent stupa rose up four yojanas high."
After a further incalculable aeon had passed, at the head of one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a great provincial chief named Jaṭila, gave a gift of robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He [the Buddha] also declared of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha."
He prophesied. The relics of the Blessed One Padumuttara also became a single solid mass.
All the gods and humans assembled and constructed a great stupa twelve yojanas in extent.
Therefore it was said:
“The Victor Padumuttara, the Buddha, attained Parinibbāna in Nandārāma;
right there his excellent stupa stood, twelve yojanas in height.
After thirty thousand aeons had passed following his time, in a single aeon, Sumedha and Sujāta [appeared].
Two Buddhas were born during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a young brahmin named Uttara, released eighty million pieces of wealth that had been set aside for burial;

he gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, heard the Dhamma, established himself in the refuges, went forth from the household life, and was ordained. He, too, [prophesied] regarding him in the future...
He prophesied, "He shall become a Buddha. However, the relics of the Blessed One Sumedha were scattered;
therefore it was said:
"The supreme Victor Sumedha, the Buddha, attained Nibbāna in Medhārāma."
“The expansion of his relics was widespread in various regions.
Subsequently, a Teacher named Sujāta appeared. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch, heard that a Buddha had arisen;
he approached him, listened to the Dhamma, and together with the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha—
Having given the sovereignty over the four great continents with their seven treasures, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
All the inhabitants of the kingdom, taking up the burden of the realm, performed the duties of monastery attendants and constantly offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, he will become a Buddha. As for the relics of the Blessed One Sujāta—
The inhabitants of Jambudīpa became as one solid mass; they built a stūpa three gavutas in height.
Therefore it was said:
"The Well-Born, the Supreme Victor, the Buddha, has attained Nibbāna in Sīlārāma."
"And right there was his cetiya, three gavutas in height.
Subsequently, in the eighteenth century of aeons, within a single aeon, three Buddhas appeared: Piyadassi, Atthadassi, and Dhammadassi.
During the time of Buddha Piyadassi, the Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Kassapa. Regarding these three...

Having mastered the Vedas and heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he built a monastery by relinquishing a hundred thousand crores of wealth and established himself in the refuges and the precepts. Then the Teacher prophesied of him:
"After the passing of eighteen hundred kappas, he will become a Buddha. Furthermore, the relics of the Blessed One Piyadassi were entirely solid and unified.
The inhabitants of Jambudīpa gathered together and constructed the Great Thūpa, three yojanas in extent.
Therefore it was said:
“The noble Sage Piyadassi attained Parinibbāna in Salalārāma;”
"Right there his Jina-stupa rose three *yojanas* high.
Subsequently, in that time, the Blessed One named Atthadassi appeared.
Then the Bodhisatta, having been a powerful and majestic ascetic named Susima, heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, gained confidence, and [offered] celestial *mandārava* flowers.
Having brought flowers such as the *paduma* and *pāricchattaka*, he rained down a shower of blossoms like a great cloud over the four continents;
having fashioned flower pavilions, flower canopies, and archways on all sides, he honored the One of Ten Powers with a parasol of *mandārava* flowers.
The Blessed One, in turn, prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha named Gotama."
Furthermore, the relics of that Blessed One were scattered.
Therefore it was said:
"The supreme Victor Atthadassi attained Nibbāna in Anomārāma."
"The expansion of the [Buddha's] elements occurred throughout various kingdoms.
Subsequently, a Teacher named Dhammadassi arose.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of the gods, and he performed worship with divine fragrant flowers and divine musical instruments, thinking, "He too will become a Buddha."
He prophesied. However, the relics of the Blessed One Dhammadassi remained as a single solid mass. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa erected a stupa three yojanas in height.
Therefore it was said:
“The Great Hero Dhammadassi attained Nibbāna on Kelāsāra Mountain.”
"In that very place, his excellent stupa rises three *yojanas* high.
Following that, at the end of ninety-four *kappas*, in one particular *kappa*, there appeared a single Teacher named Siddhattha.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, possessing great majesty and endowed with the power of higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), became an ascetic named Maṅgala.
Having brought a great jambu fruit, he gave it to the Tathāgata. After the Teacher had consumed that fruit, he prophesied:
"At the end of ninety-four kappas, you will become a Buddha. The relics of that Blessed One also did not scatter;
they constructed a stupa made of jewels four yojanas in extent.
Therefore it was said:
“The excellent sage Siddhattha, the Buddha, attained Nibbāna in Anoma-rāma;
right there his sublime stupa rose up four yojanas high.”
In a later period, ninety-two aeons ago, three Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa appeared in a single aeon.
During the time of the Blessed One Tissa, the Bodhisatta was born as a kshatriya of great wealth and great fame named Sujāta.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life and attained great supernormal power, he heard that a Buddha had arisen; [thereupon,] with divine mandārava flowers...
Taking lotus and pāricchattaka flowers, he honored the Tathāgata as he was proceeding through the midst of the fourfold assembly.
The flowers remained suspended in the air like a floral canopy; the Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the ninety-second aeon from now, he shall become a Buddha.
The relics of that Blessed One did not scatter; having taken the relics, they erected a stupa three yojanas in height.
Therefore it was said:
"The noble Victor, the Buddha, attained Parinibbāna at Nandārāma;
right there his excellent stupa rises three yojanas high."
In a later period, a Buddha named Phussa appeared.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a kshatriya named Vijitāvin, renounced his great sovereignty and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.

Having mastered the Three Piṭakas and delivered discourses on the Dhamma to the multitude, he fulfilled the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). That Buddha likewise prophesied concerning him in the same manner.
However, the relics of the Blessed One were scattered.
Therefore it was said:
"The supreme Victor, the Teacher Phussa, attained Parinibbāna in the Sunandārāma."
"It was widespread throughout various regions.
Subsequently, ninety-one aeons ago from now, a Buddha named Vipassī appeared.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, possessing great psychic power and great majesty, having become a Nāga king named Atula, [offered] a great golden throne inlaid with the seven precious gems.
He gave [the relics] to the Blessed One, who prophesied: "In the ninety-first aeon from now, he will become a Buddha.
Furthermore, the relics of that Blessed One did not disperse; all gods and humans, having prostrated themselves, took the relics and constructed a stupa seven yojanas in height.
Therefore it was said:
“The noble Victor Vipassī, the Hero, attained Nibbāna at Sumittārāma;
right there a supreme stupa seven yojanas in size was constructed for him.”
In a later period, thirty-one aeons ago from now, two Buddhas were born: Sikhi and Vessabhu.
During the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, the Bodhisatta, having been King Ariṇḍama, offered a great almsgiving including robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha;
he gave the Elephant-Treasure adorned with the seven gems and [elephants] the size of an elephant.
Having prepared them, he gave them as allowable articles; he, in turn, prophesied: "In the thirty-first aeon from now, he shall become a Buddha.

The relics of the Blessed One Sikhi remained as a single solid mass, but all the people dwelling in Jambudīpa took those relics and constructed a stupa three yojanas in height, made of the seven precious gems, with a splendor like the Himavat mountain.
“The Sage Śikhin, the Buddha, attained Parinibbāna in the Dussārāma grove;
right there his excellent stupa rose three *yojanas* high.
After him, a Teacher named Vessabhū appeared. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Sudassana.
Having offered a great gift of robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he went forth into homelessness in his presence.
Endowed with proper conduct and virtue, he was filled with abundant joy through his deep veneration for the Jewel of the Buddha; the Teacher prophesied of him:
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, he shall become a Buddha. Furthermore, the relics of the Blessed One Vessabhu were scattered.
Therefore it was said:
"The supreme Victor Vessabhū, the Teacher, attained Nibbāna at Khemārāma;
his relics were widespread throughout various regions."
In the subsequent period of this eon, four Buddhas appeared: Kakusandha, Konāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One.

During the time of the Blessed One Catuṣsandha, however, the Bodhisatta, having been King Khema, gave a gift of robes along with medicinal ointments and other remedies to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he went forth; the Teacher also made a prediction concerning him. However, the relics of that Blessed One did not scatter;
they all gathered together, and having taken those relics, they erected a stupa one *gāvuta* in height.
Therefore it was said:
“Kakusandha, the supreme Victor, attained Parinibbāna at Khemārāma;
right there his excellent stupa rose up a quarter-league into the sky.
After him, a Teacher named Konāgamana appeared, and at that time the Bodhisatta was a king named Pabbata.
Having performed the sacrifice, surrounded by his circle of ministers, he went into the presence of the Teacher;

having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and after distributing a great almsgiving, he gave fine woolen cloth, Chinese silk, Koseyya silk, blankets, and Dukūla cloth, as well as a golden band, and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him.
The relics of that Blessed One were scattered.
Therefore it was said:
“The Sambuddha Konāgamana attained Parinibbāna in Pabbatārāma.”
"The Dhamma was widespread among those various regions.

Subsequently, a Teacher named Kassapa arose. At that time, the Bodhisatta, being a young brahmin named Jotipāla, became proficient in the mastery of the three Vedas and was renowned both in the world and in the sky, [serving] the potter Ghaṭīkāra.
He became his friend. Together with him, he approached the Teacher, and having heard a discourse on the Dhamma, he went forth.
Being diligent, he mastered the Three Piṭakas and, through his excellence in conduct, brought glory to the Buddha’s dispensation.
The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him. As for the relics of the Teacher Kassapa—
The people dwelling throughout the whole of Jambudīpa did not disperse; having assembled, they built a stūpa one *yojana* in height,
using each of the golden bones— worth ten million coins— as the outer ornamentation, and each [bone] worth half a million coins for the internal filling,
while performing the function of clay with *manosilā* stone and the function of water with oil.
Therefore it was said:
“The Conqueror Mahākassapa, the Teacher, has indeed attained Nibbāna at Setavyā;
right there his Conqueror’s stupa rose up a yojana in height.”
And here [are the names]: Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Sumana,
as well as the Buddha Anomadassī, Nārada, and Padumuttara.
Sujāta, Piyadassī, Dhammadassi— the supreme among men—
Siddhattha Buddha, Tissa, and likewise Vipassi,
Sikhī, Kakusandha, and Kassapa: these sixteen were the great seers.
The dimensions of these stupas have been shown in the Pāli Canon itself;
therefore, I have properly revealed them all.
O people of faith, you should rightly honor these stupas with sincere respect.
Furthermore, regarding those eight Sugatas who desired the welfare [of beings] and whose relics were widely distributed in various regions:

the account of the stūpas of the Buddhas and the manner in which they were brought forth in the presence of all [those relics], as contained in the *Thūpavaṃsa* composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the minds of virtuous people, is hereby completed.
However, after the Blessed One Kassapa, there was no other being called a Buddha except for this Sammasambuddha.
Thus, having received the prophecy in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara,
the Bodhisatta fulfilled the perfections and stood in his final existence as Vessantara.
“This earth is insentient, lacking consciousness of pleasure or pain;
yet even it shook seven times by the power of my gift.
Having performed such meritorious deeds that caused the great earth to tremble, at the end of his lifespan, passing away from there, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
There, having surpassed other gods in ten respects and experiencing divine prosperity for the duration of his lifespan, [the god] will reach the end of his life in seven days by human reckoning;
at that point, his clothes become soiled, his garlands wither, sweat breaks out from his armpits, and a lack of luster comes over his body. The god no longer finds delight in his divine seat.

When these five portents had arisen, the deities—seeing them and becoming filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), realizing that "our heavenly realms will no longer be empty"—and knowing that the Great Being had fulfilled the perfections, thought:
"Now, instead of proceeding to another divine world, he will arise in the human world; once he has attained Buddhahood and performed meritorious deeds, he will pass away from here."
Thinking, "Cutā will fill the world of the gods," he said:
"From the time that I was in the Tusita host, I was then named Santusita;
ten thousand [beings] gathered and entreated me with palms joined."
“Now is the time, O Great Hero; having arisen in a mother’s womb, saving the world including the devas, awaken to the deathless state!
Thus was he entreated for the sake of attaining Buddhahood regarding the time, the island, the country, the family, the mother, and the measure of his lifespan.
Having performed the five great observations and made his resolve, he passed away from there and took rebirth in the royal family of the Śākyas.
There, being maintained in great prosperity, he gradually reached auspicious youth and,
enjoying the glory of sovereignty like the splendor of the deva-world in three palaces suited to the three seasons, went out for a pleasure excursion in the garden.

At the time of his departure, having seen the three divine messengers known as the old man, the sick man, and the corpse in succession, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and turned back.
On the fourth occasion, seeing one who had gone forth (*pabbajita*), he conceived a desire for the going-forth, thinking, "Excellent is the going-forth!
Having returned to the garden and spent the day there, he sat on the bank of the auspicious lotus pond while the barber attended him.
When Vissakamma, the son of the gods, arrived having assumed a disguise, he prepared and adorned [the city].
Upon hearing the news of Prince Rāhula’s impending execution and perceiving the intensity of his paternal affection,
he thought, "I shall cut these fetters before they are further tightened," and as he was entering the city in the evening—
“Truly extinguished is that mother— truly extinguished is that father—
truly extinguished is that woman who has such a husband as this.
Having heard this verse spoken by her paternal aunt’s daughter named Kisāgotamī, [the Blessed One] here [used] this term “extinguished” (nibbuta).
Having sent a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold to Sāvatī by means of a messenger, he entered his own palace.
Lying upon his bed of glory, he saw the disorderly behavior of the dancers who had fallen asleep under the influence of drowsiness;
with a heart full of world-weariness, he roused Channa, had Kaṇṭhaka brought, and mounting him, accompanied by Channa, [set out for] the ten-thousandfold world-system.

Having set out on the Great Renunciation accompanied by a retinue provided by the deities, and having traversed three kingdoms during the remainder of that very night, he reached the far bank of the river Anomā.
Dismounting from the back of his horse and standing upon the sandy bank of the Cālikā, which resembled a heap of pearls, he said:
"Channa, take my ornaments and Kaṇṭhaka and go; as for the ornaments..."
Having entrusted Kaṇṭhaka to others, he took his auspicious sword with his right hand and, with his left hand, cut off his topknot together with the diadem.
He threw it into the air, saying, "If I shall become a Buddha, let it stay in the sky; if not, let it fall to the ground.
The crest-jewel, having traveled a distance of one *yojana*, came to rest suspended in the sky.
Then Sakka, king of the gods, received it in a jeweled bowl one yojana in size.
As it is said:
"Having cut off his topknot, which was scented with the finest perfumes..."
The bull of the Sakyas tossed up his upper robe,
and Vāsava, the thousand-eyed one, received it upon his head with his excellent golden armlet.
Having accepted it, he led him to the deva-world and, upon the summit of Mount Sineru, fashioned a crest-jewel stupa (*cuḷāmaṇi-cetiya*) three *yojanas* in size, made of sapphire.

Then, during the time of Buddha Kassapa, his ancient companion Ghaṭīkāra Mahābrahmā, having attained the state of a *mātaṅga* for the duration of an entire interval between Buddhas (*buddhantara*), thought: "Today my companion has undertaken the Great Renunciation."
“Having set out, O ascetic, I shall go taking his requisites”:
“The three robes, the bowl, a razor, a needle, and a girdle,
along with a water-strainer— these are for a bhikkhu devoted to the practice.”

Having brought these requisites of a recluse, the Great Man gave them; having donned the robe that is the banner of the Arahants and assumed the supreme garb of renunciation, he threw the pair of garments into the air.
Brahmā received them and, in the Brahma-world, constructed a shrine for the robes twelve yojanas in size, made entirely of every kind of jewel.
“Even though his defilements were not yet abandoned at that moment,
because of the Great Being’s power alone, this crest-jewel of Dussa was thus honored.
Therefore, in the practice of those Great Bodhisattvas,”
“Who indeed would be a wise person to undertake such a great effort?
Thus ends the story of the two stupas for the Cūḷāmaṇi relic (9).
Having gone forth, the Bodhisatta eventually arrived at Rājagaha; there he wandered for alms and [stayed] at Paṇḍava.
Seated on a mountain slope, though invited by the King of Magadha to accept his kingdom, he declined that offer;

having attained omniscience, he gave his promise to go to Tissa-vijita, approached Āḷāra and Uddaka, and being unsatisfied with the specific attainments reached in their presence, he exerted himself in the Great Struggle for six years. Viśākha...
On the day of the full moon, having partaken of the milk-rice given by Sujātā in the village of Senāninigama and having sent the golden bowl down the river Nerañjarā,
he spent the day in the great forest grove on the bank of the Nerañjarā by means of various meditative attainments;
then, at evening time, having accepted a handful of grass from Sotthiya, [he sat down] with Kāḷa, the Nāga king.
Having praised his virtues and ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he spread out blades of grass and made this vow:
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging. Having thus made his promise, he sat facing the east;
and while the sun had not yet set, having shattered the army of Māra, he attained the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) during the first watch of the night.

Having attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings during the middle watch of the night, and having realized the omniscient knowledge adorned with all virtues— such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence— at the conclusion of the final watch,
he spent seven weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. On the eighth week,
while seated at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma, he fell into a state of inactivity for ten days.
When the Great Brahmā Sahampati, together with his retinue, requested him to teach the Dhamma, the Buddha,
surveying the world with his Buddha-eye and taking up the Brahmā’s entreaty, looked to see whom he should teach first;
perceiving that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, he recognized the great service rendered by the group of five monks.
Having recollected this, he rose from his seat and, traveling toward Kāsipura, consulted with Upaka along the way;
then, on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, having reached the dwelling place of the five bhikkhus of the group at Isipatana in the Deer Park,
and having instructed them after they had addressed him with an unworthy speech, "Friend," he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
He caused eighteen koṭis of beings, headed by the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña, to drink the nectar of the Deathless.
Having remained for forty years from that time onwards, he taught eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma,
delivered countless beings across the wilderness of existence, and brought all the duties of a Buddha to completion.
At Kusinārā, in the Upavattana sal grove of the Mallas, between a pair of *sāla* trees, on the full moon day of the month of Visākha,
he lay down on his right side with mindfulness and clear comprehension upon a couch prepared with its head toward the north, in the posture of one who will not rise again.
At that time, it is said, for the sake of honoring the Blessed One, the twin *sāla* trees blossomed completely from their roots all the way to their tips.
The foremost trees were covered with a single canopy. Not only were the twin *sāl* trees thus, but all the branches of every tree were in full bloom.
Not only in that very garden, but throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassa-cakkavāḷa*), fruit-bearing trees bore fruit.
On the trunks of all the trees grew trunk-lotuses (*khandhapaduma*), and on the branches grew branch-lotuses (*vallaripaduma*). In the sky...
Sky-lotuses bloomed, and lotuses with long stalks sprouted, piercing through the surface of the earth. The entire great ocean became covered with five-colored lotuses.

And the Himālaya mountain, extending for three thousand yojanas, appeared like a mass of peacock feathers gathered together, like a place draped all over with garlands and wreaths, or like a flower-ornament firmly pressed and bound.
It was exceedingly beautiful, like a flower-basket filled to the brim.
The twin *sāla* trees, their eyes and brows moved by terrestrial deities, scattered flowers over the body of the Tathāgata.
Celestial *maṇḍārava* flowers also fell from the sky; they were the color of gold.
Measuring the size of a leaf-umbrella, they catch dust the measure of a large gourd; not only mandārava flowers,
but all other flowers such as those of the pāricchattaka tree, having filled golden caskets and silver caskets again and again,
various [flowers] are scattered neither here nor there by deities stationed even in the city of the Thirty-three or in the Brahma-world.
Having offered [the oblations] and returned, they scattered the pollen and dust from the filaments of lotuses over the body of the Tathāgata.
Not only did the deities, but also the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and humans, offer sandalwood powder;
not only sandalwood powder, but all kinds of fragrant substances such as black aloe-wood, tagara, red sandalwood, and so forth; and yellow orpiment, collyrium, gold, and silver.
Powders and all varieties of perfumed incense, having filled golden and silver caskets, were cast by deities stationed at the rim of the world-system and other locations;
these did not scatter along the way, but fell only upon the body of the Tathāgata. Divine musical instruments resounded in the sky.
Not only those, but all types of stringed instruments, those covered with leather, and so forth—
The musical instruments of the devas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and humans— distinguished by their various types such as hollowed drums and the like— numbering ten thousand across the *cakkavāḷas*,
assemble within a single *cakkavāḷa* and resound in the sky.
It is said that a certain long-lived deity named Varacāraṇa, having been reborn on the human path, [beheld] the Great Being.
Having heard that he would become a Buddha, they began weaving garlands with the thought, "We shall take them on the day of his rebirth-linking.
While they were still weaving, when the Great Being was conceived in his mother's womb, they were asked, "For whom are you weaving?
They replied, "He will not remain [in the womb] yet; we shall take them on the day of his emergence from the womb. Again, when he was emerging...

Having heard, "On the day of the Great Renunciation he will depart," [they set out]; having heard, "He has departed on the Great Renunciation," [they set out]; having heard, "On the day of the Perfect Enlightenment he will depart," [they set out];
having heard, "Today he has attained Perfect Enlightenment," [they set out]; having heard, "On the day of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma he will depart," [they set out];
having heard, "He has turned the Wheel of Dhamma," [they set out]; and having heard, "On the day of the Twin Miracle he will depart," [they set out]. Today is the day of the Twin Miracle.

"Having heard that the Deva is performing [the descent], we shall go on the day of the descent. Having heard today that the Deva is performing the descent, we shall go when he releases the life-force.
Having heard that he has released the life-force, we shall go on the day of the Parinibbāna before it is finished?
"Today, between the twin Sāl trees, the Blessed One has entered the lion’s posture on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending."
When they were told, "He will attain final Nibbāna at the powerful hour of dawn; to whom among you shall you cling?", he replied: "What is this?
This very day he took rebirth in a mother’s womb; this very day he emerged from the womb; this very day he made the Great Renunciation. This very day he became a Buddha;
this very day he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion; this very day he performed the Twin Miracle."
He did so. This very day he descended from the world of the gods. This very day he relinquished the formative forces of his life-span. It is said that this very day he attained final Nibbāna.
Surely it would have been appropriate for him to remain even for the duration of a meal of rice-gruel on the second day;
for one who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained Buddhahood, such a thing would be most unseemly. Thus, taking up their flower garlands before they were even finished, they arrived.
Finding space within the circle of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) and reaching its rim,
they rushed forward, grasping hand with hand and neck with neck; and having sung in praise of the Three Jewels, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
the six-colored rays of light, the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the five hundred and fifty Jātaka tales, and the fourteen Buddha-knowledges (*buddhañāṇa*), they [praised] him.
At its conclusion, they cried out, "Friend! Friend! This occurred because of that—divine musical performances were occurring in the sky.
Yet, while such a great honor was being rendered, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the Mallas during the first watch of the night.
Having taught the Dhamma to Subhadda during the middle watch of the night, he established him in the paths and fruits;
then, having exhorted the bhikkhus during the last watch, at the time of the powerful dawn, he passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue while shaking the great earth.
When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had thus attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Ānanda informed the Malla king of that event.
Having heard this announcement, they took perfumes, garlands, all the musicians, and five hundred pairs of garments,
and went forth. Honoring, revering, esteeming, and worshipping the Blessed One’s body with dances, songs, instrumental music, garlands, and perfumes,
they constructed canopies of cloth and prepared circular wreaths, as follows:
They passed that day.
Then it occurred to the deities and the Mallas of Kusinārā: "It is now too late today to cremate the Blessed One’s body;
we shall cremate the Blessed One’s body tomorrow. And so they passed the second day as well.
In this manner they passed the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth day as well; on the seventh day, the deities of the Dosiṇāra mountain and the Mallas,
honoring, revering, respecting, and worshipping the Blessed One’s body with divine and human dances,
songs, music, garlands, and perfumes, [carried it] through the middle of the city.
Having carried it out, they deposited it at the Mallas’ shrine named Makutabandhana.
At that time, Kusinārā was strewn as far as its very crossroads with Mandārava flowers as thick as a winnowing basket.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā [prepared] the body of the Blessed One like that of a wheel-turning monarch...
They wrapped the body in new cloth; having wrapped it in new cloth, they wrapped it in carded cotton wool;
having wrapped it in carded cotton wool, they wrapped it in new cloth.
Following this same method, after wrapping it with five hundred pairs [of cloths], they placed it in an iron oil-vat, covered it with another iron vat, and [applied] all kinds of perfumes.
Having prepared a funeral pyre, they placed the Blessed One’s body upon it.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was traveling along the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks.
At that time, having inspired confidence in the elders, they had been reborn in heaven.
The deities, not seeing the Elder at that assembly, thought, "Where indeed is our own family-preceptor, the Elder?
As they were reflecting, they saw him traveling along the middle road. They then made this resolution: "Until our family-preceptor, the Elder, has been paid homage, let the funeral pyre not ignite.
Then the four chief Mallas, having bathed their heads and dressed in new clothes, [prepared] a bier adorned with a hundred jewels.
Thinking, "We shall light the sandalwood pyre," eight, sixteen, and even thirty-two men took up pairs of bellows and,
fanning with palm-leaf fans and blowing into leather bags, were simply unable to catch fire. Then the Mallas of Kusinārā,
having asked the Venerable Anuruddha for the reason why the pyre would not ignite, [proceeded as follows].
"Having heard the intention of the deities, it is said that Mahākassapa is coming with five hundred bhikkhus, thinking, 'I shall pay homage at the feet of the One of Ten Powers.
It is said that as long as he has not arrived, the funeral pyre does not ignite.
What kind of bhikkhu is this, sirs? Is he dark, fair, tall, or short? When such a bhikkhu stands before him, what will the One of Ten Powers think?"
Thinking, "This is indeed the Parinibbāna," some went out with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands;
others, having decorated the streets, stood watching the path by which [the body] would come.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Mallas' shrine called Makūṭabandhana at Kusinārā, where the Blessed One’s funeral pyre was located. Having approached, he...
Having arranged his robe over one shoulder and circumambulated the funeral pyre three times, he reflected and observed:

"The feet are in this place. Standing near the feet, he attained the fourth jhāna based on direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and upon emerging from it, he offered five hundred pairs of fine cloths, adorned with a thousand pieces of gold, together with cotton sheets for the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
Having divided the golden bowl and the reliquary stupa into two parts, he made this resolution: "May they rest upon my head, the highest part of my body.
Simultaneously with that resolve, those pairs of garments and other items, having been divided into two, emerged from between his feet like the full moon emerging from behind a cloud.
The Elder, extending his hands which resembled blossomed red lotuses, firmly grasped the Teacher’s gold-colored feet down to the ankles and placed them upon his own noble head.
When the great multitude saw this marvel, they simultaneously let out a great roar.
Having honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they paid homage to him according to their desire. And so it was.
After being saluted by the Elder, the great multitude, and those five hundred bhikkhus, they released their hands from the Elder’s hand;
yet the footprints of the Blessed One, red as lac-dye, remained fixed in their respective places without moving even slightly into the wood or other materials.
Whether the Blessed One’s feet were coming out or going in, or whether it was cotton, silk, or a thread of cloth, [they remained as they were].
Not even a drop of oil or a fragment of wood moved from its place; everything remained exactly where it was.
But when the Tathāgata had risen and vanished from sight—like the moon or the sun that has set—the great multitude wailed with a great lamentation.
There was even greater sorrow than at the time of his final passing away. Then...
Through the power of the deities, however, this funeral pyre ignited all at once from every side.
As the Blessed One’s body burned, not even so much as a trace of ash—let alone soot—was perceived from the outer skin, inner skin, flesh, and so forth;
rather, relics resembling jasmine buds, like refined gold, and like pure gold remained behind.
For the bodies of long-lived Buddhas are like a solid mass of gold, entirely compact. But the Blessed One said:
"I shall not remain for long; I will attain Parinibbāna soon. My teaching has not yet been spread everywhere;
therefore, even though I have attained Parinibbāna, let them take at least a small portion of my relics and, in their own respective dwelling places—"
He resolved upon the distribution of the relics, thinking: "By building a cetiya and honoring it, the great multitude shall have heaven as their ultimate goal.
As for his relics, how many were distributed and how many were not? These seven relics were not distributed:
the four canine teeth, the two collar-bones, and the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). The remainder were distributed. Among those, the smallest of all...
The relic was the size of a mustard seed; the great relic was the size of a split grain of rice.
The exceedingly large one was the size of a split mung bean.
When the Blessed One’s body had been cremated, [flames] the size of an outstretched arm, the size of a shank, and even the size of a palm tree trunk issued from the sky.

A stream of water fell and extinguished the funeral pyre; not only from the sky, but streams of water also issued forth from the gaps between the branches and foliage of the sāla trees standing all around, and they too extinguished it. The Blessed One’s funeral pyre was vast;
having split the earth on all sides, it proceeded as a column of water about the size of a goat’s head, resembling a wreath worn by a young girl.

The Malla kings took only the funeral pyre; having filled golden and silver jars with various kinds of scented water brought for the purpose, and having sprinkled it over the sandalwood pyre with golden and silver nozzles, they extinguished the fire.
As the pyre was burning there, the spaces between the branches, the foliage, and the leaves of the surrounding *sāla* trees—[were filled with smoke].
And when the net rose up, there was no leaf or branch that was not scorched;
even the ants, the monkeys, and the small creatures could no longer move within the nets.
Even when torrents of water fell from the sky, or streams of water issued forth from the *sāla* trees, they did not break through the earth.
Even when streams of water were poured out, it was only natural that this should be the measure.
Then, having extinguished the funeral pyre, the Malla kings had the fourfold fragrant ointments prepared in the assembly hall;

they scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient, caused a canopy of cloth to be fastened above, adorned it with golden stars, and there hung garlands of perfumes, flower-garlands, and jewel-garlands.
Having hung [the decorations], from the gatehouse as far as the auspicious hall for adorning the head—
known as the "Binding of the Diadem"— he had a screen of fine cloth erected on both sides; he had a canopy of cloth fastened above, inlaid with golden stars,
and there too he had suspended fragrant garlands, flower garlands, and jewel garlands, along with five-colored banners on jeweled poles.
Having raised banners and flags all around, having placed banana trees and full jars in the streets that were sprinkled and swept,
and having lit staff-lamps, they placed a golden bowl containing the relics upon the back of an adorned elephant;
after worshipping it with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings, they brought it into the city while performing auspicious music and entered the assembly hall.
Having placed him upon a couch made of sarabha wood, having held a white parasol over him, having had him surrounded by men with spears in their hands,
having had him surrounded by elephants striking trunk against trunk,
then by horses striking neck against neck, then by chariots striking pole against pole, and then by warriors with their arms...
They had them surrounded with bows that struck edge-to-edge as they were being brandished by those who wielded their arms.
Thus, having made the area for a distance of one *yojana* all around appear as if covered by armor, they established a guard.
But why did they do so? Because during the two preceding weeks, they [had cleared] the space for the standing and sitting of the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus.
While preparing solid food and soft food, they could find no opportunity for their games; therefore, it occurred to them:

"We shall play these seven days of games. However, it is possible that someone might come and seize the relics knowing our state of negligence; therefore, having established a guard, we shall play. Thus they did so.
Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha heard that the Blessed One had indeed attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
How did he hear it? First, his ministers, having heard the news, reflected: "The Teacher has indeed attained final nibbāna;
he cannot be brought back again. Yet there is no one equal to our king in worldly faith. If..."
"He will hear it in this very manner, and his heart will be pierced; however, the king must be protected by us.
So saying, they brought three golden bowls, filled them with the four sweet substances, went into the presence of the king, and said this:
"We have seen two dreams; for the sake of counteracting them, you should put on a fine linen cloth as follows..."
"Only the nostrils are visible; thus it is fitting to lie upon a bowl of the four sweet substances.
Having heard the words of the ministers who desired his welfare, the king accepted, saying, "So be it, dear ones," and had it done accordingly.
Then one minister, having removed his ornaments and disheveled his hair, [proceeded] in the direction where the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna.
Facing him and raising his joined palms in reverence, he said to the king:

"There is no being that can escape death. When the king heard that the Blessed One, the Teacher, who increased their lifespan and was a field of merit for the shrine site and the foundation of consecration, had passed away at Kusinārā, he fell unconscious and emitted a cloud of steam from a drona-measure of the four sweets.
They lifted the king up and laid him down in a second trough. Having regained consciousness, he asked, "Father, what are you saying?
"The Teacher, Great King, has attained final Nibbāna," they replied. He fell back into unconsciousness and emitted steam from the four kinds of sweet substances in the trough.
Then, lifting him up from there as well, they laid him down in a third trough. Having again regained consciousness, he...
"Father, what do you say? the Teacher asked. "Great King, he has attained final nibbāna. The king fell unconscious once more, and the sweet urn emitted steam.
Then, lifting him up from there as well, they bathed him and poured water over his head from jars; the king regained consciousness.
Having regained consciousness, he rose from his seat, scattered his hair— which was perfumed with scents and the color of jewels—
over his back, which was the color of a golden slab; then, as if clutching his chest, which was the color of a golden image,
with his well-rounded fingers that were the color of coral sprouts, he went down into the middle of the street in the guise of a madman, lamenting while still adorned.
Surrounded by his retinue, he departed from the city and went to Jīvakambavana.
Looking toward the spot where the Blessed One had sat and taught the Dhamma, he thought: "Did not the All-Knowing Blessed One sit in this very place and teach the Dhamma?
He dispelled my dart of sorrow; he extracted the dart of sorrow from me. I—
"I have gone for refuge to you. Yet now, O Blessed One, you do not even give me an answer! Having lamented thus again and again, he continued:
"Surely, Blessed One, we have heard that on other occasions, at such times as these, you were wandering the surface of Jambudīpa accompanied by a great assembly of monks.
But now, I hear of conduct from you that is neither fitting nor appropriate."
Having thus recited these and other verses to the extent of sixty stanzas, he recollected the virtues of the Blessed One and thought:
"My lamentation alone will not suffice; I shall have the relics of the One Possessed of Ten Powers brought here. He then dispatched a messenger and a letter to the Malla king, saying:
"The Blessed One was a kshatriya, and I too am a kshatriya; I too am worthy of a stupa for the Blessed One’s remains."
Having sent word, "Let him build a great [stūpa]," he thought: "If they grant it, that is well;
if they do not grant it, we shall take it by means of force. Thus, having arrayed his fourfold army, he himself set out.
And just as Ajātasattu did, so too did the Licchavi kings in Vesālī, the Sākya kings in Kapilavatthu, the Bulayas in Allakappa, and [the Koliyas] in Rāmagāma.
The Koḷiyans at Veṭhadīpaka and the Mallas at Pāvā each sent a messenger and likewise set out with a fourfold army.
Among them, the Pāveyyakas lived in a city closer to Kusinārā than all the others, at a distance of three *gāvutas*.
The Blessed One, having entered Pāvā, proceeded to Kusinārā. These kings, however, possessed great retinues; such were their retinues.
They were born later. All those inhabitants of the seven cities arrived and surrounded the city of Kusinārā, saying, "Let them either give us the relics of our Teacher or [give us] battle.
Then the Malla kings said this: "The Blessed One passed away within the territory of our village; we [will not give them up]."
"We sent a message, but we did not go ourselves to bring it. The Teacher himself came, sent a message, and summoned us.
Furthermore, you must not give us whatever treasure arises within the boundaries of your village;
for in the world with its devas, there is no treasure equal to the Jewel of the Buddha—such is this supreme treasure."
Thinking, "Having obtained the treasure, we shall not give it up," they thus increased their quarrel.
"It was not only by you that milk was drunk from your mother's breast; it was drunk by us as well.
You alone are men, we are not men!"—thus making mutual claims of selfhood, they sent back and forth messages of rebuke and roared at one another with the trumpeting of pride.
If there had been a battle, victory would have belonged to the Kosiṇārakas alone; why, then, did the deities who had come for the purpose of viewing the relics take the side of those [other kings]?
Then the brahmin Doṇa, having heard this dispute, thought: "These kings are quarreling over the place where the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna;
this is not fitting. Enough of this strife; I shall bring about peace. Thus he went to the Uṇṇata region.
Having stood there, he recited the discourse named *Doṇagajjita*, which consists of two *bhāṇavāras*.

At that time, during the first *bhāṇavāra*, they did not understand even a single word; but at the conclusion of the second *bhāṇavāra*, everyone cried out, "The sound of 'Bho' is like that of a teacher!
The sound of 'Bho' is like that of a teacher! Indeed, throughout the entire surface of Jambudīpa, it was said that [this was the case] in their own noble families.
Generally, he had no one who could be called his pupil; then, having heard their own words and perceiving that they had become silent, he spoke this again:
"Listen, sirs, to my single word."
Our Buddha was a teacher of patience;
for one who has attained perfection,
there can be no violence even when his body is being broken.
May all of you, sirs, being united, harmonious,
and in mutual agreement, perform the eight portions;
let the stupas spread throughout every direction.
“The majority of people have faith in the One with Vision.

Herein, the meaning is as follows: “Our Buddha was a teacher of patience” refers to the time when, even before reaching the stage of Buddhahood while fulfilling the perfections, he was the ascetic Khantivāda, the prince Dhammapāla, the elephant Chaddanta, and the nāga king Bhūridatta.

In the past, during the time of the Naga King Campeyya, the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, Mahākapi, and in many other previous births as well, he did not give way to anger toward others but practiced only patience. He praised patience alone;
how much more so now, when our Buddha, having attained the characteristic of equanimity toward both the desirable and the undesirable, was in every respect a teacher of patience.
For such a person as this, who has accomplished the goal, there can be no conflict upon the breaking up of the body.
“*Na hi sādhayanti*”: it is not good; “*sarīrabhaṅge*”: the meaning is for the sake of the breaking up of the body, that is, on account of the elements and their constituent parts;
“*siyā sampahāro*”: it is said that there should be no conflict, meaning no clash of weapons, would not be good. “*Sabbeva*... [all indeed...]
"May you all be united," means: "May all of you, sirs, be united; do not be divided. "In harmony" means:
"Be harmonious through body and speech, being gathered together as one and speaking with one voice. "Rejoicing together" means: "Be rejoicing in one another even in your hearts.
"'Let us divide into eight portions'": let us divide the relics of the Blessed One into eight portions. "'Of the Visionary One' (cakkhumato)": [refers to the Buddha].

Having stated many reasons to convince them—that the Buddha possesses the quality of "vision" through five kinds of vision, and that it is not only you who have faith in him, but that among the great multitude there is not even a single person who could be called unworthy—he persuaded them.
Then all the kings spoke thus: "In that case, Brahmin, you yourself must divide the relics of the Blessed One into eight portions."
"Divide [the relics] equally and well-apportioned. Having thus assented to those kings, the brahmin Doṇa divided the relics equally and well-apportioned.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows: it is said that after they had assented, Doṇa had a golden bowl opened. The kings arrived.
Having seen only these gold-colored relics in the bowl, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing One, said:
"In the past, we beheld your body adorned with the thirty-two marks, shimmering with the six-colored rays of a Buddha, and golden-hued;
but now, only these gold-colored relics remain. This is not fitting for you, Blessed One."
They lamented. At that time, the brahmin, perceiving their state of negligence, took the tooth relic and placed it within his turban;
afterwards, he divided it equally and with perfect distribution.
All the relics returned to their natural state, amounting to sixteen *nāḷis*. Each resident of a city received two *nāḷis*.
But while the brahmin was still dividing the relics, Sakka, lord of the devas,

looked about to see who had taken the Blessed One’s right canine tooth— the very thing that would serve as the condition for his discourse on the Four Truths to cut through the doubts of the world with its devas—
and seeing that it had been taken by the brahmin, [he realized] that the brahmin was not capable of performing the appropriate honor for the tooth.
Thinking, "I shall be able to take it," he took it from the midst of his turban, placed it in a golden casket, and having led him to the world of the gods, he enshrined it at the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.
The brahmin, having divided the relics, was unable even to ask, "Who has taken my tooth-relic? since he did not see it;
[the Buddha said: "Did you not divide the relics? What are you [saying]?"
Because he did not even first realize the existence of his own relics, seeing that he was attributing faults to himself, he was unable even to say, "Give me my share as well.
Therefore, this golden vessel too has come under the category of the relics, by which the relics of the Tathāgata were measured. To this [vessel] I—
Thinking, "I shall build a stupa," he said, "Sirs, please give this jar to me. Then the kings gave the jar to the brahmin.
The Mallas of Pippalivana, having heard that the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, thought, "The Blessed One was a kshatriya, and we too are kshatriyas;
we also deserve to receive a portion of the Blessed One’s relics."
Having sent a messenger and set out prepared for battle, they arrived and the kings spoke thus:
"There is no portion of the Blessed One’s relics; the Blessed One’s relics have been divided. Take embers from here. They took embers from there.
Then King Ajātasattu [prepared] the twenty-five-yojana road between Kusinārā and Rājagaha.
Having had a level ground eight usabhas wide prepared, the Malla kings performed worship between the Makuṭabandhana and the Saṇṭhāgāra;
having likewise performed worship along the twenty-five yojana path, they displayed the relics—
placed in a golden casket— in market stalls everywhere for the sake of preventing the world from becoming weary.
Having had it surrounded by a fence of spears, he caused the people within his own realm, extending five hundred yojanas in circumference, to assemble.
Taking those relics, they departed from Kusinārā, playing a game of "relics" as they went;
wherever they saw beautiful flowers, they placed the relics between the spears, and when those flowers were exhausted...
They proceeded. When the front of the chariot reached the rear part [of the city], they celebrated a grand festival for seven days.
Thus, seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since those who were bringing the relics arrived;
from the time of the Parinibbāna of the ascetic Gotama, the holders of wrong views had acted by force.
"Afflicted by their own frivolous play, they lamented, 'All our businesses have been ruined,' and having corrupted their minds, eighty-six thousand of them were reborn in the states of misery.
The one whose taints were exhausted (the Buddha) reflected: 'The great multitude, having corrupted their minds, has been reborn in the states of misery.
Seeing Sakka, the king of the gods, he thought, 'We shall devise a means to bring back the relics,' and [approached] him."
"Having gone there and reported this matter, tell the Great King: 'Employ a means to bring forth the relics,'" they said. Sakka replied:
"There is no ordinary person as faithful as Ajātasattu; he will not do my bidding.
However, I shall show him a terrifying specter (*vibhīsaka*) resembling the demon Māra—one that seizes, hurls, and causes consumption."
"I shall do this for you, O Great King: 'Summon the non-human beings who are angry; have them bring back the relics.
You should speak thus, and he will cause them to be brought. Then Sakka did all of that.
The elders also approached the king and said, "Great King, the non-human beings are angry; have them bring back the relics."
"Venerable sir, my mind is not yet satisfied," said the king. "Even so, let it be brought," he replied. On the seventh day, the relics were brought.
Having taken the relics thus brought, the king erected a stupa in Rājagaha;
the other kings also, each according to his own power, had them carried out and erected stupas in their respective places. Doṇa the brahmin also—
"Did the Moriyas of Pipphalivana also erect a stupa at their respective places?
There is one stupa in Rājagaha, one in the city of Vesālī,
one in Kapilavatthu, and one in Allakappa."
One stupa in Rāmagāma, one in Veṭhadīpaka,
One among the Mallas of Pācīna, and one in Kusinārā;
These are the stupas containing his bodily relics that are established on Jambudvīpa.
Together with the Aṅgārakumbha stūpas, those become ten stūpas;
