these ten stūpas of the Supreme Man, O King of Men,
have been worshipped according to their respective merit.
They are always worthy of veneration by the entire world,
including the devas; thus ends the Discourse on the Ten Stupas.

10. When the stūpas had been thus established, the Elder Mahākassapa, seeing that there was a danger to the relics, approached King Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, it is fitting to make a single deposit of the relics. The king replied, "Venerable sir, let me first undertake the work of depositing them;
but how shall I have the relics brought? [The Elder said], "Great King, the bringing of the relics is not for you."
"It is a burden; it is a burden for us. It would be well, venerable sir, if you were to bring the relics yourself; I shall construct the relic-shrine.
The Elder brought all the relics, setting aside only those portions intended for the service of various royal families.
However, the Nāgas seized the relics at Rāmagāma; there was no obstacle to them, for they were destined for the Mahāvihāra in the island of Laṅkā in the future.
This was the method for depositing the treasure in the Great Cetiya. He did not bring it there himself;
rather, having had it brought from the remaining seven cities and deposited in the southeastern direction of Rājagaha, he made this resolution:
"In this place, let the rock that exists here disappear, let the earth become perfectly pure, and let no water rise up."
The king had that spot excavated and, having fashioned bricks from the earth extracted therefrom, he caused eighty cetiyas for the great disciples to be built.
When even the great disciples asked him, "What is the king doing here? he replied, "It is for the cetiyas of the great disciples.
No one knew that it was a place where relics were deposited; however, when that area had been dug down to a depth of eighty cubits, [they found] below—
Having had the Teacher’s remains enshrined, he had a house made of copper as large as a shrine-hall built there in the Thūpārāma;
he also had eight caskets and eight shrines made of yellow sandalwood and other materials.
Then, having placed the Blessed One’s relics inside a casket of yellow sandalwood, he [placed] that casket of yellow sandalwood...
He placed that [relic] in another golden sandalwood casket, and that in yet another; thus, having combined eight golden sandalwood caskets into one,
by this same method he placed the eight caskets within the eight golden sandalwood stūpas,
and the eight golden sandalwood stūpas within the eight red sandalwood caskets, and the eight red sandalwood caskets within the eight red sandalwood stūpas.
The eight red sandalwood stūpas were placed in eight ivory caskets; the eight ivory caskets in eight ivory stūpas;
the eight ivory stūpas in eight caskets made of all kinds of jewels; the eight caskets made of all kinds of jewels in eight stūpas made of all kinds of jewels;
the eight stūpas made of all kinds of jewels in eight golden caskets; and the eight golden caskets in eight golden stūpas.
In eight golden stūpas there were eight silver caskets; in eight silver caskets there were eight silver stūpas;
in eight silver stūpas there were eight jewel caskets; in eight jewel caskets there were eight golden stūpas;
in eight jewel stūpas there were eight ruby caskets; in eight ruby caskets there were eight ruby stūpas.
He placed eight ruby stūpas within eight emerald stūpas; eight emerald stūpas within eight crystal caskets;
and eight crystal caskets within eight crystal stūpas. The uppermost crystal shrine was the size of the Cetiya in the Thūpārāma.
For him he had a house made of all kinds of jewels built; above that, one made of gold; above that, one made of silver; and above that, he had a house made of copper built.
There, having strewn sand made of all kinds of jewels and scattered thousands of water-born and land-born flowers, he [recited] five hundred and fifty Jātaka tales.
The Great Elder had the Great King Suddhodana, Queen Mahāmāyā, and all seven of their co-born children fashioned entirely out of gold.
He had five hundred and five golden and silver jars filled with water placed there;
he also had five hundred golden banners and five hundred golden lamps made, which were filled with fragrant oil and fitted with wicks of fine *dukūla* cloth.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having made the resolution: "Let the garlands not wither; let the perfumes not perish; let the lamps not go out," had the letters engraved upon a golden plate:
"In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa shall raise the royal parasol and become the Dharma-king Aśoka; he will cause these relics to be widely distributed."
The king, having honored [the relics] with all his ornaments, departed while closing the doors starting from the beginning.
Having closed the copper-iron door, he tied the key and seal to the pulling-rope and placed a great cluster of jewels right there.
He had the following inscription engraved: "In the future, may poor kings take these jewels and perform honor for the relics."
Sakka, the king of the devas, addressed Vissakamma, saying, "Dear son, Ajātasattu has made a deposit of relics.
Establish a guard over this place," and he sent him. Vissakamma arrived and arranged a canopy of wild beasts.
Having fashioned wooden figures holding crystal-colored swords within that relic chamber, he set them to patrol around it with a speed like the wind.
Having fastened it with a single pin, he constructed a stone enclosure all around in the shape of a *giñjaka* (a circular granary),
covered it on top with another [stone], filled it with earth, leveled the ground, and established a stone stupa upon it.
This is the account of the enshrinement of the relics.
11. When the enshrining of the relics was thus completed, the Elder remained for the duration of his lifespan and then attained final Nibbāna;
the king also passed away according to his karma, and those people likewise died. At a later time, Prince Piya-dāsa raised the royal parasol and became the Dhamma-king named Aśoka.
Taking those relics, he established them within eighty-four thousand cetiyas throughout Jambudīpa.
It is said that Bindusāra had one hundred sons; Asoka had them all put to death, with the exception of his own uterine brother, Prince Tissa.

Having ruled for four years without being formally consecrated while putting them to death, at the end of those four years—two hundred years after the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata—[he was consecrated].
In his eighteenth year, he attained the consecration as sole monarch over the entire Jambudīpa.
By the power of that consecration, these royal supernormal powers (rājiddhi) arose: his command prevailed for a distance of one *yojana* beneath the great earth, and likewise in the sky above;
and from Lake Anotatta, sixteen water-jars were brought by eight carriers every single day.
The deities brought [the water]. Having conceived faith in the Teaching, he gave eight jars to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
two jars to about sixty bhikkhus who were masters of the Tipiṭaka; two jars to the chief queen Asandhimittā;
and four jars he used himself. Indeed, there is something called "tooth-stick-creeper" (dantakaṭṭhanāgalatā) in the Himālayas, which the deities themselves provide.

It was glossy, soft, and flavorful; they enjoyed it day after day, by means of which the daily task of tooth-cleaning was accomplished for the king, the chief queen, the sixteen thousand dancers, and the sixty thousand monks.
Day after day, deities brought him *agada*-myrobalan, *agada*-pumpkin, and gold-colored, fragrant [tooth-sticks].

They brought mangoes cooked in honey; likewise, for the burning Chaddanta elephant, they brought five-colored lower and upper garments, a yellow-colored hand-towel, and a divine, knowledge-bestowing cloth.
Furthermore, they brought daily ointments and perfumes from the Nāga realm, as well as a priceless *sumana* flower-cloth not made of thread for his wearing, and precious collyrium.
The dragon kings bring [the rice]. From the very day the Chaddanta elephant rises, nine thousand carts daily bring fine rice.
The mice remove the husks and chaff so that not even a single broken grain remains.
In all places belonging to the king, only this rice is consumed. Honey-bees produce honey.
In the smithies, hammers strike the anvils with a clear sound. The jackals shake their hides, and the karavīka birds, having arrived, perform an offering for the king by warbling in sweet tones.
Endowed with these supernatural powers, the king, on a certain day, sent a golden chain as a bond for the four [elephants].
Having brought the Naga King Mahākāḷa— who possesses a form visible to the Buddhas and who lives for an eon—
and having seated him upon a magnificent throne beneath a white parasol, she performed worship with hundreds of varieties of lotuses,
terrestrial flowers, and golden blossoms, while sixteen thousand dancers adorned with every ornament stood all around.

Having surrounded [him], he manifested [the form] with these words: "Bring the form of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Wheel-Turner of the sublime True Dharma, whose knowledge is infinite, within the range of these eyes.
Thus it was produced, adorned with the secondary marks and made resplendent by the beauty of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, like a blooming lotus flower or a white water-lily.
The surface of the waters was as radiant as the sky, its splendor expanded by the spreading mass of rays from the clusters of stars;
it was like the peak of the Golden Mountain, encircled by the glow of twilight, the hue of the sun, rainbows, and streaks of lightning, and adorned with a garland of pure banners of various colors,
enveloped by the play of a fathom-wide halo of light interwoven with rays of diverse hues such as blue, yellow, and red.
Beholding the form of the Buddha— the beauty of whose head was brilliantly illuminated and who was like an elixir for the eyes of the hosts of Brahmas,
devas, humans, nāgas, and yakkhas— the King performed what is known as the "eye-worship" for seven days.
It is said that after receiving his consecration, the King followed the external heretical sects for only three years.
In his fourth year of the Buddha’s dispensation, he established a permanent provision of food for sixty thousand members of the Brahmin caste,
heretics, and white-robed wanderers (pāṇḍaraṅga paribbājaka).
While King Asoka was distributing the alms previously instituted by his father in the same manner within his own palace, one day, from the lion-window—
Standing there, seeing those who were outside the sphere of tranquility eating with improper conduct, their faculties uncontrolled and their deportment undisciplined, he thought:
"Having examined such a gift, it is right to give it to those who are worthy. Having thought thus, he said to his ministers:
"Go, sirs, and bring into the inner palace those ascetics and brahmins whom each of you considers most virtuous."

Thinking, "I shall give a gift," the ministers replied to the king, "Very well, Your Majesty," and having brought those various white-robed wanderers, Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and others, they said, "Great King, these are our Arahants.
Then the king, having arranged high and low seats in the inner palace, said to those who had arrived, "Let them come. To each one as they arrived, he spoke.
"Sit down on seats suitable for each of you," he said; accordingly, some sat on fine chairs (*bhaddapīṭhaka*) and others on wooden benches (*phalakapīṭhaka*).
Seeing this, the king realized, "These men have no inner wealth," and having given them food and hard provisions suitable for them, he dismissed them.

As time passed in this manner, one day, while standing at the lion-window, he saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the royal courtyard—tamed, guarded, with senses calmed, and endowed with perfect deportment. Who was this Nigrodha?
He was the son of Prince Sumanarāja, the eldest son of King Bindusāra. Herein is the sequential account of Bindusāra:

It is said that while the king was still weak, Prince Aśoka abandoned the kingdom of Ujjain which he had obtained, came [to Pāṭaliputra], brought the entire city under his own control, and seized Prince Sumana.
On that very day, Queen Sumanā, the consort of Prince Sumana, became pregnant. She...
Having departed in disguise, they were traveling toward a certain village of Caṇḍālas not far away;
hearing the sound of a deity dwelling in a banyan tree near the house of the chief Caṇḍāla as she was escorting Sumanā from there,
they went into her presence, and the deity, by her own supernatural power, fashioned a sala tree.
"Stay here," she gave him this instruction. She entered that *sāla* tree. On that very day, she gave birth to a son.
Because he was protected by the deity of the *nigrodha* tree, she gave him the name Nigrodha.
From the day he was born, the eldest Caṇḍāla, regarding her as his own sister, began to provide for her constantly.
The princess lived there for seven years. At that time, Prince Nigrodha had also reached the age of seven.
Then, a certain Arahat named Mahāvaruṇa Thera, while residing there, perceived the boy’s perfection of causal conditions and thought, “This boy is now seven years old;
it is time to ordain him. Having informed the princess, he ordained Prince Nigrodha. The prince—

He attained Arahatship even while still at the threshold of his studies. One day, having attended to his body early in the morning and performed the duties toward his teacher and preceptor, he took up his bowl and robes and set out, thinking, "I shall go to the door of my mother, the female lay-devotee.
He entered the city through the southern gate, passed through the center of the city, and departed by the eastern gate. His mother’s residence was located there.
Having gone out, he had to proceed; at that time, King Aśoka, the Dharma-king, was walking back and forth in the eastern direction facing the east within the lion-window.
At that very moment, the novice Saṅgharakkhita reached the royal courtyard, his faculties calmed and his mind tranquil, [seeing] the distance of a yoke.

"Beholding. This is why it was said. One day, while standing at the lion-window, he saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the royal courtyard—tamed, guarded, with senses at peace, and endowed with perfect deportment. Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
"All these people have distracted minds; they are like a forest path. But this boy has an undistracted mind."
His looking forward and looking around, as well as his contracting and extending [the limbs], were so graceful that [the king thought], "Surely there must be some supramundane quality within him.
At the mere sight of the king, the novice’s heart became serene. Affection was established;
why? It is said that formerly, at the time he was performing meritorious deeds, this man had been the king’s elder brother, a merchant.
Then the king, having conceived affection and great respect for the novice, sent his ministers with the command, "Summon the novice.
When [the king] thought, "He is taking too long," he sent two or three more, saying, "Let him come quickly! But the novice came at his own natural pace.
The king, recognizing that a suitable seat had been prepared, said, "Be seated. Looking here and there, [the king saw] that there was no other monk present.
Having approached the royal couch, which was adorned with a raised white parasol, he signaled to the king that he wished to receive the bowl. Seeing him approaching the couch, the king thought:
"Today this novice will become the master of this house. The novice placed the bowl in the king's hand, ascended the couch, and sat down.
The king presented him with all the varieties of rice gruel, curry, and cooked rice he had prepared for his own use. The novice accepted only as much as was necessary for his own sustenance.
At the conclusion of the meal, the king said, "Do you know the instruction given to you by the Teacher?
"I know it, Great King, in part. "My dear, tell it to me as well. "Very well."
"Great King," he said, and for the sake of offering thanks, he recited the "Appamāda-vagga" (Chapter on Heedfulness) from the *Dhammapada*, which was appropriate for the king.
Upon hearing the verses, "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death," the king said at the conclusion of the thanksgiving, "I have understood, dear father;
please finish [the recitation]. Having received thirty-two portions of choice food, on the following day, thirty-two monks...
Having taken [the alms], he entered the royal palace and performed his meal. The king [thought],
"Let thirty-two other monks also receive alms together with you," and by this very means, increasing [the number] day after day,
he cut off the food supply for sixty thousand brahmins and wanderers, and [provided it] for sixty thousand [monks] within his own residence.
He established a permanent meal offering for the monks out of the very same faith he had felt upon meeting the Elder Nigrodha; and the Elder Nigrodha,
having established the king and his retinue in the three refuges and the five precepts,
caused them to establish an unshakable faith in the Buddha’s teaching through a faith that transcends the level of ordinary worldlings.
Furthermore, having caused the great monastery named Asokārāma to be built, he established alms-food for sixty thousand bhikkhus.
Throughout the eighty-four thousand cities of all Jambudīpa, he had eighty-four thousand monasteries constructed.
Adorned with eighty-four thousand cetiyas, these were built solely through righteousness and not through unrighteousness, in a single day.

It is said that after King Aśoka had given a great almsgiving at the Asokārāma and sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of sixty thousand bhikkhus, he invited the Saṅgha with the four requisites and asked this question: "Venerable sirs, how much is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One?
"Great King, there are nine divisions; according to the sections, there are eighty-four thousand divisions of Dhamma."
The king, having gained confidence in the Dhamma, thought, "I shall honor each section of the Dhamma with a monastery.
On that very day, he disbursed ninety-six crores of wealth and commanded his ministers: "Come, sirs!
Having built one monastery in each city, cause eighty-four thousand monasteries to be constructed throughout the eighty-four thousand cities."
He himself began the construction work for the great monastery of Asoka at the Asokārāma.
The Saṅgha appointed the Elder Indagutta—possessed of great psychic power, great majesty, and whose taints were exhausted—as the overseer of the new construction.
Whatever portion of the work was not yet finished, the Elder brought to completion through his own supernatural power. Thus, in three...
Within a year, he completed the construction of the monasteries. On a single day, letters arrived from all the cities; the ministers informed the king:
"Your Majesty, the eighty-four thousand monasteries are finished. Then the king approached the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and asked:
"Venerable sirs, eighty-four thousand monasteries have been built by me; from where shall I obtain the relics?"
"Your Majesty, we have heard that there is indeed a deposit of relics, yet it is not known in which specific place it lies.

Not finding the relics after having had the Cetiya demolished at Rājagaha, the King had a replica made and, taking with him the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, he went to Vesālī.
Not finding them there either, he went to Kapilavatthu; and not finding them there either—
He went to Rāmagāma; however, at Rāmagāma they did not allow him to break open the Nāga Cetiya. The spade fell upon the cetiya and broke into pieces.
Thus, having failed there as well, he went to Allakappa, Pāvā, and Kusinārā.
Everywhere, having attempted to break open the cetiyas but failing to obtain the relics, he restored them to their original state and returned to Rājagaha. There, the four...
Having convened the assembly, he asked: "Has anyone previously heard that there is a relic deposit in such-and-such a place?
Thereupon, an elder of eighty years spoke: "I do not know of a relic deposit in such-and-such a place.
However, when I was seven years old, my grandfather elder had me take a flower-basket and said, 'Come, novice, to such-and-such...'"
"There is a stone stupa in another forest; let us go there. Having gone and paid homage, he said, "It is fitting for the novice to investigate this site.
He replied, "Great King, I know only this much.
The king, saying, "This very spot is it," had the grass cleared away and the stone stupa and the earth removed, and beneath...

He saw a floor made of plaster. Then, having had the plaster and the bricks removed, he gradually descended through the surrounding cloisters and saw seven kinds of jewel-sand and eighty wooden figures turning around.
Having summoned the yakṣa-servants and caused them to perform an offering ceremony, he still could not find the end or the limit, even as he paid homage to the deities.
"I shall take these relics and deposit them in eighty-four thousand monasteries, performing honors for them so that the deities do not create obstacles," he said.
King Sakka, while wandering on his tour, saw this and, addressing Vissakamma, said: "Dear one, King Asoka is a righteous monarch..."
Thinking, "I shall remove the bones," he entered the courtyard. Having gone there, [the king] said, "Take away the wooden forms.
Then, having come in the guise of a boy from Pañcacūḷagāma, he stood before the king with a bow in his hand and said, "I shall take them away, Great King. "Take them, dear boy," [the king replied].
Taking an arrow, he pierced it right at the joint, and everything was scattered about.
Then the king took the key and seal fastened to the ring, and saw the heap of jewels;

seeing the inscription, "May future poor kings take this jewel and pay honor to the relics," he became angry and thought repeatedly, "How can it be fitting to call a king like me a 'poor king'? Having searched the door and entered the interior of the house...
He entered. The lamps, which had been lit more than two hundred and eighteen years prior, blazed forth just as before;
the blue lotus flowers appeared as if they had been brought and arranged at that very moment;
the floral carpet seemed as if it had been spread at that very instant; and the perfumes seemed as if they had been ground and set out just a moment ago.
The King took a golden plate and read: "In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa shall raise the royal parasol and become the Dharma-king named Aśoka;
he shall take these relics and cause them to be widely distributed.
Having said, "I have been seen by you, venerable Mahākassapa Thera," he folded his left hand and struck with his right hand.
Thus, having left only a small portion of the relics for veneration at that site and taking all the remaining relics, he closed the relic-chamber in the same manner as it had been previously sealed;
having restored everything to its original state and established a stone cetiya on top, he enshrined the relics in the eighty-four thousand monasteries. In this way...
On the surface of Jambudīpa, King Aśoka, the Dharma-king, caused eighty-four thousand cetiyas to be built.
All these stupas are the sole lamps for the entire world; they bring heaven and liberation to all. Abandoning all other duties, people should worship them in every way at all times.
The Discourse on the Eighty-Four Thousand Stupas.

12. Thus, after King Aśoka, the Dharma-king, had established eighty-four thousand monasteries, he paid homage to the Great Elder and asked, "Am I, venerable sir, an heir to the Buddha's Dispensation? "Of what are you an heir, Great King? You are an outsider to the Dispensation.
"Venerable sir, having disbursed ninety-six crores of wealth, I have built eighty-four thousand monasteries together with their shrines."

"Having had [the stūpas] built, I am not the heir; who else is the heir? "Great King, you are indeed a donor of requisites, but he who causes his own son and daughter to go forth is called an heir to the Teaching.
When this was said, King Aśoka, aspiring to the status of an heir to the Teaching, [looked at] Prince Mahinda standing nearby.

"Having seen this, my dear, will you be able to go forth? he asked. The prince, who had already been desirous of going forth by his own nature, upon hearing the king's words, was filled with exceeding joy and said, "I shall go forth, Your Majesty; having ordained me, be a successor to the Dispensation.
At that time, the king’s daughter Saṅghamittā was also standing in that place; seeing him, she said, "You too..."
“Mother, will you be able to go forth? “Very well, dear one,” she replied. Since the king did not obtain his wish, he was delighted at heart;
he approached the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and said, “Venerable sirs, please ordain these children and make them heirs to my dispensation.
The Saṅgha accepted the king’s words, and [ordained] the prince by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.
He was granted the going-forth by his preceptor, the Elder Mahādeva, and his teacher. He received full ordination with the Elder Majjhantika as his teacher;
at the very moment of his ordination, he attained Arhatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
The Elder Āyupālā was the name of the teacher for the princess Saṅghamittā, while the Elder Dhammapālā was her preceptor.
...was his name. Then, from the time he was ordained, the Elder Mahinda,
while mastering both the Dhamma and the Vinaya in the presence of his own preceptor, learned the Theravāda— including the Tipiṭaka as compiled in the two councils together with its commentaries—
within three years, and [taught it] to his own preceptor’s pupils.
He was the leader of about a thousand bhikkhus.
Now at that time, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, while investigating where in the future the Teaching would be well-established,
perceived that it would be well-established in the border regions.
Having assigned specific responsibilities to various bhikkhus, he dispatched them to their respective regions.
He sent the Elder Majjhantika to the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra, saying, "Go to this kingdom and establish the Teaching there.
Having spoken likewise to the Elder Mahādeva, he sent him to the Mahiṃsaka territory. To the forest-dwelling Elder Rakkhita, he said:
He sent the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita to Aparanta, the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita to Mahāraṭṭha, and the Elder Mahārakkhita to the Yonaka world.
He sent the Elder Majjhima to the region of Himavanta, and the Elders Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
To his own pupil, the Elder Mahinda, he entrusted [the mission] along with the Elders Itthiya, Uttiya, and Bhaddasāla.
"Go together with the Elder Saṃbhala to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Dispensation there.
Thus they all departed for their respective directions, each accompanied by four others as his retinue.
In every place they reached, all the Elders won over the people and established the Dispensation.

But when the Elder Mahinda, having been requested by his preceptor and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Dispensation, reflected, "Is now the time for me to go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?", he considered the advanced age of King Muṭasīva.
[He thought: "This great king is old; it will not be possible to take hold of him and establish the Dispensation."
"Now, however, his son Devānampiyatissa will rule the kingdom. Having gained him, it will be possible to uphold the Dispensation;
therefore, until that time arrives, let us observe our kinsmen, and see whether we shall come back to this country again or not."
Having thus reflected, and having paid homage to his preceptor and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
he departed from the Asoka Monastery. Together with those four elders, Itthiya and the others, and with the novice Sumanas, the son of Saṅghamittā, and the lay follower Bhaṇḍuka,
he set out on a journey toward the city of Rājagaha, traveling through the southern district of Upavattaka.
Looking for his kinsmen, he passed six months; then, traveling by stages, he arrived at the place where his mother lived, a city named Veṭḍiṣa.

Upon seeing the Elder there, the queen—his mother—worshipped the Elder’s feet with her head, gave him almsfood, and led the Elder up to the monastery she herself had built on Mount Veṭṭhiṣa, known as the Veṭṭhiṣa Giri Vihāra.
Seated in that monastery, the Elder reflected: "The duties we had to perform here are finished.
Is now the time to go to Laṅkādīpa? Then he thought: "Let His Majesty Devānampiyatissa first enjoy the consecration sent by my father, and let him hear of the virtues of the Triple Gem;
and for the sake of the festival, let him depart from the city."
"Let him ascend Mount Missaka; then we shall see him there. Thereafter, he remained dwelling in that very place for another month.
When the month had passed, Sakka, lord of the gods, approached the Elder Mahinda and said this: "Venerable sir, King Muṭasīva has passed away;
now King Devānampiyatissa rules the kingdom. And by the Perfectly Enlightened One, you were..."
"It has been prophesied that in the future, a monk named Mahinda will cause the island of Tambapaṇṇi to be converted.
Therefore, venerable sirs, it is now the time for you to go to that excellent island; I too shall be your companion.
Having accepted his words, the Elder, being the seventh among them, rose into the air from the Veṭṭhī mountain monastery.
In the eastern direction of Anurādhapura, he established himself on Mount Missaka—which even today is known as Cetiya-pabbata.
On that very day, it was the lunar mansion called Jeṭṭhamūla in the island of Tambapaṇṇi;
the king, having caused the proclamation of the festival, commanded his ministers, "Celebrate the festival," and departed from the city accompanied by a retinue of forty thousand men.
Having departed, he set out for Mount Missaka, desiring to sport with deer;
then a deity dwelling on that mountain, thinking, "I shall show the king the elders," assumed the form of a red deer and wandered nearby as if grazing on grass and leaves.
Seeing that it was now improper to pierce him while he was heedless, the king pulled back his bowstring.
The deer began to flee by way of the Ambaṭṭha road, and the king, pursuing him closely from behind, also ascended the Ambaṭṭha mountain.
The deer vanished not far from the elders.
The Elder Mahinda, having resolved, "May the king see only me and no others as he approaches," said, "Tissa! Tissa! Come here!
Upon hearing this, the king thought, "In this island of Tambapaṇṇi, there is no one capable of addressing me by the name 'Tissa,' for I am the one born here.
Yet this man, wearing tattered and torn robes and clad in saffron-colored cloth..."
"The one who addresses me by name—could this be a human or a non-human? The Elder replied:
"We are recluses, Great King—the disciples of the Dhamma-King—and out of compassion for you alone, we have come here from Jambudīpa."
At that time, King Devānampiyatissa and King Aśokadhamma were friends who had never met.
By the power of King Devānampiyatissa’s merit, three bamboo poles appeared at the foot of Mount Chāta in a bamboo grove:
one called the creeper pole, one called the flower pole, and one called the bird pole.
Their names are as follows: among them, the support for the creeper is naturally silver-colored, and the creeper that grows there, having adorned it, appears golden in color;
on the support for the flowers, however, flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and black appear with their stalks, petals, and filaments clearly and beautifully arranged;
and on the support for the birds, there are birds such as swans, chickens, and jīvañjīvaka birds.
Various kinds of four-footed creatures appeared as if they were alive, and from the ocean there arose many sorts of jewels, such as pearls, gems, and beryl.
Furthermore, on Tambapaṇṇi there arose eight kinds of pearls: the fear-pearl, the elephant-pearl, the chariot-pearl, and the myrobalan-pearl.
There were pearls from Ceylon, finger-ring pearls, *kakudha* fruit pearls, and natural pearls;
he sent those staffs, those pearls, and many other jewels as a gift to King Aśoka, the Dharma-king.
King Aśoka, being pleased, sent back five royal insignia as well as many other gifts for his consecration.
And not only this material gift, it is said, but he also sent this gift of the Dhamma:
"I have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha;
I have declared myself a lay follower in the teaching of the Sakyan Son."
“O Supreme among Men, having inspired confidence in these three grounds of upliftment, take refuge with faith.
The King, recollecting the news of the Dispensation’s arrival from the son of the Aviri people, [addressed] the Elder: “This is the asceticism of the Great King, O Maharaja, of the Dhamma-King...”
Hearing the words "disciples," he thought, "Has the Noble One arrived? and immediately laid aside his weapons and sat to one side, exchanging pleasantries with him.
While they were still engaged in friendly conversation, those forty thousand men arrived and surrounded him; at that moment, the Elder showed them to the others as well.
The king, having seen them, asked, "When did these come? [The Elder replied: "Along with me, O Great King. "But now, are there other such ascetics in Jambudīpa?
"Great King, at present Jambudīpa is illuminated by the saffron robes and surrounded by the power of the seers. Regarding them:
'They have attained true knowledge and psychic powers, and some possess the knowledge of others' minds...'"
“The Arahants whose taints are destroyed are many disciples of the Buddha.
Then the king said, “Venerable sir, tomorrow I shall send a chariot; having mounted it, you should come,” and having spoken thus, he departed.
Not long after the king had left, the Elder addressed the novice Sumana: “Come, Sumana, it is time for the hearing of the Dhamma.”
"Ghoṣeti" means that the novice, having entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), emerged from it and made a resolution;
then, with a concentrated mind, while sounding across the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, he proclaimed the time for hearing the Dhamma.
Hearing the novice’s voice, the earth-dwelling deities (bhummā devatā) raised their voices; by this means, [the sound reached] as far as the Brahma-world.
A sound went forth. Because of that sound, a great assembly of deities gathered.
Seeing that vast gathering of deities, the Elder preached the Samacitta Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by incalculable deities.
Many nāgas and supaṇṇas were established in the refuges. Then, during that night...
After some time, the king sent a chariot for the Elders. The Elders said, "We do not mount a chariot.
Go ahead; we shall follow later," and having ascended into the air, they descended at the site of the Paṭhamaka Cetiya in the western direction of Anurādhapura.
The king, having dispatched his charioteer and prepared a pavilion within his residence, thought:
"Will the noble ones sit upon the seats, or will they not sit?
Even as he was thinking thus, the charioteer reached the city gate and saw the elders who had arrived earlier, fastening their waist-bands and putting on their robes.
Seeing them, he became exceedingly joyful in mind; returning, he announced to the king, "Your Majesty, the elders have arrived.
The king asked, "Have they mounted the chariot? "They have not, Your Majesty; rather, having departed from behind, they have come first and are standing at the eastern gate.
Upon hearing that they had not mounted the chariot, the king said, "In that case, my man, spread a carpet on the ground."
Having said, "Prepare the seats in brief," he went out to meet them. The ministers, having spread mats on the ground, arranged various coverings above them, such as woolen rugs and the like.
The king also went forth, paid homage to the elders, took the bowl from the hand of Thera Mahinda, and with great honor and worship, [served] the elders with excellent food.
Having personally satisfied them with solid and soft foods, he summoned Queen Anulā and five hundred women led by her, saying,
"Let them pay homage to the Elders and perform acts of worship and honor," and sat down to one side. The Elder,
raining down the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma upon the king and his retinue, [recited] the *Petavatthu*, the *Vimānavatthu*, and the *Saccasaṃyutta*.
He preached the Dhamma. Having heard it, those five hundred women also realized the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Then, when the citizens heard of the elders’ virtues, they lamented, saying, "We do not get to see the elders.
Thereupon, the king, thinking, "There is no space here," said, "Go, my men! Cleanse the elephant stable, scatter sand over it, and [prepare it for them]."
“Having scattered flowers of five colors and hung up a canopy, prepare seats for the elders at the place where the auspicious elephant stands,” he said;
the ministers did accordingly.
The Elder went there, sat down, and preached the Devadūta Sutta; at the conclusion of the discourse, a thousand beings [attained the fruits of the path].
He was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Likewise, at the southern gate in the Nandana Grove, they prepared a seat for the Elder, saying, "The elephant stable is crowded.
The Elder sat there and preached the *Āsīvisūpama Sutta* (The Simile of the Venomous Snake).
Having heard that as well, one thousand beings attained the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, on the second day after the day he arrived, [to] two thousand five hundred...
There was a realization of the Dhamma by thousands of beings.
While the Elder was conversing with the women who had come from various noble families—the daughters-in-law and young maidens of those houses—in Nandanavana, evening arrived.
Perceiving that it was time, the Elder rose, saying, "I shall now go to Missaka Mountain."
The ministers lodged the elders in the Mahāmeghavana monastery. When that night had passed, the king went into the presence of the elder;
having asked whether they had slept well, he asked, "Venerable sir, is a monastery suitable for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?
The elder replied, "It is suitable, Great King."
The king, being pleased, took a golden water-pot, poured water into the Elder’s hand, and gave him the Mahāmeghavana garden.
On the following day as well, having eaten at the royal palace, the Elder preached the Anamataggiya discourses in the Nandana Grove.
On the next day, he preached the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta. In this same manner, he preached for seven days.

There was a realization of the Dhamma for five thousand people who were dancing. On the seventh day, however, the Elder, having preached the *Appamāda-sutta* (Discourse on Heedfulness) within the royal palace, went back to Cetiyagiri itself.
Then the King thought: "The Elder came here of his own accord after being invited; therefore, it would be appropriate for him to depart even without taking leave."
Having reflected thus, he mounted his chariot and went to Cetiyagiri with great royal splendor;
upon arriving and approaching the presence of the elders, he drew near appearing exceedingly exhausted. Then the elder said to him, "Great King, why have you come so weary?
[The king replied,] "After you gave me such strict exhortation, I now wish to depart."
"Nukho" means "for the purpose of knowing, venerable sir. "Great King, we do not wish to go;
rather, it is proper for one called a *samaṇa* to know the time when the rains-retreat (*vassa*) begins.
At that very moment, the king, having surrounded the Karaṇḍaka Cetiya courtyard and commenced work on the sixty-eight caves, returned to the city itself.
The Elder Tepi and the great multitude, instructing the people, spent the rainy season retreat at Cetiyagiri.
Then, after the Venerable Mahāmāhinda had completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, on the full-moon Uposatha day of the month of Kattika, he said this to the King:

"Long has it been, Great King, since we have seen the Perfectly Enlightened One, the occasion for our paying homage, our rising to greet him, our joining of palms in salutation, and our performing acts of courtesy."
“There is none; therefore we are despondent. “Venerable sir, you said, ‘The Perfectly Enlightened One has attained final Nibbāna.
“Great King, although he has attained final Nibbāna, his bodily relics still remain. “In that case, venerable sir, I shall have another stupa erected.
Search for a suitable site. “But from where shall we obtain the relics? [He replied: “Together with Sumanas...”
"By means of mantras, O Great King," [said the sage]. Then the king approached Sumanas and asked, "Venerable sir, from where shall we now obtain the relics?
Sumanas replied, "Be at ease, Great King. Have the streets cleaned, have them adorned with banners, flags, full water-jars, and the like;
together with your retinue, observe the Uposatha vows, station all the musicians, and [prepare] the auspicious elephant."

Having had [the image] fashioned adorned with all ornaments and having a white parasol raised over it, at evening time he set out toward the Mahānāgavana garden, thinking, "In that place I shall surely obtain the relics. The King accepted this, saying, "Very well.
The Elder, however, went straight to Cetiyagiri.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahinda Thera said to the novice Sumana: "Go, novice, approach the noble King Asoka Dhammaraja in Jambudipa and speak these words in my name:
'Great King, your friend Devānampiya Tissa has placed his faith in the Buddha's teaching and desires to establish a stupa; it is said that the relics of the Blessed One are in your hands.'"
“Give me that alms-bowl and the relic which are there,” he said. Taking them, he approached Sakka, the king of the gods, and said:
“Great King, it is said that in your hands there are two relics:
the right canine tooth and the right jawbone. Therefore, you should worship the right canine tooth, but give the right jawbone to me. And so he spoke to him.
"Tell me, Great King, why did you neglect us after sending us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?
"Very well, venerable sir," Sumana replied, accepting the elder's words.
He immediately took his bowl and robe, rose into the air, descended at the gate of Pāṭaliputta, went into the presence of the king, and reported the matter to him.

The king, being pleased, took the bowl from the novice’s hand, fed him, and then, having rubbed the Blessed One’s bowl with perfumes and filled it with relics resembling excellent pearls, he gave it back.
The novice took it and approached Sakka, the King of the Devas. Seeing the novice, Sakka, the King of the Devas, asked: "What is it, Bhante?"
"Sumana, you are wandering about," he said. "Great King, why do you neglect us after having sent us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?
"I have neglected them, Venerable Sir; tell me, what shall I do? "It is said that there are two relics in your hands:
the right canine tooth and the right collarbone. Therefore, you should worship the right canine tooth and [worship] the right collarbone."
"But give it to me. "Very well, Bhante," replied Sakka, Lord of the Devas;
he opened the jewel-stupa measuring one *yojana* in size, extracted the right jawbone, and gave it to Sumanas.
He took it and established it right there on Cetiya Mountain. Then all those great *nāgas*, headed by Mahinda—
Having enshrined the relics bestowed by King Aśokadhamma right there at Cetiyagiri,
they took the right jawbone and went to the Mahānāga forest park during the increasing shade. The king,
having performed the aforementioned honors and worship with Sumanas, mounted the back of a noble elephant in the evening, with a white parasol held over the head of that auspicious elephant.
Carrying [the relic], the Great Elephant reached the royal park.
Then this thought occurred to him: "If this is the relic of the Perfectly Enlightened One, let the umbrella turn downward;
let the auspicious elephant kneel upon the ground; and let the relic-casket rest upon my head."
Simultaneously with the King’s thought, the parasol was lowered, it rested upon the knees of the elephant, and the relic casket settled upon the King’s head.
With his body as if anointed with the Deathless and filled with supreme joy and gladness, the King asked:
"Venerable sir, what shall I do with the relic? "O Great King, place it right here on the elephant’s forehead," he replied.
The king placed the relic casket upon the forehead of an elephant. The delighted elephant trumpeted a cry like a thundercloud;
a great rain cloud arose and poured down a shower of lotuses, reaching as far as Ukada. A great earthquake occurred, and even in the border regions it was said:
"The relics of the Perfectly Enlightened One shall be established here!"
Then that noble elephant, surrounded by many musicians and being honored with exceedingly magnificent offerings and respect,
retreated facing the western direction; having gone as far as the eastern gate of the city,
he entered the city through the eastern gate, while magnificent worship was being performed throughout the entire city, and [emerged] through the southern gate.
Having gone out, there is, it is said, a place called Pabhajavathu in the western direction of the Thūpārāma;

having gone there, he turned back again toward the Thūpārāma itself. That was the site where a shrine had been established for the water-strainer, the waist-belt, and the rain-cloak belonging to the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones. This is that very place.
"Even though the shrines have fallen into ruin, it remains surrounded by various thickets with branches bristling with thorns through the power of the deities.
Let no one defile it with leftover food or impure refuse.
Then, the king’s men went before that elephant, cut down all the thickets, and cleared the ground.
They made that spot level as the palm of a hand. The elephant went there and, having placed that spot in front of him, stood at its western side on the site of the Bodhi tree.
Then they began to lower the relics from his head, but the elephant would not allow them to be lowered.
They asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, why does the elephant not allow the relics to be lowered?"
"Your Majesty, it is not fitting to remove that which has been ascended. At that time, the water in the Abhayavāpī had run dry;
the ground all around was cracked, and the clods of earth were easy to extract. Then the great multitude quickly brought earth and made a site the size of a hand or a jar.
At that very moment, they began to fashion bricks for the purpose of building the stupa.
They began the work. Until the bricks were finished, the elephant-nāga remained for several days during the day at the site of the Bodhi tree in the elephant stable.
At night, he walked around the ground where the stupa was to be established.
Then, having had the site measured out, the king asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, what kind of stupa should be built? [He replied: "A heap of rice."

"It is fitting, Great King," [the Elder replied]. "Excellent, Bhante," the King said, and having caused a stupa of the height of a man's leg to be built, he performed great honors for the purpose of enshrining the relics.
Then all the citizens and the people of the countryside gathered together, assembling for the purpose of seeing the relics. And when they had assembled—

In the midst of that great multitude, the relics of the One Possessing the Ten Powers rose into the air from the elephant’s frontal globe to the height of seventy palm trees and displayed the Twin Miracle.
From various parts of those relics, six-colored rays of light, streams of water, and masses of fire issued forth.
This was the miracle displayed by the Blessed One at the foot of the Gaṇḍamba tree in Sāvatthī.
The miracle was exactly the same. And that was neither by the power of the elders nor by the power of the deities, but rather by the power of the Buddhas alone;
for it is said that while the Blessed One was still living, he made this resolve:
"In the island of Tambapaṇṇi, in the southern direction from Anurādhapura, at the site of the cetiyas of the three previous Buddhas, [let there be] my [cetiyas]."
"May the Twin Miracle take place on the day the relic of the right collarbone is established.
Thus, the Buddhas and the Buddha-qualities are inconceivable;
for those who have faith in these inconceivables, the result is inconceivable.
Emerging from the relic-body, with its drops of water, there was not a single spot on the entire surface of the island of Tambapaṇṇi that was not touched by them.

Thus, having extinguished the heat of the land of Tambapaṇṇi with those water droplets and having displayed a miracle for the great multitude, that relic-body descended and came to rest upon the head of the king.
Considering the attainment of human birth to be fruitful, he paid great honor and established the relic.

Simultaneously with the establishment of the relic, there was a great earthquake; and when the stupa was completed, the king, his brothers, and the queens each built individual stupas that inspired wonder among gods, nāgas, and yakkhas.
Thus, even though the Conqueror has passed away,
his physical relics can still bring about the welfare of people and manifold happiness through the many teachings of the Dhamma.
For one who stands firm should emulate the Lord.
This concludes the account of the Thūpārāma within the *Thūpavaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the minds of virtuous people.
Now, when the worship of the relics was completed and the noble relic had been established, the Elder Mahinda [entered] the Mahāmeghavana monastery itself.
Having gone there, he established a residence. At that time, Queen Anulā, desiring to go forth into the religious life, informed the king.
Having heard her words, the king said this to the Elder: "Venerable sir, Queen Anulā desires to go forth; please let her go forth. [The Elder replied:
"Great King, it is not permitted for us to ordain women. However, in Pāṭaliputta, my sister..."
"There is an elder nun named Saṅghamittā; summon her, O Great King.

On this island, the Bodhi trees of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones have been established, and our Blessed One’s Bodhi tree must also be established by means of the radiance emitted from its heart.
Therefore, you should send a message so that Saṅghamittā may come taking the Bodhi tree."
The king, having accepted the elder’s words, consulted with his ministers and said to his own nephew named Ariṭṭha:
“Dear boy, will you be able to go to Pāṭaliputta and bring back the noble Saṅghamittā Therī together with the Great Bodhi tree?
“I shall be able to do so, Your Majesty, if you grant me permission to go forth,” he replied.

"Go, dear son, bring the Elder and receive the going-forth. Having received the message from both the King and the Elder, and by virtue of the Elder’s supernormal power (*adhiṭṭhāna*), he traveled in a single day to the port of Jambukola;
there he boarded a ship, crossed the ocean, and went to Pāṭaliputta, where he delivered the King's message: "Your Majesty, your son, the Elder Mahinda..."
He spoke thus: "It is said that the sister-in-law of your companion, King Devānampiyatissa, named Queen Anulā, desires to go forth.
You should send the noble Elder Saṅghamittā to ordain her, and together with the noble lady, you should bring the Great Bodhi tree.
Having delivered this message to the Elder, he approached the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā and spoke as follows: "Noble Lady, for you..."
"Brother Mahinda Thera has sent me to you, saying:
'Queen Anulā, the sister-in-law of King Devānampiyatissa, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred female attendants, desires to go forth;
please come and ordain her.'"
"Your Majesty, she then went with great haste and reported the matter to the king. Then she said, 'I shall go, O Great King, to the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
He replied, 'In that case, mother, take the Mahābodhi and go.
Having had the road prepared from Pāṭaliputta as far as the Mahābodhi tree, he set out from Pāṭaliputta with a vast army seven *yojanas* long and three *yojanas* wide."
Having departed, he took the Noble Saṅgha and went to the vicinity of the Great Bodhi tree.

He surrounded the Great Bodhi tree with an army that displayed raised banners and flags, was variegated with various jewels, adorned with many ornaments, strewn with diverse kinds of flowers, and resounded with the clash of many musical instruments; then the king [honored it] with flowers, perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
Having worshipped him, performed three circumambulations to the right, and prostrated at eight places, he rose and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Desiring to receive the Bodhi tree through an act of truth (*saccavacana*), he ascended the jeweled throne, took up a stylus, and drew a design with *manosilā* (lapis lazuli).
He declared: "If the Great Bodhi is to be established in the island of Laṅkā, and if I am [devoted] to the Buddha’s teaching..."
"May I be free from doubt; may the Great Bodhi tree itself descend and be established in this golden vessel," he thus performed an act of truth.

Simultaneously with that act of truth, a branch of the Bodhi tree, having been severed by means of emerald-cutting tools at the spot where it was marked, stood upon the golden vessel filled with fragrant paste.

Then the king, having brought the Great Bodhi tree from the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) to Pāṭaliputta with great honor and having provided all necessary provisions, placed the Great Bodhi tree upon a boat on the Ganges.
He himself departed from the city, crossed the Vindhya forest, and after seven days, reached Tāmaliptī by way of stages; along the way, gods, nāgas, and humans [honored him].
They performed a magnificent worship of the Great Bodhi tree.
The king, too, having placed the Great Bodhi on the seashore for seven days and rendered it great honor,
boarded a ship together with the Bodhi tree and the Elder Saṅghamittā and her retinue, saying, "Let us go to the presence of the One of Ten Powers."
Crying out, "The Great Bodhi Tree is emitting a web of rays! he stood with palms joined in reverence, shedding tears.
As he watched, the Great Bodhi, having ascended the ship, plunged into the surface of the great ocean right before the Great King's eyes;
and for a league all around within the great ocean, the waves were stilled and five-colored lotuses blossomed.
In the sky, divine musical instruments resounded; celestial beings dwelling on land and in water offered an exceedingly magnificent worship from the air.
Amidst such great honor, the ship entered the port of Jambukola.
King Devānampiyatissa, for his part, had the road cleared from the Northern Gate all the way to the port of Jambukola.
On the day he departed from the city after being adorned with ornaments, while standing at the site of the Saddhasālā near the northern gate,
he saw the Great Bodhi tree approaching across the great ocean by means of the Elder’s supernatural power; with a joyful heart, he emerged and,
scattering flowers of five colors along the entire path, offered flower-gifts at intervals.
Setting out, he reached the port of Jambukola in a single day; surrounded by all the musicians and honoring [the Bodhi tree] with flowers,
incense, perfumes, and other offerings, he descended into water reaching up to his neck and, with a mind full of faith, thinking,
"This is indeed the Bodhi tree that radiates a network of rays from the essence of the Blessed One," he lifted the Great Bodhi tree and placed it upon his head, the supreme limb.
Having established the Mahābodhi tree and surrounded it, he descended from the ocean together with sixteen clans possessing noble birth who had come to attend upon it.
Having set the Bodhi tree on the shore of the ocean, he honored it for three days with the entire sovereignty of Tambapaṇṇi.
Then, on the fourth day, taking the Mahābodhi tree and performing magnificent worship, he proceeded by stages toward Anurādhapura.

When [the Bodhi tree] arrived in Anurādhapura, they accorded it great honor; on the fourteenth day, during the waxing phase of the moon, they brought the Mahābodhi into the city through the northern gate, carried it through the center of the city, and exited through the southern gate.
At a spot five hundred *dhanus* from the southern gate—where our Perfectly Enlightened Buddha had entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—they established it.
Having entered [that meditative attainment], he sat down. And the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones had also sat down after entering that same meditative attainment.

He established [the Bodhi tree] at that place which was the Tilaka-tree of the Mahāmeghavana garden—the site where the Blessed One Kakusandha’s Sirīsa-Bodhi, the Blessed One Konāgamana’s Udumbara-Bodhi, and the Blessed One Kassapa’s Nigrodha-Bodhi were established.
Having prepared the ground for the site of the royal palace, including the gates and ramparts, he established the Great Bodhi tree there.
Thus, for the welfare of Laṅkā and for the growth of the Sāsana,
the Great Bodhi was established in the delightful Mahāmegha Grove.
14. The Story of the Arrival of Bodhi.
Queen Anulā, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred male attendants—thus accompanied by a thousand women—went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā;
and before long, she and her retinue were established in Arahatship.
Ariṭṭha, the king’s nephew, also went forth in the presence of the Elder together with five hundred men;
not long after, he and his retinue were established in Arahatship. Then one day, the king, having paid homage to the Bodhi tree, was proceeding with the Elder toward the Thūpārāma.
When he arrived at the site of the Lohapāsāda, his men [brought] flowers.
They brought flowers and the king gave them to the Elder. The Elder worshipped the site of the Lohapāsāda with those flowers.
When the flowers had merely fallen to the ground, a great earthquake occurred.
The king asked, "Venerable sir, why did the earth quake? [The Elder replied: "Great King, in this place, in the future, for the Saṅgha..."
"There will be a Uposatha hall; this is its omen," he said.
Again, when he reached the site of the Mahācetiya, *campaka* flowers were brought to him. The King gave those too to the Elder.
Having worshipped the Mahācetiya site with flowers, the Elder paid homage; at that very moment, the great earth trembled. The King asked, "Venerable Sir, why did the earth tremble?"
He asked. "Great King, in this place there will arise in the future a great stupa for the Blessed Buddha, peerless;
this is its omen," he said. "I myself shall build it, Bhante. "Enough, Great King; you have much other work to do.
But your nephew named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya shall cause it to be built."
Then the king said, "Venerable sir, if he will build it for me, I shall consider it as already built.

Having had a stone slab twelve cubits in length brought, he caused the inscription to be written: "In this place, Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, the grandson of King Devānaṃpiyatissa, is building a stūpa," and he established it there. Then King Devānaṃpiyatissa [erected] the Cetiya-pabbata.
The relics, which had been brought by filling the alms-bowl of the Perfectly Enlightened One and placing it upon the back of an elephant, were deposited;
and having caused stūpas to be built at every league throughout the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, he established the relics therein.
As for the Blessed One’s bowl, however, he placed it in the royal palace and paid it worship.
Having enshrined the relics of the Fully Enlightened One, which were only the size of alms-bowls,
he caused great royal stūpas to be built, each one a *yojana* in extent.
This is the discourse on the *yojana*-stūpas.
Then the king, having performed many other meritorious deeds, reigned for forty years.
Upon his passing, his younger brother Uttiya reigned for ten years. Upon his passing, his younger brother Mahāsīva reigned for exactly ten years.
Upon his passing, his younger brother Sūratissa [reigned] for exactly ten years.
Then his son Assanāvika reigned. Two Damila sons of Assanāvika took Sūratissa and reigned righteously for twenty-two years.
Having taken him [from them], Muṭasīva’s son named Asela reigned for ten years.
Then, having come from the Coḷa kingdom, a Damila named Eḷāra seized King Asela.
Having captured Eḷāra, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya reigned for forty-four years.
To illustrate this matter, here is the sequential account:
It is said that King Devānampiyatissa had a younger brother who was a viceroy named Mahānāga. Then, regarding the king—
Desiring the kingdom for her own son, the queen prepared a mango laced with poison for the viceroy, who was having a lake constructed by raft;

she sent it to the queen’s sons. When they set out with the viceroy, as soon as the vessel was opened, the prince himself took the mango, ate it, and died. The viceroy, understanding the reason for this, [reported it] to the queen.
Frightened by that very [threat], he took his queen and his army and went to Rohaṇa.
On the way, his chief consort gave birth to a son at the monastery named Yaṭṭālavihāra; the brother named him Tissa.
Having gone from there and residing in Mahāgāma, he ruled the kingdom in Rohaṇa. After his passing, his son Yaṭṭālatisso [ruled].
He ruled his kingdom precisely at Mahāgāma. Upon his passing, his son named Goṭhābhaya likewise ruled there. Goṭhābhaya’s son, named Kākavaṇṇatissa, likewise ruled there.
It is said that King Kākavaṇṇatissa had as his chief queen, the consort Vihāramahādevī, the daughter of King Kalyāṇatissa; she [was] the king’s...
She was dear and pleasing to him. Living in harmonious union with her, the king dwelt performing meritorious deeds.

Then one day, after the queen had given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus right there at the royal palace, she took perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in the evening and went to the monastery to hear the Dhamma;
there she saw a virtuous man who was lying down, severely ill and near death.
Seeing the novice, she honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings; then, describing her own prosperity, she entreated him, saying, "Venerable sir, pray aspire to have me as your son.
He did not wish for it, yet she entreated him again and again. The novice, thinking that such being the case, he might thereby provide assistance to the Dispensation, [consented].

Having accepted the invitation of Sakka, and despite the celestial realm appearing before him through the sign of his future destination, he took rebirth in the womb of the queen who was traveling in a golden palanquin out of longing [for him].
After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son. They gave him the name Abhaya Gāmaṇī. Later on...

They gave him another name as well: Tissa. As Prince Gāmaṇi gradually grew up, he reached the age of sixteen and became skilled in the arts of elephant training, endowed with splendor, strength, and prowess.
Then King Kākavaṇṇatissa [appointed] Nandhimitta, Suranimmala, Mahāsena, Goṭhayimbara, and Theraputtābhaya—
Having placed these ten great warriors—Yo-bharana, Veḷusumana, Khañjadeva, Phussadeva, Labhiyya, and Vasabha—near his son, he had them reside there.
Their history of origin should be taken from the *Mahāvaṃsa*. The king bestowed upon the ten great warriors honors equal to those given to his own son.
He appointed Prince Tissa to protect the countryside and stationed him at Dīghavāpī.
Then one day, seeing the excellence of his own army and vehicles as he was departing for the village, the prince sent word to the king, saying, "I shall fight with the Damilas.
The king, wishing to protect his son, forbade him, saying, "Enough, O son; stay here. He sent word a second and even a third time, but the king [remained firm].
"Having become angry, fashion a golden chain and bind him; thus I shall guard him. Abhaya, having become angry with his father the king, fled and went to the Malaya region.
From that time on, because of his malice toward his father, the king became known as Duṭṭhagāmaṇī.
For the purpose of bringing his sons to the place of their quarrel, the king had the warriors take an oath.
Then King Kākavaṇṇatissa, having had sixty-four monasteries constructed, passed away after reigning for exactly sixty-four years.
When Prince Tissa heard that his father had died, he came from Dīghavāpi;
having performed the funeral rites for his father’s body, he took his mother and the elephant Kaṇḍula and fled to Dīghavāpi out of fear of his brother. The ministers—
Having assembled and reported that situation, they sent him into the presence of Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Tissa.
Having heard that message, he came to Bhuttasāla and dispatched messengers to his brother;
then, having come from there to Mahāgāma and received the consecration, he sent letters to his brother up to three times, requesting that he send his mother and the elephant Kaṇḍula.
Knowing his state of mind, he went forth for battle. The prince also, having prepared himself for war, went forth.
A great battle took place on the back of Cūḷaṅgaṇiya between the two brothers.
It is said that because those warriors had taken an oath, they did not become allies in their fight. At that time, [there were] many thousands of the king’s...
The people died. Having been defeated, the king fled, taking with him the minister Tissa and the horse Dīgha-tuṇika.
The prince pursued him closely from behind. Along the way, the monks constructed a mountain.
Seeing it, the prince realized it was the work of the Saṅgha of monks and turned back. The king, having fled, reached the ford of Jalamāla on the Kappaṇḍakara River.
"Go and eat," he said. The minister brought out food placed in a golden bowl and gave it to him.
The king, observing the time, thought, "I shall eat after giving to the Saṅgha. He then had the meal-time announced by dividing the food into four portions:
for the Saṅgha, for the minister, for the mare, and for himself. At that time, from Piyaṅgudīpa, there was a monk named Kuṭumbiya Tissa Thera.
Having arrived, he stood before him. When the king saw the Elder, his heart was filled with faith;
he placed the portion set aside for the Saṅgha and his own portion into the Elder’s bowl. The minister also placed his own portion into it, and the mare likewise desired to give.
Knowing her intention, the minister placed her portion as well into the bowl.
Thus the king gave the elder his full alms-bowl. The elder took the bowl and went, giving it to the elder named Gotama.
He fed five hundred bhikkhus and then filled the bowl again with the portions obtained from there;
he threw it into the air, and the bowl traveled and stood before the king. Tissa took the bowl, fed the king, and—
Then, having eaten himself, he fed Vaḷava. Then the king made his armor into a cushion and sent forth the bowl.
It traveled on and came to rest in the hand of the Elder.
The king returned again to Mahāgāma, assembled his army, took sixty thousand troops, and fought with his brother once more; at that time, for the prince—many...
A thousand men fell [in pursuit].
The prince fled, entered a monastery, and went into the house of a great elder.
The king, following closely behind, realized he had entered the monastery and turned back; afterwards, the elders...

The two brothers forgave one another. Then the king, having sent Prince Tissa to Dīghavāpi to oversee the agricultural works, himself also caused the proclamation of the drum to be made and carried out the farming operations.
Then, having shown favor to the great multitude and enshrined the relic in a spear, he went to Tissārāma surrounded by a powerful army and [addressed] the Saṅgha.
Having paid homage, he said, "Venerable Sir, I shall go beyond the Ganges to illuminate the Dispensation; give me a monk who will travel with me so that I may honor it.
The Saṅgha gave him five hundred monks. Taking the Saṅgha of monks, the king mounted the elephant Kaṇḍula and set out with his warriors.
Surrounded by a great army, he set out for battle and, having arrived at Mahiyaṅgaṇa, fought there with the Damilas and erected the Kañcuka Thūpa at Mahiyaṅgaṇa.
To explain the history of that stupa, this is the sequential account:
It is said that nine months after the Blessed One attained enlightenment, he came to this island and stayed on the bank of the Gaṅgā, which was three yojanas long and one yojana wide.

Having come to the Yakkha assembly in the Mahānāgavana park and standing in the air above those Yakkhas at the site of the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Thūpa, he terrified the Yakkhas with rain, wind, darkness, and so forth.
When they requested safety from him, he said: "I shall grant you safety; give me a place to sit together as a united group."
"Yakkhas, dear sir, we give this entire island to you. Grant us safety," they said.
Then the Blessed One, having dispelled their fear, spread out his leather mat upon the ground given by them;
sitting there, he attained the fire-kasina (tejokasiṇa) and caused the leather mat to blaze all around and expand. They were overwhelmed by the leather mat.
On all sides, as far as the ocean’s edge, [the mountains] had become a single mass;

the Blessed One, by the power of his supernormal might, brought the island named Giridīpa here, caused the *yakkhas* to enter it, and having placed the island back in its original location, he folded away his leather mat.
At that time, there was a gathering of deities. In that assembly, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma.
“There was a realization of the Dhamma for many millions of beings,
and countless others became established in the refuges and the precepts;
having attained the fruit of stream-entry on Mount Sumanakūṭaka,”
The deity Mahāsumana, having worshipped and questioned him, made his request; then,
having touched his head with hair that was dark and pure,
the Jina gave him from his own hand a handful of hair, the measure of which was the span of a hand.
Thus, taking that golden casket from the Teacher and placing it upon a heap of various jewels prepared at the place where he was seated,
he set his hair— seven cubits in height— upon it and covered it with a stupa of sapphire, and paid homage to it.
But when the Blessed One had attained parinibbāna, a certain elder named Sarabhū, a pupil of the Elder Sāriputta— the General of the Dhamma—
came surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, having taken a neck-bone relic from the funeral pyre;
he enshrined it in that very cetiya, covered it with stone slabs the color of clouds, and caused a stupa twelve cubits high to be built.
He departed. Then King Devānampiyatissa’s brother, named Cūḷābhaya, having seen that wonderful cetiya, had a cetiya thirty cubits high constructed.
Now, when King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya arrived at Mahiyaṅgaṇa, he subdued the Damilas there and, having caused a Kañcuka-cetiya eighty cubits high to be built, performed worship.
Thus, even while performing urgent work, those who are mines of virtue and possess wisdom perform meritorious deeds, fearing the rush of *saṃsāra*.
The Story of the Mahiyaṅgana Stupa 17.
Then the King, having fought with the Damilas and captured Chattadamila, [saw] many Damilas there...
Having slain [them], he arrived at Ambatittha and captured Ambadamiḷa within four months.
Then, descending [to the river], he captured Mahabbala and the seven Damiḷas in a single day.
After that, he captured Mahākoṭṭha at Antarasobbha, Gavara Damiḷa at Doṇagāma, Hālakola at Mahissariya, Nāḷika Damiḷa at Nāḷisobbha, and Dīghābhaya at Sagalla.
He captured Dīghābhaya the Daṃila. Then, at Kacchatittha, he captured Kiñcisīsa the Daṃila after four months.
Next, at Veṭhanagara, he captured Tāla the Daṃila; at Vahiṭṭha, Vahiṭṭha the Daṃila;
at Gāmaṇi, Gāmaṇi the Daṃila; at Kumbugāma, Kumbu the Daṃila; and at Naṇdikagāma, Naṇdika the Daṃila; and at Khāṇugāma...
At that time, in the village of Tambunna, two Damilas— maternal uncle and nephew—
were captured by Khāṇu. Hearing that "these people are killing their own kinsmen without knowing it was their own army," the lord performed an act of truth (saccakiriya) there.
"Effort for the sake of the pleasure of kingship—this has never been mine;
this is mine only for the establishment of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s dispensation.
By that truth, may my army and the equipment accompanying it [be protected]."
"Let it be like the color of a net"—thus it was exactly so at that time.
In this manner, the king had the Damilas slain on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Having been killed, they all returned and entered the city of Vijita.
Then, the king saw Naṇdimitta approaching to investigate whether he could capture the city of Vijita.
He released Kaṇḍula. When Kaṇḍula came to seize him, Nandimitta firmly grasped both its tusks with his hands, squeezed them, and forced it to sit down in a squatting position.
After testing both [the elephant and the horse], the king returned to the conquered city.
Then, a great battle between the warriors took place at the southern gate, while Veḷusumana [fought] the horse at the eastern gate.
Having mounted [the elephant], he slew many Damilas; the Damilas, having drunk [his blood] inside, closed the gate. Then the king dispatched his warriors:
Kaṇḍula-hatthi, Naṇdhamitta, and Suranimmala performed their duty at the southern gate, while Mahāsoṇa, Goṭhayimbara, Theraputtābhaya, and three others performed their duty at the other three gates.
That city was surrounded by a triple moat and possessed strong ramparts and gate-towers; it had iron doors.
Kaṇḍula, standing on his knees, broke through the stone, plaster, and bricks and reached the iron door.
Then the Damiḷas, stationed at the gate-tower, hurled various weapons, as well as red-hot iron balls and molten pitch, from the backs of elephants.
They threw him in. Then Kaṇḍula, tormented by pain, went to a body of water and plunged into it.
At that time, Goṭhayimbara said, "This is not a drinking of liquor; this is called the opening of the iron gate. Go, open the gate!
Hearing this, Jātābhimata let out a trumpeting cry, emerged from the water, and stood upon dry land. Then the elephant trainer—
Having washed the wound, he applied medicinal herbs. Then the king, having mounted his elephant and stroked the frontal globe with his hand,
gratified him by saying, "I give the entire kingdom of Laṅkā to you," and after feeding him choice food,
he bandaged the wound with a cloth, made it well-padded, and fastened a sevenfold buffalo hide upon the back of the armor.
Having bound a leather oil-skin over it, he released it; roaring like a thunderbolt, it went and pierced the threshold with its fangs and struck the door-jamb with its foot.
With a great roar, the iron gate fell to the ground along with its bars.
Then, seeing the building materials at the city gate falling from the backs of elephants, Nandimitta—
Striking with his arms, Kaṇḍula then overturned it and cast off the pain caused by the pressure of the fangs.
Thereupon, Kaṇḍula looked toward Nandhimitta for the purpose of mounting his back.
[Nandhimitta thought], "I will not enter by the path you have made," and so he struck with his arm against the wall eighteen cubits high, [leaping] a distance of eight usabhas.
Having caused a section of the wall to fall, he looked out as clear as a god;
he too, unwilling to follow the path made by him, leaped over the wall and fell inside the city. Goṭhayimbara, Soṇa, and Theraputtābhaya also each broke down a gate and entered from there.
Hatthigahetvā [took] a chariot wheel, Rathacakka-mitta a cart-fence,
Goṭha a coconut tree, Nimmala an excellent sword,
Mahāsoṇa a palmyra tree, and Theraputta a great medicine.

Having thus crushed the conquered city in four months and slain the Damilas, he then went to the place called Gariloka and captured the Damila Giriya.
From there, he went to the city of Mahela and, in four months, [captured] King Mahela.
Then the king, while proceeding toward Anurādhapura, encamped his army at a place called Paritōkāsa-pabbata;
having had a reservoir constructed there, he engaged in water-sports during the month of Jeṭṭhamūla.
Eḷāra, for his part, having heard that Duṭṭhagāmaṇi was approaching, consulted with his ministers and made the firm resolve: "We shall do battle tomorrow."
On the following day, having equipped himself for battle, Mahāpabbata mounted his elephant and set out, surrounded by a great army.
Gāmaṇī, too, after consulting with his mother, had thirty-two defensive enclosures constructed;
he stationed royal effigies holding parasols here and there, while he himself stood within the innermost enclosure.
Then, while the battle was raging, a great warrior of King Eḷāra named Dīghajānu took up his sword and shield,
rose eighteen cubits from the ground into the sky, severed the king’s form, and broke through the first military rampart;
having likewise broken through the remaining ramparts, he arrived at the military rampart standing upon the Great Jewel.
Then Suranimmala, seeing him approaching the king, announced his own name and reviled him.

Hearing this, Dīghajantu became enraged, thinking, "I shall kill him first," and having ascended into the air, he saw Suranimmala descending upon him and offered his own shield. The other [Dīghajantu] likewise struck him with his shield.
Thinking thus, he struck the shield. The other released the shield;
Dīghajantu, while cutting through the shield, fell to the ground. Suranimmala struck him with a spear;
at that moment Phussadeva blew his conch, which sounded like a clap of thunder, and the people became as if driven to madness. Thereupon, the Damila army broke.
Eḷāra fled, yet even then he caused many Damiḷas to be slain.
There, the water of the pond became turbid with the blood of those who were killed;

Having had the drum beaten there, King Duṭṭhagāmiṇī said,

Pursuing Eḷāra, he arrived at the southern gate;

Having made Laṅkā a single canopy of shade, he entered the city.

Having had [the offense] punished, he granted an exemption. Even today, kings do not have drums beaten upon reaching that place.

Phussadeva, while adjusting the king’s earring, drove an arrow into his mouth;

Having won the victory, the king returned to the city, had the arrow brought, and having had it set upright by its feather, he made a heap of kahāpaṇas equal to that measure.
