"There is war, O Great King," he said. When asked, "Now that a single kingdom has been established, what kind of war is there?
he replied, "I shall fight with the thieves that are the mental defilements (*kilesa*). The king repeatedly tried to dissuade him, but he likewise requested permission again and again.

Having received the king's consent, he went forth into homelessness. Practicing the work of insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* and came to be surrounded by five hundred disciples whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
Then the king, having beheld his great prosperity while reclining on his royal couch upon the terrace of his palace, recalled the destruction of his unshakeable army.
As he recalled it, a great fear arose within the king: "May this become an obstacle to my path to heaven.
At that time, the Arahants on Piyaṅgudīpa, knowing the king’s mental state, dispatched eight Arahants to comfort him.
Having arrived and announced their arrival, they ascended to the palace floor. The king, having paid homage to the elders and seated them on thrones, asked the reason for their visit.

The elders explained the purpose of their coming and, having made the king understand that such actions would create obstacles to heaven and liberation, they departed. Having heard their words, the king regained his composure.
Having paid homage to them (and dismissed them), he went to his royal bedchamber and thought again:
"My mother and father made us take an oath that we should never eat food without the Saṅgha;
has there been any food eaten without first giving to the community of monks, or not? While reflecting thus, through a lapse of mindfulness—
At the time of breakfast, he saw that only a single roll of pepper had been consumed without having first given any to the Saṅgha.
Upon seeing this, he thought, "I have acted improperly; I must perform a penance.

Then, when seven days of the auspicious *chatta* festival had passed, the king, with great royal majesty and a grand display of festivities, prepared to engage in water-sports, as was the custom for those who have been consecrated.
And for the purpose of observing the conduct of a king, he went to the Tissavāpī reservoir.
They placed all the king’s regalia, including his sandals and parasols, at the site of the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery.
There, at the location of the stupa, the king’s men set up the king’s spear together with the relic upright. The king spent the day there.
Surrounded by his harem, he played until evening had fallen and said, "We shall go to the city; raise the spear!
When the king’s men tried to take the spear, they were unable to move it. Seeing that marvel, the royal army gathered together and honored it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
The king, too, seeing this great wonder, was delighted at heart; having established a guard all around, he entered the city.
Then the king, having had a palisade constructed around it, had that cetiya enclosed and built a monastery.
The monastery was completed in three years. For the sake of the monastery festival, the king convened the Saṅgha;
one hundred thousand bhikkhus and ninety thousand bhikkhunīs assembled for that gathering, and there the king [addressed] the Saṅgha.
Having paid homage, he spoke thus: "Venerable sir, having forgotten, I consumed black pepper without the Saṅgha;
let there be a disciplinary act for me on that account. He said, "I have had a monastery built at Maricavaṭṭika with a shrine;
may the Saṅgha accept this 'shrine-monastery' (sacetiya-vihāra). Having poured out the water of donation, he gave the monastery to the community of monks.
He had a great pavilion constructed all around the monastery for the sake of seating the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
the pillars of the pavilion were established in the water of the Abhayavāpī pond. There was no other space remaining.
Having seated the Saṅgha there and given a great almsgiving for seven days, he presented all the requisites. There, by the senior elder of the Saṅgha...
The requisites he received were worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Thus:
"In battle and in giving, the hero among heroes, the third jewel..."
With a clear and pure mind, desiring to illuminate the Teaching,
that grateful king— beginning with the construction of the stupa—
erected great monasteries in order to worship the Triple Gem.
“Having relinquished here those priceless things for which wealth was sacrificed,
the remainder amounts to nineteen crores less one.
Thus, the wise man remains far removed from that which is hollow and essence-less.
Having transcended attachment to the body and wealth,
and having performed merit for the sake of attaining happiness,
one should constantly strive to grasp the essence.

Thereupon, the king thought: "The Elder Mahā-Mahinda has said this concerning my grandfather, King Devānampiya Tissa:
'Your great-nephew, O Great King, Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, [will build] a stupa with a golden garland a hundred cubits high.'"

He will have it built. Furthermore, thinking, "He will have a nine-storeyed iron palace built for the Sangha as its Uposatha hall," he looked around and saw a golden tablet inscription placed in a casket in the royal palace; having read it, [he learned]:
"In the future, after four hundred years have passed, Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, the son of Kākavaṇṇatissa..."
Hearing that he would have this and that built, he was thrilled and elated, and he clapped his hands, saying: "It seems the noble one has seen me as a great Mahinda!
Then, early in the morning, he went to the Mahāmeghavana, convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and said this:

"Venerable sirs, having constructed an Uposatha hall for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I shall build a palace like a celestial mansion; and having sent it to the world of the gods, I shall depict the form of the mansion on a cloth."
"Having had it written, give it to me. The Sangha dispatched eight arahants.

They went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and [beheld] a gabled palace twelve yojanas in height, forty-eight yojanas in circumference, adorned with a thousand [features], nine stories high, with a thousand chambers, produced by the power of the merit of the milk-ocean goddess, and situated in the sky.
Having gazed upon the Jewel Palace, they painted its likeness on a cloth with vermilion, brought it back, and presented it to the Saṅgha of monks;
the Saṅgha then sent it to the king.
Upon seeing it, the king was delighted in heart and subsequently had a bronze palace constructed that was identical to the painting. The commencement of the work.
At that time, he had eight hundred thousand pieces of gold placed at the four gates;
furthermore, at the four gates, he had a thousand bundles of cloth, as well as thousands of jars of molasses, oil, sugar, honey, and cakes, set out.
Having caused a drum to be beaten with the proclamation, "No groundless accusation shall be made against the palace," he [investigated] any groundless accusation that was brought forward.
Having had it appraised, he caused the builders to be paid their wages.
The palace was one hundred cubits by one hundred cubits on each side, and its height was likewise;
it had nine stories, and on each story there were one hundred gabled chambers, all of which were inlaid with jewels and surrounded by rows of golden bells.
Their gabled chambers were adorned with various jewels and featured coral railings;
their lotuses were likewise variegated with diverse gems. Similarly, there were thousand-pillared halls inlaid with various jewels and decorated with latticed windows.
Having heard of the celestial chariots of Vessavaṇa’s women, he had a jeweled pavilion constructed in the center in their likeness.
Thus, it was adorned all around with many jeweled pillars in the forms of lions, tigers, and other animals, as well as divine figures,
and encircled by a network of hanging pearls; its coral railings were of the same kind as previously described,
and in the center of the pavilion, variegated with the seven precious gems, there was a couch made of ivory upon a floor made of ivory.

The backrest was also made entirely of ivory; it was adorned here and there with golden solar discs, silver lunar discs, and pearl stars, as well as various lotuses and birth stories (*jātaka*) made of diverse gems according to their suitability, which were pleasing to the eye, and interspersed with golden creepers. Upon it was spread a costly coverlet.
Having spread out a beautiful rug, he placed a tooth-fan there. He had sandals made of coral.
Likewise, above the couch, upon a floor of wool, he had a white parasol made with a silver handle.
Therein, he had the eight auspicious symbols made of the seven precious gems interspersed among them, as well as rows of four legs made of jewels and pearls. At the edge of the parasol...
Rows of jeweled bells hung down from it.
There were four priceless and costly items: a palace, a parasol, a couch, and a pavilion.
Costly beds and seats were arranged there, and he had costly woolen blankets spread out as floor coverings. In the water-pot was a ladle.
And they were made entirely of gold. There was no need to mention anything regarding the other articles of use;
even the gateway-tower was surrounded by a captivating wall. However, because the palace was covered with copper and red stone, it became known as the "Copper Palace" (*Lohapāsāda*).
Having thus completed the palace, which was like the assembly hall of the gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he convened the Saṅgha. [The story of] Maricavaṭṭi.
The Saṅgha assembled like a gathering at a monastery. On the first stage, only worldlings (*puthujjana*) stood;

on the second stage, those versed in the Tipiṭaka; on the three stages beginning with the third, stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), and non-returners (*anāgāmin*) respectively;
and on the four higher stages, only those whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) stood. Having thus assembled the Saṅgha, [he led them] to the Saṅgha’s palace.
Having given [these], he offered a great almsgiving for seven days, as was done at the festival of the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery.
Regarding this, it is said: “For the sake of the palace, thirty koṭis were set aside by the king of great generosity, after setting aside those things that were priceless.”

Then one day, the king, having dispatched a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and performed a great worship of the Bodhi tree, was entering the city.
Seeing the stone stupa established at the site of the [Great] Stupa and recollecting the words spoken by the Elder Mahinda, he resolved, "I shall cause the Great Stupa to be built.
Having entered the city, ascended Mount Mahāntala, and partaken of excellent food, he went to his royal bedchamber and thought thus:
"While suppressing the Damilas, I have oppressed this world excessively."
"By what means indeed can we obtain bricks suitable for the Great Cetiya in accordance with the Dhamma and justice, without causing oppression to the world?
Having perceived that the King was thinking thus, the deity residing in the royal umbrella proclaimed: "The King has thought this!
Upon learning this, a great clamor arose throughout the world of the gods. Knowing this, Sakka, the King of Devas, addressed Vissakamma: "Dear son!"
"Vissakamma! King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya thought of the need for bricks for the Mahā Cetiya.
He sent [a messenger], saying: 'Go and, at a place one *yojana* from the city on the northern side, fashion bricks on the bank of the deep river and return.
Knowing this, the divine son Vissakamma came and fashioned bricks right there that were suitable for the Mahā Cetiya."
He went straight to the city of the gods. On the following day, a certain dog-hunter, taking his dogs, went into the forest;
wandering here and there, he reached that spot, but finding no bricks, he departed.
At that moment, a terrestrial deity, assuming the form of a large lizard, appeared before the hunter and his dogs in order to show him the bricks.
Having shown himself and being followed by them, he vanished after pointing out the bricks.
When the dog-catcher saw the bricks, he thought, "Our king wishes to build a stupa;
what a magnificent gift we have received! With a joyful heart, he returned early the next morning and [reported] the gift of bricks he had seen.
He reported this to the king. Having heard that message, the king was delighted; he had great honor shown to him and had that very same brick buried once again.
Then the king said, "I myself shall go to look for the brick; lengthen the spear."

At that very moment, they brought another report: at a place three *yojanas* from the city, on the northeast corner in the village of Ācāraviṭṭhi, while it was raining throughout the three watches of the night, golden seeds sprouted in an area measuring sixteen *karīsas*.
In size, the largest were one span (*vidatthi*) long, and the smallest were eight finger-breadths (*aṭṭhaṅgula*) long.
When the night had turned to dawn, the village dwellers, seeing the golden seeds, thought, "Aha!
What a treasure has appeared! They established a guard all around, filled a bowl with the golden seeds, and brought them to show them to the king.
The king, having accorded them due honor, appointed them as the very guardians of the gold.

Then, at that very moment, they brought another report. On the eastern side of the city, at a place seven yojanas away, in a district called Tambaviṭṭhi on the further bank of the Gaṅgā, copper had appeared.
Villagers came having filled their bowls with the copper and presented it to the king; the king, having caused them to receive honors appropriate to their merit, [continued].
They made them into cowherds.
Immediately thereafter, they brought another message.
At a place four yojanas ahead, at the southeastern corner, in the village of Sumanavāpi, many jewels—blue lotuses, kuruviṇḍas, and mixed gems—appeared; the villagers [filled] a bowl...
Having filled [the vessels] and returned, the Mānas showed them to the king. The king, having caused honor to be shown to them as well, appointed them as cowherds.

Immediately thereafter, they brought another message: "In the Ambaṭṭha-kola district, at a place eight yojanas to the south of the city, silver was produced in a certain cave; at that time, a resident of the city..."

A certain merchant, having gone to the Malaya region with many carts for the sake of turmeric, ginger, and other goods, unyoked his carts not far from a cave and climbed that mountain while searching for a wooden goad. There he saw a jackfruit tree;
on its trunk was a single jackfruit as large as a jar, which, when the stem was bent down, rested upon a stone surface below.
He stood there. Seeing that the tree was bent down by the weight of its fruit, he approached, touched it with his hand, and knowing it was ripe, he cut the stalk.
The jackfruit stem rose up and remained in its original position.
The merchant, thinking, "I will eat this after giving the first portion," called out the time. Then, four monks whose taints were exhausted arrived and stood before him.
They appeared. Seeing them, the merchant was delighted; he paid homage at their feet, had them sit down, and with an axe, cut around the stalks of the fruit, peeled away the rind, and removed it.
Juice flowed out from all sides and filled the pit where the rind had been set aside.
The merchant filled his bowl with the jackfruit juice, which was the color of water infused with lapis lazuli, and gave it to them. Those whose taints were exhausted...
Even as he was looking on, they rose up into the air and departed.
He called out for more alms; four other arahants arrived.
Taking the bowls from their hands as well, he filled them with golden-colored *samiñja* beans and gave them to them. Of these, three elders departed through the air, while the other...
The Elder named Indagutta, an arahant whose taints were exhausted, wishing to show him that silver, descended from the mountain above and sat down not far from that cave;

there he consumed the kernel of a jackfruit. When the lay devotee had departed, the Elder ate the remaining kernel himself, wrapped the leftovers in a bundle, and set out with it. On his way, he saw the Elder.
He gave him water and a branch for washing the bowl.
The Elder, having cleared a path leading from the entrance of the cave toward the vicinity of the cart, said, "Go by this path, lay follower.
Having paid homage to the Elder, he proceeded by that path; upon reaching the entrance of the cave, he looked all around at the cave.

Having seen that heap of silver, he took a lump of silver, cut it with a sword, and having ascertained its nature as silver, he took a large ball of it, went to the wagons, and stationed the wagons in a place well-supplied with grass and water.
He then went quickly to Anurādhapura, showed it to the king, and reported the matter; the king bestowed upon him the appropriate honor.

Immediately after that, they brought another message: "In a place five *yojanas* to the west of the city, on Mount Uruvelā, sixty pearls the size of large myrobalans, mixed with *pacāḷa* stones, have emerged from the ocean onto dry land, measuring as much as sixty cartloads.
When the fishermen saw them, thinking, 'Ah, what merchandise fit for a king has appeared,' they gathered them into a heap and established a guard over them."
Having given [the items], filled the vessel, and returned, they showed it to the king and reported the matter to him. The king also accorded them due honor as was fitting.

Again, another message was brought: "In a place seven yojanas from the northwestern corner of the city, at the edge of a sandbank in a ravine descending into the Peḷivāpi reservoir, there is a footprint the size of a *nisada* fish, four fingers long and two spans wide."
Four great jewels, the color of jasmine flowers, appeared. Then a certain dog-hunter named Matto, wandering there with his dogs, reached that place;

having seen them, he thought, "These are indeed treasures worthy of a king," and covering them with sand, he returned and informed the king. The king likewise accorded him the honor he deserved. Thus...
On the very day the king heard that bricks and other materials had been obtained for the construction of the stupa, it received its name from the place where the bricks and silver were produced. 20.
Then the king, having caused gold and other materials to be brought for the construction of the stupa, had them piled up in the treasuries.

Then, when all the materials were gathered together, O Visākha, on the full-moon Uposatha day under the Viśākhā constellation, they began the preparation of the ground for the construction of the Great Thūpa.
The King had the stone thūpa that had been erected at the site of the original thūpa removed;
and for the sake of stability, he had the ground excavated all around with an elephant-enclosure as its boundary and a depth of one hundred ratanas.
Having had the dust cleared away, he had the soldiers spread out sugar-stones and had them pounded with iron hammers until they were reduced to powder.
Then, having had the area trampled by great elephants with their feet bound in leather, he had fresh butter-clay spread over the stone pavement.
From the place where the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā fell, droplets of water rose up on all sides.
In an area measuring thirty *yojanas* where self-growing rice (*sayañjātasālī*) grows, that place is called the Ninti-sīsakoḷa forest because it is always moist.
There, the fine clay is called "butter-clay" (*navanītamattikā*).
Novices whose taints are exhausted fetch this from there; by means of it, one should know that the function of clay is fulfilled everywhere. Above the clay...
He had bricks laid down. Upon the bricks, he had a surface of hard plaster (*kharasuka*) applied; upon that, a layer of *kuruviṇḍa* stone; upon that, a network of iron;
upon that, fragrant *mārumba* flowers brought from the Himalayas by novice monks whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*);

upon that, a layer of milk-stone (*khīrapāsāṇa*); upon that, a layer of *eḷika*-stone; and upon that, he had the moral precepts (*sīla*) laid down. For all the work involving clay, only butter-clay (*navanītamattikā*) was used.
Upon the stone slab, he had a copper-iron plate eight finger-breadths thick laid down, which was made level by means of a liquid resin of wood-apple;
over that, he had a silver plate seven finger-breadths thick spread, which was leveled by means of emerald oil.
Having thus caused the ground to be prepared in every respect, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha, the king...

On that day, having assembled the community of monks, he spoke thus: "Tomorrow, on the full-moon Uposatha day under the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā, I shall establish the auspicious foundation stone at the Great Cetiya.
Tomorrow, let the entire Saṅgha gather at the site of the Thūpa.
He had a drum beaten throughout the city, [announcing]: "Let the great multitude, having observed the Uposatha and taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, assemble at the site of the Thūpa."
Then he commanded two ministers named Visākhasiri and Deva: "Go and decorate the site of the Mahā Cetiya.
They went there and had sand the color of silver plates strewn all around;
they scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient, raised plantain-leaf archways, set out full water-jars, and [fixed] a five-bannered flag upon a bamboo pole the color of jewels.
Having had it enclosed and having had various kinds of flowers, endowed with fragrance, strewn about, they adorned that place in many ways.
Then, at the break of dawn, the king had the entire city and the road leading to the monastery adorned;
he had barbers for shaving, bathers for washing, and those for providing ornaments stationed at the four gates of the city.
Having had variously colored garments, perfumes, garlands, and the like, as well as sweet meals complete with soups and condiments, prepared by the barbers, he had it announced by officials:
"Let all from the cities and the provinces come to the site of the Great Cetiya,
having had their hair and beards groomed as they please, bathed, eaten, and adorned themselves with clothes and ornaments."
He too, adorned with all ornaments and having become an observer of the Uposatha together with forty thousand men,
protected by ministers who were themselves many and beautifully decorated and adorned, surrounded by dancing women like celestial maidens,
like the King of the Gods surrounded by hosts of immortals, delighted the great multitude with his own glorious splendor.
While many musical instruments were resounding, he approached the site of the Great Thūpa in the afternoon.
For the sake of auspiciousness at the site of the Great Cetiya, he had one thousand and eight bundles of cloth placed there.
He had piles of cloth made on the four sides and also had oil, honey, sugar, molasses, and other items set out.
Then many bhikkhus came from various countries; from Rājagaha, the Elder Indigutta arrived through the air, taking eighty thousand bhikkhus with him;
likewise, from the Mahāvihāra at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī, the Elder Dhammasena arrived with twelve thousand bhikkhus; and from the Jetavana Vihāra in Sāvatthī, Piyadassi...
The Elder Nāma [brought] sixty thousand bhikkhus from the Great Forest at Vesālī;

the Elder Buddharakkhita [brought] eighteen thousand bhikkhus from the Ghosita Monastery at Kosambī; the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita [brought] thirty thousand bhikkhus from the Dakkhiṇagiri Mahāvihāra at Ujjenī; and the Elder Dhammarakkhita [brought] forty thousand bhikkhus from Pāṭaliputta.
From the Aśokārāma, the Elder Mittiṇṇa [brought] one hundred and sixty thousand bhikkhus from the kingdom of Gandhāra;
the Elder named Attiṇṇa [brought] two hundred and eighty thousand bhikkhus.
From Mahāpallavabhoga, the Elder Mahādeva [brought] four hundred and sixty thousand bhikkhus from the Yona kingdom.
From Alasanda city, the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita [brought] thirty thousand bhikkhus.

From the monastery at the entrance of the Viñjhā forest, the Elder Uttara [brought] eighty thousand bhikkhus. From the Mahābodhimaṇḍa monastery, the Elder Cittagutta [brought] thirty thousand bhikkhus.
And from the Vanavāsibhoga region, the Elder Caṇḍagutta [brought] eighty thousand bhikkhus. From Kelāsa...
From the Mahāvihāra, the Elder Suribhagutta took ninety-six thousand [monks] and went through the air.
Regarding all the monks dwelling on the island who had arrived,
no limit in number has been spoken by the ancients.
Of all the bhikkhus who had assembled together in that gathering,
those described as having exhausted their taints numbered ninety-six koṭis.
Then the Saṅgha, like a [circle] enclosed by a coral railing, stood facing one another in the center where the King’s seat was placed.
He stood there without striking [the drum]. On the eastern side, the Elder Khīṇāsava named Buddharakkhita stood, having taken with him five hundred Arahants whose names were identical to his own.

Likewise, on the southern, western, and northern sides, the Elder Khīṇāsavas named Dhammarakkhita, Saṅgharakkhita, and Ānanda stood, each having taken with him [five hundred] whose names were identical to their own.
Five hundred and fifty arahants stood [there], and the elder named Piyadassi, an arahant, stood at the northeastern corner taking the great community of bhikkhus with him.
It is said that as the king was entering the midst of the Saṅgha, he thought: "If the work on the cetiya being performed by me proceeds without obstacle..."

He reached the conclusion: "Let the elders named Buddhārakkhita, Cammarakkhita, Saṅghārakkhita, and Ānanda, each taking five hundred monks whose names are identical to their own, stand at the eastern, southern, western, and northern sides;
and let the elder named Piyadassi stand at the northeastern corner, taking the community of monks with him. The elders, too, [acted] according to the king's...
But the Elder Siddhattha, saying, "She stands thus, having understood his intention," stood facing the east,
surrounded by these eleven elders— Maṅgala, Sumana, Paduma, Sīvali, Caṇḍagutta, Sūriyagutta, Indagutta, Sāgara, Cittasena, Jayasena, and Acala—
and placing full water-pots before him.
Then the king, seeing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus standing thus, with a devout heart offered them perfumes, garlands, and other gifts;
having performed a circumambulation and paid homage at four places, he entered the hall of the full water-jar (*puṇṇaghaṭa*).
There, upon a golden pillar, stood a silver revolving staff, adorned and decorated on both sides by his well-born parents for the sake of good fortune.
Having had it measured by a minister’s son who was highly esteemed, he began to have a great circular terrace for the cetiya constructed.
However, while he was thus having it built, the Elder Siddhattha forbade him. It occurred to him:
"If the Great King constructs a large cetiya, he will die before it is finished, and in the future it will be difficult to maintain. At that moment—
"O Great King, the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus is great; it is fitting to do as the Elder says," he said.
Having understood the intention of the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus and thinking, "The Elder will do it," the King asked, "Venerable Sir, what kind of measurement shall I make?
The Elder replied, "Have a stupa-railing built from wherever I go," and so saying, he gave instructions.

Having entered [the city] by way of the gate, he departed. The king, having had a circular monument (*cetiyāvaṭṭa*) constructed for the Elder in the manner described, approached the Elder, asked his name, and honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.

After the king had circumambulated him and stood surrounding him, he approached the remaining eleven Elders, honored them, paid homage, and asked their names. Then, [he questioned] the staff-bearer who was wandering about...
The minister asked his son about them.
When the boy replied, "My lord, my name is Suppatiṭṭhita Brahmā," he asked, "What was your father's name?
Upon hearing, "His name was Naṇḍisena," he asked for the mother's name. When he heard, "Her name was Queen Sumanā," [he noted that] the names of all were considered auspicious.
Thinking, "The stupa work being performed by me will certainly reach completion," he became joyful; then the king,
having had eight golden jars and silver jars placed in the center, and surrounding them, had one hundred and eight full jars placed there.
Then he had eight golden bricks set up. Surrounding each of these, he had one hundred and eight silver bricks set up, and one hundred and eight cloths as well.
Then, having had a son of a minister named Suppatiṭṭhita-Brahma take hold of one golden brick, [he had others] with names identical to his, while still living...
Together with his parents and seven sons of his ministers, he caused the rest of the army of seventy thousand to be seized.
At that moment, an elder named Mittatthera placed a lump of fragrant paste upon the ground where a line had been drawn circling toward the eastern direction.
An elder named Jayasenatthera poured water over it, smoothed it down, and made it level.

On an auspicious lunar mansion, the Brahmā Suppatiṭṭhita first established the first set of eight auspicious objects in that place, which was thus fashioned with various kinds of auspicious benefits. The Elder named Sumanā honored it with *jātisumana* flowers.
At that moment, the great earth shook, bounded by the waters. In this same manner, the remaining sets of eight were also established.

Then the king, having established the *rajaṭiṭṭhaka* (the royal insignia), having honored [the Elder] with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and having completed the auspicious rites, had flowers placed in a golden casket.
He approached the Mahā-Buddharakkhita Thera, who was standing in front of the Saṅgha of monks on the eastern side;
having honored him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and having paid homage, he likewise [honored] the monks standing surrounding the Thera.
Having asked their names, he then approached the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita standing on the right side,
the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita standing on the rear side, and the Elder Ānanda standing on the left side;
having honored them with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and having paid homage by prostrating himself at the five points, he likewise asked their names and [stood] facing the northeast.
Having gone to Kaṇṇa, he paid homage to and made offerings to the Elder Mahāpiyadassi who was staying there; having asked his name, he stood in his presence.
The Elder, increasing his good fortune, taught the Dhamma to the king.

At the conclusion of that discourse on blessings, forty thousand among the assembly of householders who had gathered attained the state of Arahants, and forty thousand attained the fruit of Stream-entry. One thousand...
One thousand attained the fruit of once-returning; one thousand attained the fruit of non-returning; eighteen thousand monks, moreover, reached arahantship;
and fourteen thousand bhikkhunīs [reached the same].
This concludes the narrative concerning the Stupa.
21. Then the king, having paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, requested: "May the Saṅgha of bhikkhus accept alms from me until the Great Cetiya is completed.
The bhikkhus did not consent. Requesting again in due order, he obtained consent for seven days from the Upajjhāya-bhikkhus;
and at eighteen locations around the site of the Thūpa, pavilions were erected.
Having had it constructed and having seated the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he gave a great almsgiving for seven days;
providing oil, honey, molasses, and other medicinal requisites for everyone, he dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then, having caused a drum to be beaten in the city, he summoned all the bricklayers. They numbered about five hundred.
Among them, one said, "I am able to build the Great Cetiya after winning the King's favor," and he went to see the King.
The King asked, "How will you do it? He replied, "Your Majesty, having taken a hundred female slaves, I shall perform the work by clearing away one cartload of earth each day.
The King said, "If that is the case, it will be a mound of dust; there will be no grass, trees, or such things."
Thinking, "They will arise, but the duration [of my life] does not proceed," he warded that off.
Another said, "I take a hundred men and perform labor for one day, clearing away a single heap of dust.
Another said, "I perform labor for five measures of dust."
Another said, "I shall perform the work by exhausting two *ammaṇas* [of earth]. The king rejected him as well.

Then another wise man, a bricklayer, said, "O King, I am a mason; having pounded the earth with mortars, rolled it with rollers, and smoothed it with trowels, I shall exhaust one *ammaṇa* of dust in a single day, and taking a hundred workers, I shall perform the work.
The king accepted this, thinking, "In that case, there will be no need for grass and such at the Great Cetiya, and it will endure for a long time," and asked again: "But what shape will you make it?"
At that moment, the divine son Vissakamma took possession of the carpenter’s body.
The carpenter filled a golden bowl with water, took it in his hand, and struck the surface of the water.
A great bubble of water, like a jar of oil, rose up. "O God, I shall do such a thing," he said.
The king, accepting his words with the exclamation "Excellent!", gave him a pair of garments worth a thousand,
a golden ornament named Puṇṇaka likewise worth a thousand, sandals worth a thousand, twelve thousand kahāpaṇas,
and had a house and a field granted to him in a suitable location.
Then, during the latter part of the night, the king thought, "How indeed might I have bricks brought without oppressing the people?
The deity, knowing the king's thought, made it so that the bricks were exhausted at each of the four gates of the Cetiya one day at a time;
on that very night, they formed a heap of bricks. When the night had passed, the people saw it and reported it to the king. The king was pleased.
He appointed a carpenter to oversee the work. By this same method, the deities brought bricks every day until the completion of the Mahācetiya;
yet, in the place where the work was done during the entire day, neither clay nor brick-dust could be seen. At night, the deities made them disappear.
Then the King, for the sake of providing wages and materials for the laborers working on the Great Cetiya and for the fourfold assembly,
at each of the four gates provided sixteen thousand kahāpaṇas,

as well as clothing, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, oil, honey, drinks, the five pungent medicines, various kinds of soups and condiments, meals, rice-gruel, solid foods, and the eight kinds of permissible items.
Having had various drinks and five kinds of betel-leaf preparations for oral fragrance set out, he issued this command:
"Let householders or renunciants performing work at the Great Cetiya take what they desire according to their needs; do not give anything to those performing work who have not paid the price.
Then, one elder, desiring to be a companion in the construction of the Cetiya, [took] clay similar to that at the work site...

Having fashioned himself into a molded lump of clay, he took it with one hand and a garland with the other, ascended to the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, deceived the royal officials, and gave them to the carpenter. As the carpenter was receiving them, he realized they were not ordinary clay;
he looked at the Elder’s face, and upon discerning his expression, a great commotion arose there.
Gradually, having heard this, the king came and asked the carpenter: "Is it true, my man, that a certain bhikkhu gave you a lump of clay without any basis? He replied:
"For the most part, the masters come bringing flowers in one hand and lumps of clay in the other."
“Because of that, not knowing him, I assigned him to labor, thinking only this: ‘This one is a newcomer; this one is a resident.
“Therefore, show that elder to this man,” he said. He stationed an elderly man of strength near the carpenter.
When the carpenter returned, he showed the elder to the man of strength. Recognizing him, he informed the king.

The king gave him instructions: "When you have gathered three pots full of *jātisumana* buds into a heap in the courtyard of the Great Bodhi tree and set out perfumes, and at the time when the one who has gone to the courtyard of the Great Bodhi tree arrives, give the perfumes and garlands presented by the king for the purpose of honoring the visiting elder.
Following the king's directions, the soldier [did so] for that Bodhi...
When he went to the courtyard, he gave him that perfume and garland.
He too, being filled with joy, washed the stone seat, adorned it with perfume,
prepared a stone slab, and having offered flowers, prostrated at the four points and extended his joined palms at the eastern gate, [experienced] rapture.
Having offered a flower-pūjā, he stood there gazing [at it].
At that time, a soldier approached the elder, paid homage, and spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, the King intends to inform you that he has provided the funds for the lump of clay given to you for the purpose of assisting in the work on the cetiya."
"By worshipping yourself, you cause others to worship. Upon hearing this, the Elder was displeased.
The man said, "Venerable sir, let alone those three; even golden flowers as large as *sumana* buds do not equal the value of this lump of clay.
Venerable sir, please compose your mind," and with these words, he departed.
At that time, there was an elder living at the Piyaṅgalla Monastery in the Koṭṭhivāla district who was a kinsman of the bricklayer.
Having arrived and consulted with the bricklayer, he determined the dimensions of the bricks required for the long and thick construction;
then, having gone there, he himself carefully kneaded the clay, fashioned the bricks, fired them, and placed them in his bowl-bag.

Having returned after depositing [the brick], he took a brick for the king with one hand and a flower with the other, and gave the king’s brick together with his own brick. The mason took it and applied it to the work.
With a mind filled with joy and gladness, the Elder dwelt in the Iṭṭhakasāla Pariveṇa while performing the work on the Great Cetiya.
That deed of his became known. The king asked the mason: "My man, it is said that a certain nobleman gave us bricks without payment.
"It is true, Your Majesty; a certain nobleman gave us bricks, and they were brought into the work as being identical to our own," he replied.
When the king asked, "Do you recognize those bricks? he replied, "I do not recognize them, out of deference to my kinsmen."
The king, thinking, "If it is thus, give him to this man," stationed him as a soldier; he presented himself to that soldier just as before.
The soldier went to the monastery cell, sat down nearby, and having exchanged greetings, asked: "Venerable sir, are you a newcomer or a resident?
"I am a newcomer, lay follower. "In which kingdom do you live, venerable sir? "In the district of Koṭṭhivāla."
“Lay follower residing at Piyaṅgalla Vihāra, stay right here; do not go,” [the Elder said]. “We do not stay here;
we shall depart on such-and-such a day,” he replied. “Soldier, I too will come along with you. My village is also in this very province;
it is called such-and-such a village,” he said. “Very well,” the Elder accepted. The soldier reported this matter to the king.
The king had the horse trainer give the elder a pair of garments worth a thousand pieces,
a costly red woolen blanket, a pair of sandals, a tube of fragrant oil, and many other requisites for a recluse.
Having received these requisites, the trainer went to the monastery cell, stayed there with the elder for the night, and departed together with him at dawn.

Having traveled by stages until he reached a place where the Piyaṅgalla Monastery was visible, he had the Elder sit in the cool shade, washed his feet, anointed them with fragrant oil, and gave him water mixed with sugar to drink. Then, having fastened on his sandals, he said:
"These requisites were taken by me for the sake of the Elder who visits our family; I now give them to you. But as for this pair of robes—"
"This was taken for the auspicious blessing of my son; you should make it into a robe and wear it," he said, and placed it at the feet of the Elder.

The Elder placed the pair of cloths into his bowl-bag, made a bundle of the remaining requisites, put on his sandals, took up his staff, and set out on the road. The soldier walked with him for a short distance.
"Wait, venerable sir; this path belongs to me," he said, and then, in the same manner as previously described, he delivered the king’s message to the Elder.
Upon hearing it, the Elder became overcome with grief, thinking that the work accomplished with such great effort was as if never done;
shedding a stream of tears, he said while still standing, "Lay follower, take back your requisites yourself."
"He discarded all his equipment out of pride; what indeed can you say, venerable sir?
Even though this king gives requisites making the summit of existence (*bhavagga*) his limit, he is not able to act in accordance with your desires.
However, he has it built with the intention: 'I shall perform the work at the Mahācetiya in such a way that others have no share in it. But as for you, venerable sir..."
Having said, "Take the requisites you have obtained for yourselves and gladden your hearts," he instructed the Elder and departed.
There is no measure to the number of beings who, having performed work as wages at this cetiya and gladdened their hearts, were reborn in the heavenly realms.
It is said that when the goddesses reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven looked upon their own prosperity, they wondered, "By whom was what..."
Reflecting, "We have obtained this prosperity through our karma," and realizing that it was gained by performing work as service at the Great Cetiya,
they thought, "If such is the fruit even of work done as service, what will be the fruit of work performed with one's own resources out of faith?
Having thus reflected, they took divine perfumes and garlands during the night.
Having arrived and made offerings, they paid homage to the cetiya.
At that moment, the Elder Mahāsīva, who resided at Bhātivanka, had gone there to pay homage to the cetiya;
seeing them paying homage, he stood near the Mahāsattapaṇṇi tree and, after they had finished their homage as they pleased, he questioned them as they were about to depart.
“By the light of your bodies, the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi has become one vast light. What work did you perform? “Venerable sir, we have no work of our own;
rather, having inspired confidence in this cetiya, we performed work as hired laborers,” they said.
Thus, even work performed as hired labor with a mind of faith in the Buddha’s teaching yields great fruit. Therefore—
“Knowing that ‘By the mere clarity of mind toward the Sugata, the highest state is attained,’ the Buddha performed worship at the stupa.
Thus, while having the construction of the cetiya carried out, the king completed the three flower-offerings. That was for the sake of the stability of those whose taints were exhausted.
Having leveled it with the ground, they caused it to sink; in this manner, they caused it to sink nine times as it was repeatedly built up.
The king, not knowing the reason for this, became displeased and convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Eighty thousand bhikkhus assembled.
Having honored the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and having paid homage, the king asked: "Venerable sirs, regarding the three flower-offerings at the Mahācetiya..."
"Even after nine times, we do not know," the Saṅgha of bhikkhus said. "Great King, there is no obstacle to your work or to your life.
This [collapse] was caused by those possessing psychic power for the sake of future stability; from now on, they will not cause it to collapse.
Without allowing any alteration, complete the Great Thūpa. Having heard this, the king was delighted and carried out the work on the Thūpa.
The ten flower-vases were completed with ten crores of bricks.
When the three flower-vases had been finished, the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus commanded two novices named Uttara and Sumana, both of whom were Arahants with taints destroyed:
"Build for me each a stone palace, square and symmetrical, eight cubits thick, eighty-eight cubits in height, and adorned with the six colors."
"Bring them," he said. Having assented with "Very well," they went to Uttarakuru and,
having brought stones of the color of fat in various sizes and shapes resembling *bhaṇḍi* flowers, they spread one stone upon the floor of the relic chamber,
arranged four stones at the four corners, and [placed] another in the eastern direction for the purpose of closing the relic chamber.
They placed it near the sand wall, making it invisible.
Then the King had a Bodhi tree made of every kind of gem, endowed with every excellence and captivating to the mind, erected in the center of the relic chamber;
for it was established upon a floor of sapphires, and its roots were made of emeralds.

The trunk was eighteen cubits high and made of silver, variegated with the eight auspicious symbols beginning with the *śrīvatsa*, as well as rows of flowers, rows of creepers, and rows of four-legged birds and swans.
Its five great branches were also eighteen cubits long;
its leaves were made of jewels, pale yellow leaves were made of gold, and [other] leaves were made of silver.
The fruits were made of coral. Likewise, he had a cloth canopy fastened over the sprouts.
At its edges, on all sides, a network of pearl bells hung down. Rows of golden bells and golden garlands hung here and there.
At each of the four corners of the canopy, a single cluster of pearls worth nine hundred thousand [pieces of gold] hung down.
Therein, lotuses were manifested in various precious gems according to their respective forms, including the shapes of the moon, the sun, and the stars.
Costly cloths of many colors, numbering one thousand and eight, hung down.
Then, having had railings made of the seven precious gems constructed all around the Bodhi tree, he had them spread with great myrobalan and pearls.
Between the pearl railings, he had rows of full jars made of the seven precious gems placed, filled with scented water.
In those [rows], the golden jars had flowers made of coral; the coral jars had flowers made of gold;
the gem jars had flowers made of silver; the silver jars had flowers made of gems; and the jars made of the seven precious gems...
The flowers were made of the seven precious gems.
To the east of the Bodhi tree, upon a gem-encrusted throne worth a koti, she had a golden image of the Buddha seated on a thickly paved couch.
The twenty nails of that image and the white parts of its eyes were made of crystal.
The palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, the coverings of his tusks, and the red parts of his eyes were made of coral;
his hair and eyebrows, as well as the dark parts of his eyes, were made of sapphires; and his fine body hair was made of silver.
Then Sahampati Mahābrahmā stood holding a silver parasol over him. Thereafter, in the two worlds of the gods...
He depicted Sakka, the king of the gods, together with the deities, holding the Vijayuttara conch and bestowing anointment;
and the divine son Pañcasikha, playing the *beḷuva-paṇḍu* lute as a musician;
and the Great Black Nāga King, surrounded by Nāga maidens, praising the Tathāgata with various sounds of hymns.
Having fashioned a thousand arms reaching for Vāsava, and having seized various weapons such as tridents and clubs,

he caused [Māra] to mount the back of the elephant Girimekhala with a thousand jars, surround the Māra-force, and come to the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) while manifesting many terrifying sights.
In the other directions, in the eastern quarter, there was a peak resembling a cross-legged throne (pallaṅka).
Having had three couches worth ten million pieces of gold spread out, he had a ivory staff and a coral fan placed there.
Having made the trunk of the Bodhi tree the headboard, he had a silver bed worth ten million pieces of gold and adorned with various jewels spread out.
For seven days, the place where the One of Ten Powers gazed at the Bodhi throne with an unblinking eye after attaining full enlightenment [was likewise honored].
The place where he walked upon the Jewel Walk; the place where he looked out from the Jewel Walk for seven days;
the place where, having entered the Jewel House, he sat reflecting on the Dhamma; the place where he went to the root of the Mucalinda tree and sat down;
and the place where the Naga Mucalinda, having encircled him seven times with his coils and spread his hood over him, stood guard. From there...
[The account of] going to the root of the Ajapāla banyan tree and the place where he sat;
then, when food was brought, [the account of] having the bowl accepted by the Four Great Kings at the Rājāyatana tree;
then, the Brahmā’s entreaty, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the going forth together with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and the going forth of the Bhaddavaggiya group.
The taming of the matted-hair ascetic Triśaṅku, the visit to Bimbisāra in the Laṭṭhivana grove, the entry into Rājagaha, the acceptance of the Veḷuvana monastery,
and the ordination of eighty great disciples; thereafter, the journey to Kapilavatthu, the place where he stood upon the Jewel Walk,
the renunciation of Rāhula, the renunciation of Nanda, the acceptance of the Jetavana, and [the events] at the foot of the Gaṇḍamba tree.
In the world of the gods, he performed the Twin Miracle.
According to some accounts, while seated there,
he delivered the Abhidhamma teaching, performed the miracle of the Descent from Heaven, and presided over the assembly for the Elder’s Questions.
Likewise, the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Rāhulovāda Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Pārāyana Sutta, the Samāgama, the taming of Dhanapāla,
Āḷavaka, Aṅgulimāla, and Apalāla; the relinquishing of the life-faculty (āyusaṅkhāra), the partaking of sūkaramaddava, the acceptance of the pair of Siṅgivaṇṇa robes,
the drinking of clear water, the Parinibbāna, the lamentation of gods and men, and the Elder Mahākassapa’s prostration at the feet of the Blessed One.
He had the cremation of the Teacher’s body performed with fire, the funeral rites at the pyre, and the distribution of the relics carried out by that same brahmin.

Likewise, he had five hundred and fifty Jātakas carved. While having the Vessantara Jātaka carved, however, he had Sañjaya the Great King, Phusatī the Queen, Maddī the Queen, Prince Jāliya, and Kaṇhājina carved. Then, Paṇḍava...
The gift of the elephant; the great gift of seven hundred [attendants]; the inspection of the city; the gift of the *siṇdhava* (sindhic) horses;

the carrying of the chariot by deities due to the praise of Rohitassa; the gift of the chariot; taking fruit himself from a tree that bent down of its own accord and giving honey and meat to the children;
and the gift of a golden needle to the hunter while in the guise of a renunciant on the slopes of Vaṅka Mountain.
The site of the dwelling; the gift of children to the worshipper; the gift of a wife to the Brahmin Sakka;
the place where the worshipper, having taken the two children by the power of a deity, went before King Sañjaya;
from there, the gathering of the six Khattiyas in the interior of Vaṅka Mountain; the consecration of Vessantara and Maddī; and the place where he entered the city.
He described in full detail the place where the rain of the seven treasures fell, the place where he was reborn in the Tusita heaven after passing away from there,
the place where the deities of ten thousand world-systems entreated him to become a Buddha,
his irreversible descent into the mother’s womb, Queen Mahāmāyā and King Suddhodana, and the place where he was born in the Lumbinī grove from the sky.
He caused [the following to be depicted]: the falling of two streams of water; his taking seven steps facing north;
the Great Man’s footprint remaining upon the head of Kāḷadevala’s matted locks; the shadow of the Jambu tree never passing beyond the spot where he stood;
and the place where, having seen the negligence of the nurses, he sat cross-legged on a glorious couch and attained meditative absorption (jhāna).
Then he caused Rāhula’s mother and Rāhula himself to perform auspicious rites.
Thereafter, at the age of twenty-nine, while on his way to the pleasure garden for recreation, he saw three divine messengers reckoned as the aged, the diseased, and the dead;
on his fourth visit, seeing the form of one who had gone forth at the place where he turned back, he conceived the thought, "Excellent is this going forth," and proceeded to the pleasure garden.
Having enjoyed the splendor of the pleasure grove, at the time of evening twilight, having bathed and sat down upon the auspicious stone slab,
he rose from his place of adornment; then, at midnight, seeing the disorder of the dancers,
he mounted the noble horse Kaṇṭhaka and departed for the Great Renunciation, accompanied by the deities of the ten thousand world-systems.
He described the ritual of worship at the site of Kaṇṭhaka’s turning back, his renunciation on the bank of the river Anomā, his entry into Rājagaha, his reclining on Mount Paṇḍava,
his request for King Bimbisāra to rule the kingdom, his acceptance of the milk-rice porridge offered by Sujātā,
his consumption of the porridge on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, and the distribution of the remaining porridge across the river.

He related in full detail the miracle at the Sāla grove, the place where he went for his midday rest, the acceptance of the *kuśa* grass offered by Sotthiya, and the place where he sat after ascending the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Then he had it performed for the seven who arrived together, headed by the Elder Mahinda. In the four directions, [men] stood with swords in their hands.
He had the four Great Kings made; then the thirty-two sons of the gods; then thirty-two divine maidens holding golden-staffed lamps;
then the twenty-eight yakṣa generals; then the deities standing with palms joined in reverence;
then the deities standing holding clusters of jewel-encrusted flowers; and then those holding golden jars.
Then there were deities of stability; then deities of dance; then deities of instrumental music;
then deities standing holding mirrors ten cubits in size, each worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold];
then deities standing holding flowering branches, each worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]; then deities standing holding the lunar disk, and the solar disk.
Then the deities standing holding lotuses; then the deities standing holding parasols;
then the sons of the Malla deities wearing variegated garments; then the deities standing holding cloth-wrappings;
then the deities standing holding jeweled censers; then the deities standing holding wheels of Dhamma; then...

He had deities made as sword-bearers, and deities standing with golden bowls upon their heads—each bowl the size of five hands, filled with scented oil, and containing a blazing lamp wrapped in fine linen cloth.
Then, at the four corners [of the pavilion], he placed four large gems atop crystal pillars. At the four corners, he established these.
He had four heaps made of gold, gems, pearls, and diamonds; then he had lightning streaks fashioned upon a cloud-colored stone wall;
then jeweled creepers; then chowries; and finally, having taken blue lotuses, he had figures of nāgas fashioned holding them.
The king had single coins made of solid gold for the pavement; he also had the remainder of the ritual offerings made entirely of the seven precious gems.
Furthermore, the articles worthy of worship mentioned here were infinite and immeasurable;
for instance, the Elder Cittagutta, who resided at Ambapāsāna, [saw] twelve [monks] assembled below the Lohapāsāda.
While preaching the Dhamma to a thousand bhikkhus, having begun with the Rathavinīta Sutta, he paused his discourse and spoke,
suspecting that some would not believe him as he was extolling the great relic treasure. At that moment, the Elder Mahātissa,
a dweller of Koṭapabbata who was an arahant, sat nearby listening to the Dhamma and said, "Friend Dhamma-preacher..."
"There is something lacking in your account," he said. "As a descendant, speak in detail.
Then, on this very island, there was a great king named Bhātiya who was devoted to the Buddha’s teaching;
every evening and morning, he would eat only after paying homage to the Mahācetiya. One day, while sitting in the court of justice, as he was deciding a difficult legal case, it became too late.
Having risen from his seat, he forgot to pay homage to the stupa. When food was brought to him, he reached out his hand and asked the people, "Did I pay homage to my grandfather today, or not?
For ancient kings used to address the Teacher as "grandfather.
The people replied, "You did not pay homage, O Lord."

At that moment, the king dropped the morsel of food he was holding in his hand into his bowl, rose up, had the southern gate opened, and having arrived, ascended the Great Cetiya courtyard by the eastern gate.
While paying homage, he heard the sound of the recitation of the Dhamma by the Arahants within the relic chamber; thinking it was coming from the southern gate, he went there.

Having seen this, and having gone to the other doors in the same manner, not seeing [the relic] there either, and thinking that the noble ones were wandering about reciting the Dhamma, he stationed men at the four gates for the purpose of watching. Having himself wandered about again and still not seeing it, he questioned the men;
knowing from them that it was not outside, he concluded that it must be inside the relic chamber.
Having made this resolution, he lay down near the eastern gate facing the Great Cetiya, stretching out his hands and feet, having renounced life and made a firm vow:
"If these noble ladies do not cause me to behold the Relic Chamber, I shall remain without food for seven days;
though I wither away like a handful of dust scattered upon the ground, I shall not rise. As he—
Through the power of his virtues, Sakka caused the palace to appear as if on fire.
Sakka, reflecting upon this and understanding the cause, did not go there himself, but spoke thus to the elders who were reciting the Dhamma:
"Venerable sirs, this righteous king, who has faith in the Buddha’s teaching, heard the sound of the recitation in this place and [went] to the relic chamber."
Having made a firm resolve, "I shall not rise until I have seen [it]," he lay down;
if he does not see the relic chamber, he will die right there. "Bring him in and let him look upon the relic chamber," they said.
Out of compassion for him, the elders commanded one elder to bring the king and show him the relic chamber. Having brought the king in, they had him look upon the relic chamber.

"Send him back," [the king said]. He took the king by the hand, led him into the relic chamber, and after having him pay homage as he pleased, sent him back once everything had been observed. Later on, the king returned to the city;
having had portions of the images seen by himself in the relic chamber decorated with gold, he had a great pavilion constructed in the royal courtyard, and within that pavilion...
Having had those images fashioned and assembled in the city, he said, "Such golden images as these were seen by me in the relic chamber.
Because they were made according to the proportions of those [original] images, they became known as "proportional images" (*niyāmaka-rūpaka*).
Year after year, the king had those images brought out and showed them to the citizens; this was the first time.
At the time it was revealed, the citizens were filled with faith; they brought forth one boy from each family and ordained them.

Again, the King, thinking, "There are many who do not know this matter, O Noble Ones, and I shall inform them as well," went to the monastery, assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus beneath the Lohapāsāda, and having himself taken his place on the Dhamma-seat, [remained] in the Dhātugabbha throughout the three watches of the night.

Having explained the introductory section, he rose even before he was able to conclude it. Thereupon, one bhikkhu asked the king: "Great King, you arrived after having already eaten your morning meal.
Having spent three watches of the night expounding [the Dhamma], you were not even able to finish the ritual for worshipping the relic chamber; is there much more to be said?"
"What shall the king say, venerable sir? What I have described to you does not even equal one-tenth part [of what is there].
I spoke only of what I had personally observed. Venerable sir, the arrangement of offerings within the relic chamber is infinite.
Thus he said; the articles worthy of worship are infinite, filling each of the eighty cubit-long sides of the square [chamber].
It would not have been easy to fill the relic chamber even continuously, let alone to arrange everything there appropriately;
indeed, let alone the relic chamber, it would have been impossible to fill even the area bounded by the sand rampart of the Great Cetiya continuously.
Therefore, as for how all those objects worthy of worship were brought there, what needs to be said has already been stated by the ancients.

It is said that the Elder Mahāsīva, who was well-versed in the three Piṭakas and possessed a straight back, sat in the royal palace and, while explaining to the king how he had heard the lion’s roar of the Ten-Powered One, described the enshrining of the relics and concluded the discourse. The king spoke thus to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, this relic chamber is perfectly square; from each side, it measures eighty cubits."
"Who will believe that such venerable treasures are kept here? the Elder asked. "Have you ever heard before, sir, how large the Indasāla Cave is?
the King replied, "Venerable sir, it is about the size of a small couch.
Then the Elder said, "Great King, on the day our Teacher delivered the *Sakkapañha Sutta*, how large was the assembly gathered in the cave?"
"‘Osaṭā’ means ‘previously heard. "Venerable sir, I have heard that there are deities in two worlds of the gods," the king said.
When the Elder asked, "If that were so, O Great King, would you not believe even that? the king replied, "But that was due to the supernatural power of the gods;
for supernatural power, venerable sir, is indeed inconceivable."
Then, O Great King, the Elder became [invisible] by means of that very power of the gods (*deviddhi*).

He said, "This, however, has arisen through these three types of supernormal power (*iddhi*): the king’s royal power (*rājiddhi*), the gods’ divine power (*deviddhi*), and the noble ones’ noble power (*ariyiddhi*).
The king, accepting the Elder’s words with the exclamation "Excellent!", honored the Elder with a white parasol and held the parasol over his head.
Having brought [the relics] to the Mahāvihāra, he again offered a parasol to the Mahācetiya for seven days and performed an offering of jasmine flowers.
To establish this very point, many other instances have been shown; let those suffice, as we remain indifferent to them here.
Furthermore, in this case, the king was one of great influence and power, who had fulfilled the perfections and made his formal resolve.
By virtue of that [work], the majesty of the gods is to be understood; for it was fashioned by the divine son Vissakamma, commanded by Sakka, having been infused from the very beginning.

By virtue of that, the supremacy of the gods is to be understood. The Elder Indagutta, who presided over the work, performed it by following even the minor and lesser details of the construction; and not only the Elder, but all the Noble Ones as well did so.
It should be understood that they applied themselves with diligence to the duties to be performed by each individually through these three kinds of psychic power (iddhi).
For this was said in the Mahāvaṃsa:
"The great elder Indagutta, possessed of the sixfold direct knowledge (chaḷabhiñña) and great wisdom..."
"The one who presides over karma has here ordained all this:
all this by means of royal power, by the power of deities, and by the power of the Noble Ones; it stands established without obstruction."
23. Discourse on the Description of the Relic Chamber and its Adornment:
Thus, having completed the work to be done in the relic chamber, the king went to the monastery on the fourteenth day and convened the community of monks;
those assembled were thirty thousand monks. The king [addressed] the community of monks...
Having paid homage, he spoke thus: "The work that was to be done by me in the relic chamber is finished;

tomorrow, on the Uposatha day of the Āsāḷha month under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation, the enshrinement of the relics will take place. 'Venerable sirs, please look after the relics,'" he said, entrusting the responsibility to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and returned to the city itself.

Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, searching for a bhikkhu to fetch the relics, saw a novice named Soṇuttara who was sixteen years of age, possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā), and residing as a worshipper in the Pariveṇa; having summoned him, they said:
"Friend Soṇuttara, the King, having completed the relic chamber, has made the task of bringing forth the relics a burden for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"Therefore, you must bring the relics. "Venerable sir, from where shall I obtain the relics? he asked.
The community of monks said to him: "Friend Soṇuttara, while the Tathāgata was lying on his deathbed, he addressed Sakka, the king of the gods, saying:
'Of my bodily relics, which amount to eight *doṇas*, one *doṇa* has been honored by the King of the Koliyans.'"
He said, "In the future, it will be established at the Mahācetiya on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Then, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the brahmin Doṇa divided the relics into eight portions and gave them to the inhabitants of eight cities.
They each had a cetiya constructed in their own city and maintained it; among those, [the portion] in Rāmagāma was [received] by the Koḷiyas.
When the Katacaitya was broken by a great flood, the relic casket entered the ocean and came to rest upon a bed of jewel-sand, overspread with six-colored rays of light.
When the nāgas saw this, they went to the Mañjerika nāga abode and informed King Mahākāḷa; he [sent] ten koṭis...
Surrounded by a thousand *nāgas*, he arrived, paid homage with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings,
and raised banners of gold, coral, crystal, and silver. Amidst the playing of five-fold musical instruments and various *nāga* dances,
he placed the relic casket (*dhātughaṭikā*) in a jeweled box, took it upon his head, and leading it back to the *nāga* realm while performing great honor and veneration, brought it there.
Having honored the relic with ninety-six crores of wealth and having constructed both the stupa and the stupa-shrine with all kinds of jewels, he maintained the relics.

While the Elder Mahākassapa was enshrining the relics for Ajātasattu, he deposited the relics at Rāmagāma and brought the remaining relics to present them. The King asked, "Why were the relics not brought from Rāmagāma?"
The Elder said, "Great King, there is no obstacle for them; they will be established in the future at the Mahācetiya in Tambapaṇṇidīpa.
King Asoka, the Dhamma-king, having opened the deposit of relics and looking within, did not see the eighth measure of relics;
he asked, "Venerable sir, where is another measure of relics? [The Elder replied: "Great King, it is in the cetiya built by the Koḷiyas on the bank of the Gaṅgā."
Once it was firmly established, when the stupa was broken by a great flood, it entered the great ocean.

Seeing it, the *nāgas* took it to their own *nāga*-abode and preserved it; thus spoke those whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "Great King, my *nāga*-abode is the place where my commands are carried out;
I shall bring that too, Venerable Sir," he said. "Great King, those relics in the future..."
“They will establish [the relics] at the Mahācetiya on the island of Tambapaṇṇi,” they said, and thus they prevented him.
Therefore, Mañcherika, go to the Nāga abode, inform the Nāga king of this matter, and bring back the relics; tomorrow the relic treasury will be established.
Soṇuttara, having accepted with “Very well,” went to his own cell.
The King, too, having entered the city, caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: "Tomorrow there will be the enshrinement of the relics;
let the citizens, having adorned themselves according to their respective means and taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, descend upon the courtyard of the Great Cetiya.
Sakka, for his part, commanded Vissakamma: "Tomorrow there will be the enshrinement of the relics at the Great Cetiya."
"May you adorn the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi! On the following day, he leveled the island of Tambapaṇṇi, which was nearly eighty *yojanas* in extent, making it as even as the full orb of the moon;
he covered it with sand resembling silver plates and filled it with clusters of five-colored flowers.
He had rows of full water-jars placed all around, enclosed the area with cloths, and spread a canopy of fine cloth above.
Having bound them to the surface of the earth, he displayed land-lotuses upon the ground and hanging lotuses in the sky, arranging it like the adorned assembly hall of the gods.
He also caused the great ocean to appear as if still and covered with five kinds of lotuses.
By the power of the relics, the entire Cakkavāḷa was made to appear as if prepared for the occasions of the descent into the womb, the enlightenment, and so forth.
The citizens of the city, having swept the streets and strewn them with sand like pearls, scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient,
hoisted banners and flags of various colors, and adorned [the city] with golden jars, plantain arches, garlands, and flower-stands,
prepared the city for the festival. At the four gates of the city, the King [provided for] those who were destitute...
For the enjoyment of the people, he had various kinds of hard and soft foods, perfumes, garlands, clothing, ornaments,
the five kinds of betel-leaf preparations, and betel leaves set out. Then the king, adorned with all his ornaments,
mounted his excellent chariot yoked to four thoroughbred Sindhu horses, which were the color of white water-lilies.
Placing an adorned, musth-elephant in front and holding a golden vessel upon his head,
he stood beneath a white parasol. At that moment, thousands of female dancers resembling celestial maidens, adorned with various ornaments like the nymphs of the gods,
as well as the ten great warriors and the fourfold army, [surrounded him].
They surrounded the king.
Likewise, one thousand and eight women, carrying full water-pots, surrounded him.
One thousand and eight men and one thousand and eight women, each measuring a sarasapramāṇa [in height], carried flower-caskets and staff-lanterns.
They surrounded him, taking up banners of various colors. Thus the King, with great royal majesty, set out for the Nandana Grove like a king of the gods.
At that time, with the sounds of various musical instruments and the rattling of elephants and chariots, it was as if the great earth were being split asunder.
At that moment, Soṇuttara, sitting right in his own cell, learned from the sound of the musical instruments that the king had departed.

He entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and by means of his resolve, he submerged into the earth and appeared before the Great Black Nāga King in the Mañjerika Nāga realm. Upon seeing Soṇuttara, the Nāga King—
Rising from his seat, having paid homage, washed their feet with scented water, and honored them with flowers endowed with color and fragrance,
he sat down to one side and asked, "Venerable sirs, from where have you come? When they replied, "We have come from the island of Tambapaṇṇi," he asked, "For what purpose?"
Great King, while King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya was having the Mahācetiya constructed, he entrusted the relics to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
About thirty thousand bhikkhus assembled at the Mahāvihāra;
the relics deposited for the purpose of enshrining them in the Great Thūpa were placed in the presence of King Mahākāḷanāga, who reported this matter to him.
"Having spoken thus, they sent me, saying, 'Bring the relics,' and therefore I have come here," he said.
Upon hearing this, the Naga king, as if overwhelmed by a mountain and overcome by great dejection of mind, thought:
"We believed that by honoring these relics we would be released from the states of misery and reborn in heaven."
"But this bhikkhu possesses great psychic power and great majesty;
if these relics were situated in this place, he would be able to take them away even by overcoming us. It is fitting to remove the relics," he thought.
Looking at the assembly, he saw his own nephew named Vāsula-datta standing at the edge of the crowd, and [addressed] him...
Having understood his maternal uncle’s intention, he gave him his consent; then, having gone to the Cetiya-house,
he took the relic casket, swallowed it, and went to the foot of Mount Sineru—
a mountain that is one hundred yojanas in circumference and three hundred yojanas in height.
Having extended his many thousands of hoods, that one of great psychic power,
smoking and blazing at the foot of Mount Sineru,
lay down upon the sandy ground with his coils folded.
Having had many thousands of snakes, similar to himself,
constructed, he had them laid down, surrounded on all sides;
then many gods and nāgas descended there.
"We shall fight both of these elephants.
Then, the Naga King, having learned from his nephew that the relics had been removed, spoke thus:
"The relics are no longer in my possession. Without making any delay here, go quickly and report this matter to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus."

Thinking, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus will seek the relics elsewhere," the novice, from the very beginning, spoke of the arrival of the relics and urged him, saying, "The relics are right here with you; give them without delay.
Then the Nāga king, realizing that the novice had grasped the matter by the root, [thought], "By whatever means possible, the relics..."
Thinking, "It is proper to send him away without giving anything," he led the novice to the Relic Chamber and showed him both the Cetiya and the Cetiya-house.
That Cetiya and Cetiya-house were made entirely of all kinds of jewels.
For it is said in the Mahāvaṃsa:
“Behold, O monk, this well-constructed shrine and shrine-house, beautifully fashioned from many various jewels.
Having thus shown it, he descended from the shrine-house and stood upon a coral lotus on the Half-Moon Rock. Then, regarding him—
"Venerable sir, please determine the value of the cetiya and the cetiya-hall," said the novice. "We are unable to determine the value, Great King;
even all the jewels on the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi are not worth this crescent-shaped stone," he replied.
The Nāga king thought: "If this is so, it is improper to take the relics from a place of such great honor to a place of little honor."
"Is it not so, O Bhikkhu? he asked. The novice replied: "O Great King, those called Buddhas are indeed reverent toward the Dhamma, not reverent toward material things.

Even though you have had a jeweled house built the size of a world-system, filled with all kinds of gems, and carry about the relics, there is not even a single Nāga capable of attaining the realization of the Dhamma. Why is this?
“O Naga, even for you, the realization of the Truths does not yet exist. It is indeed fitting that the relics be led to the place where the realization of the Truths occurs.
For the Tathāgatas arise for the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra; this is the manifestation of the Buddha’s splendor.
Therefore, I shall lead the relics, for the King himself shall perform the enshrinement of the relics this very day.”
"Therefore, without making a fuss, give me the relic quickly," he said.
When this was said, the Naga king, being unable to refuse and thinking that the relics were being guarded by his own nephew, spoke thus: "Venerable sir, you say 'Give it!
Give it! without knowing whether the relics exist in the stupa or not. I [say] they do not exist."
"I say: 'If you see him, take him and go. [The king says: 'I will take him, Great King. [The king says: 'Take him, monks!
Having thus obtained the promise three times—'I will take him, Great King' and 'Take him, monks'—and having had a fine net woven, he stood there with the monks."
Placing his hand upon the face of his nephew, he immediately said,
"Nāga, take this casket of relics and stand here!
Having submerged himself into the earth, he emerged within the monastic courtyard.
Then, the assembly of devas and nāgas, having gathered thinking, "We shall witness the battle between the novice and the nāga," saw the victory of the monk-nāga;
delighted and overjoyed, they returned with him while worshipping the relics.
When the nāga king had departed after deceiving the monk by saying, "I have been sent [here]," he was thrilled and joyful regarding the relics.
Having taken it, he sent a message to his nephew so that he might come.
Then the nephew, not seeing the basket in his mother’s womb,
came weeping and informed his maternal uncle.
Then that Naga king cried out, "We have been deceived!
and all the Nagas together lamented.

Thereupon, all the Nagas having assembled in the Naga abode, they loosened their hair and, grasping their hearts with both hands, shed streams of tears from eyes like blue lotuses, as if their very sorrow were melting away.
“Lamenting, the nāgas came into the presence of the Saṅgha and lamented in many ways, distressed by the removal of the relics.
And having lamented, they spoke thus to the community of monks: “Venerable sirs, without causing distress to anyone, through the power of our merit...”
"Having obtained these relics that have been worn by the hem of his robe, why did you not take them all? You are creating an obstacle for our attainment of heaven and liberation!
Out of compassion for them, the Saṅgha caused a small amount of the relic to be given.
Satisfied with that, they departed and brought offerings for worship.
Then Sakka, Lord of the Devas, addressed Vissakamma, saying, "Construct a pavilion made of the seven precious gems at the place where the novice stands.
At that very moment, he constructed the pavilion.
Then Sakka, surrounded by a retinue of devas from two celestial realms, arrived carrying a jeweled couch together with a golden spittoon. Therein—
Having established it within the pavilion and taken the relic casket from the hands of the novice, he placed it upon that couch.
At that time— “Brahmā held the parasol, Santusita the yak-tail fan,
Suyāma the jeweled palm-leaf fan, and Sakka the conch-blower with its water.”
But four great kings stood there with swords in hand,
and thirty-two sons of the gods, possessed of great psychic power,
stood there holding out their hands and worshipping with *pāricchattaka* flowers.
Thirty-two maidens also stood there holding staffs and lamps;
having driven away the wicked yakkhas,
