twenty-eight yakkha generals then stood guard, providing protection.
There, Pañcasikha stood playing the lute,
while Timbaru provided the sound of musical instruments;
and many sons of the gods were engaged in singing excellent songs, having prepared the stage.
The Naga king Mahākāla was praised in manifold ways;
celestial musical instruments resounded, divine songs were performed,
and divine perfumes rained down as the deities caused them to fall.
Then the Elder Indagutta, for the purpose of warding off Māra, fashioned an iron canopy in the sky extending as far as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
The Elders belonging to the five Nikāyas surrounded the relics and, sitting in five places, performed the communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*).
At that time, the King came to that place, removed the golden casket from his head, and [placed] the relic-casket [upon it].

Having placed it in his own lap, set it upon a throne, and worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he prostrated himself at the five points, raised his joined palms to his head, and stood gazing at it with wide-open eyes.
At that moment, while the white parasol atop the relic was visible, the Brahmā who held the parasol was not seen; likewise, the palm-leaf fan [was visible, but its bearer was not].
Fanning-fans and such were seen, but no holders were seen; the sounds of celestial musical instruments and songs were heard, but no gandhabba deities were seen.
Having witnessed this marvel, the king said this to the Elder Indagutta: "The deities have honored me with divine parasols;
I, however, honor them with human parasols. The Elder replied, "It is fitting, Great King. The king—

Having honored him with his own golden image under a white parasol, he took a golden pitcher, offered the consecration water, and on that very day bestowed the sovereignty over the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Then all the musical instruments were sounded; having honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they paid him great reverence once again.
The king asked the Elder: "Venerable sir, our Teacher bore two umbrellas, one divine and one human.
Were there not two umbrellas, or three umbrellas, Great King? "I see no other umbrella, venerable sir.

[The Teacher’s umbrella was] that which has virtue as its base, concentration as its handle, the faculties as its spokes, the powers as its rim, and is covered by the leaves of the paths and fruits; it is the supreme white umbrella of liberation.
Having raised [the Dharma], attained the consecration of knowledge, and set in motion the wheel of the jewel of the Dharma,
he exercised sovereignty over the ten thousand world-systems, bringing the kingdom of the Buddha into his own hands. Thus, saying,
"I give the kingdom three times to the Teacher who holds the three umbrellas," he honored the relics with the kingdom on three occasions.
Then, while gods and humans were offering divine perfumes, garlands, and the like, and while the sounds of many musical instruments were resounding,
the King took the relic casket upon his head, emerged from the jeweled pavilion, and, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
circumambulated the Great Cetiya, ascended by the eastern gate, and entered the relic chamber. Then...
Surrounding the Great Cetiya, ninety-six koṭis of Arahants stood there.
The King, intending to remove the relic casket from his head and place it upon a magnificent couch, thought thus;
at that very moment, the relic casket moved seven tāla trees' distance away from the King's head and settled of its own accord.
The elements, having ascended into the sky, assumed the form of a Buddha— adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
the eighty minor characteristics, and a fathom-wide aura; beautified by the splendor of Ketumāla and blazing with a manifold web of rays in various colors such as blue, yellow, and red—
and performed at the foot of the Gaṇḍamba tree a twin miracle identical to the twin miracle [performed by the Buddha].
Having seen that miracle of the relics and having gained confidence, twelve koṭis of gods and humans attained Arahatship,
while those who attained the remaining three fruits were beyond counting. Thus, after displaying various miracles through the relics,
they relinquished their Buddha-forms, entered the casket, descended with it, and came to rest upon the head of the king.
As if anointed with nectar, the king, considering his attainment of human birth to have become fruitful,
took the relic casket with both hands and, surrounded by dancers, approached the decorated couch.
Having placed the relic box upon a jeweled throne and washed his hands with scented water, he rubbed them with various kinds of fragrant unguents.
Having searched through the jewel casket and taken the relics, he thought:
"If these relics remain undisturbed by anyone,
and if they shall stand as a refuge for the people..."
"Let them lie down upon a well-prepared, most costly couch in the manner of the Teacher lying down at the time of his final nibbāna.

Having thought thus, he placed the relics upon the surface of that excellent couch; at that very moment, by the power of the king's intention, the relics lay upon the costly couch in the likeness of the Buddha.
"On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha,
during the Uposatha, under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha, the relics were thus established.
Simultaneously with the establishment of the relics, the great earth trembled, and manifold miracles occurred in many ways."
On that very day, making the waters its boundary, this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked;
the great ocean surged, lightning bolts flashed in the sky, and a brief rain fell. A single tumult arose throughout the six celestial realms.
Having seen this marvel, the King was filled with faith and placed the relics upon his own golden palanquin beneath a white parasol.

Having worshipped [the relics] and granted sovereignty over the island of Tambapaṇṇi for seven days, he removed his ornaments worth three hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and offered them in worship.
Likewise, all the female dancers, the ministers, the rest of the great multitude, and the gods also worshipped with all their ornaments; therefore—
Whether one should worship with devotion the Sugata, honored by the three worlds, while he is still present,
or whether a person should worship his relic even as small as a mustard seed—
the fruit of their merit is equal, provided that their faith is the same.
"Knowing that even though the Sugata has attained final Nibbāna,

the wise person should honor his relics"— thereupon the king gave robes, garments, and medicinal requisites such as sugar and ghee to the Saṅgha, and had the communal recitation of the scriptures performed throughout the entire night.
On the following day, he caused the drum to be beaten in the city, and the great multitude [prepared] perfumes, garlands, and other offerings for this seven-day period.
Thinking, "Let them take [the relics] and go to pay homage," the Elder Indagutta also resolved:
"May all the people in the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi who wish to pay homage to the relics come at this very moment, pay their respects, and then return to their respective places.
They did exactly so; having paid homage to the relics, they departed. The King, meanwhile, offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha for seven days.
After seven days had passed, he informed the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, I have completed the work that was to be done for the relic chamber; please close the relic chamber.
The Saṅgha addressed the novice Uttarasumana, saying, "Close the relic chamber with the stone the color of fat that you brought previously. They accepted, saying, "Very well."
They closed the relic chamber.
Then those whose taints were exhausted [made this vow]: "In the relic chamber, let the perfumes not fade; let the garlands not wither; let the lamps not go out;
let the jewels not lose their luster; let the objects worthy of worship not perish. Let the stone slabs, colored like fat, be joined together."
They resolved, "May there be no opportunity for our enemies.
Thus, after the King had enshrined the relics, he again caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:

"Having enshrined the relics at the Great Cetiya, let them bring the relics back and perform a re-enshrinement. Then the great multitude, according to their respective means, [prepared] gold, silver, and so forth.
Having had a casket made and having placed the relics therein, they deposited them upon a stone slab the color of fat above the relic-chamber.
Thus, all the relics collected together amounted to about one thousand.
Thus ends the account of the depositing of the relics in the *Thūpavaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the minds of virtuous people.
24. Then the king, having enclosed all that [area], while constructing the cetiya, completed the four-sided base together with the dome.
However, before the work on the parasol and the plastering was finished, he fell ill with a terminal disease;
becoming emaciated, he summoned his younger brother and [entrusted] the unfinished work on the parasol and the plastering of the cetiya to him.
"Father, finish it quickly and satisfy me," he said. Knowing the king's weakness, [the architect] realized that he would not be able to complete the work in the interim;
therefore, he had a tunic made of pure cloth and had it fastened to the Cetiya.
Then, by means of painters, he had a railing, full vases, and rows of five-fingered hands fashioned upon the top of the tunic.
The basket-makers, having had a bamboo umbrella made, fashioned a railing upon the top of it consisting of rough-leaf discs representing the sun and moon;
they decorated it with lacquer and red arsenic and reported to the king, "The work on the stupa is finished.
The king said, "In that case, show me the Great Cetiya," and lying down in a palanquin, he performed a circumambulation of the Cetiya.
Having prepared a bed on the ground at the southern gate and lying there upon it, he lay on his right side facing the Mahāthūpa and on his left side facing the Lohapāsāda;
looking upon them, his heart became filled with serene faith.
Then, perceiving how greatly the King’s message had benefited him, the monks who had come from various places to inquire after his health—
Ninety-six crores of people stood surrounding the king. Then the Saṅgha, having split into various groups, engaged in communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*).
Not seeing the Elder Theraputtābhaya at that assembly, the king thought thus:
"He did not retreat even when twenty-eight great battles were being waged against me by the Damiḷas; now, while this battle for death is taking place—"
"Thinking that he does not come because he has seen my defeat," [the king thought]. Then the Elder, dwelling on a mountain ablaze at the head of the Karinda River,
knowing the king's reflection, arrived through the air surrounded by five hundred who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) and appeared before the king.
When the king saw the elder, he had him sit before himself and spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, having taken ten great warriors with you, you fought against the Damilas; now, alone, I have begun to fight against Death.
Yet, I am unable to defeat Death, that enemy. Then—
"O Lord of Men, do not fear! Until the enemy of the defilements has been conquered, the host of Death remains unconquerable.

Having said this, he instructed him thus: "Great King, in this entire world of living beings, everyone is followed by birth, pursued by old age, overcome by sickness, and struck down by death. Therefore, [he said]:"
"Just as vast mountains, having struck against other peaks,
might roll around on all sides, crushing [everything] in the four directions;
even so do old age and death overwhelm living beings."
Whether it be a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudda,
a caṇḍāla, or a pukkusa, he avoids nothing at all— he tramples everything down.
There is no ground there for elephants, nor for chariots, nor for infantry.
"Nor can he be conquered by a battle of spells or by wealth.

Therefore, this so-called death has not overcome those of great renown such as Mahāsammata and others; those of great merit such as Jotiya and others; those of great strength such as Baladeva and others;
those possessed of psychic power such as Mahāmoggallāna and others; and those possessed of wisdom such as Sāriputta and others, who attained [liberation] through their own self-arisen knowledge.
It falls without any doubt even upon those who have realized the Truths, the Paccekabuddhas endowed with all virtues,
and even the Sammasambuddhas— how much more so, then, upon other beings?
Therefore—
All those excellent kings of great lineage, beginning with Mahāsammata, have passed away;
likewise, Baladeva and others of great strength have gone to the state of impermanence.
Those who possessed merit and attained renown, such as Mahaddhana, Jotiya, Meṇḍaka, and the rest, have also departed.
All those who possessed enjoyments entered the mouth of Death like the moon and its retinue entering the mouth of Rāhu;
even he who was renowned as the most excellent among the sons of the Tathāgata endowed with psychic powers—
that Elder— along with the Great King himself, entered the mouth of Death by the power of his own psychic strength.
"O Great King, among all beings, with the exception of the Victor (the Buddha), there is no one equal to him in wisdom.
Even he, the Dhamma-Senāpati, though a disciple, has gone to impermanence.
O Great King, even the Self-Become One (the Buddha) has gone to peace through the power of his own self-arisen knowledge."
All of them, though endowed with the power of knowledge, did not transcend impermanence;
even the Lord of the Three Worlds, that Supreme Person, having transcended the state of impermanence,
O King, was unable to go further— of other beings there is no need to speak.
Therefore, O Great King, all beings in the realms of existence have never been liberated from death.
Reflect thus: "All conditioned things are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
For even in your second existence, your desire for the Dhamma was indeed great.
Having abandoned the celestial bliss of the divine world that had presented itself to you,
you came here and performed manifold meritorious deeds;
even for the sake of a single kingdom, you acted thus to illuminate the Teaching.
"Great King, whatever merit you have performed up until this very day, remember it all;
it will immediately become happiness.

Hearing this, the king was delighted in heart and said, "Venerable sir, even in the battle with death, I have you as my support," and, finding relief, he ordered the scribe to read the Book of Merit. The scribe read the Book of Merit as follows:
“One hundred and nine monasteries were caused to be built by the Great King;
one hundred and nine crores were spent on the monastery and the Maricaṭṭi [stupa];
the supreme Lohapāsāda was caused to be built for thirty crores.”
Twenty-four priceless [relics] were enshrined in the Mahāthūpa;
the remaining ones in the Mahāthūpa were enshrined by Subuddhi,
O Great King, and they are worth a thousand koṭis once again through you.
In the land of Maleya, there was a merchant named Koḷamba who,
having given two very costly earrings and taken them back,
[offered them] to the five supreme Great Elders who had destroyed the taints.
With a mind full of faith, he gave a handful of sour millet;
[this was done] by Cūḷaṅgaṇiya, who, having been defeated in battle and fleeing,
caused a proclamation to be made for his death, and then returned through the air.
To the one whose taints were destroyed, the self-restrained one, who was indifferent to himself, he read out the merit-register, saying, "A bowl of rice has been given.
Hearing this, the king was delighted and said, "Stop! Stop! Read on! Thus he spoke during the seven-day festival for the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery.
During the seven days of the festival for the Thūpa-āramha, I bestowed a most precious and great almsgiving upon the Saṅgha of both the four quarters.
I performed twenty-four great Visākha-pūjās; three times I gave robes to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus on the island of Tambapaṇṇi;
seven times I gave the kingdom of Laṅkā to the Sāsana; and five times I gave ghee, oil, and perfectly pure [offerings].
At twelve locations along the road, I lit seven thousand lamps;
at eighteen locations, I caused medicine and food to be constantly provided for the sick by physicians. At forty-four locations, I gave oil-lamps;
at exactly those same locations, I caused ghee-filled cakes and honey-cakes to be constantly given along with the meals.
Month after month, on the eight Uposatha days, I caused lamp oil to be provided for all the monasteries in the island of Laṅkā.
Having heard that the gift of Dhamma is greater than the gift of material things, I sat upon the Dhamma throne below the Lohapāsāda and began to recite the Maṅgala Sutta;
yet, out of reverence for the Saṅgha, I was unable to complete the recitation. From that time forth, regarding those who teach the Dhamma...
Having honored them, I had Dhamma discourses delivered in all the monasteries;

and for each Dhamma preacher, on the eight Uposatha days of every month, I caused to be given ghee, molasses, and sugar in measures of a *nāḷi*, and *yaṭṭhi-madhuka* in the measure of a four-fingered handful, as well as two garments. All of this was given by me while established in power.

"He wins over the mind. But "he wins over only the two gifts given by me while I was in a state of wretchedness, regardless of my own life"—having heard this, the Elder Abhaya, O Great King, felt faith precisely toward that which is inspiring of faith.
For those two portions of alms-food were obtained without causing distress to others and were righteously acquired; thus, he did not look to himself and remained unattached.
"Because it was given; because it was given after making it sufficient for the recipients; because it was given having generated joy and gladness; because it was given with powerful faith;
and because the gift was consumed without remainder—by these five reasons it is great.
Having said this, he continued: "O Great King, among the elders who received the *kaṅgu* and *ambila* alms, the Elder Maliyamahādeva [is foremost] at Samantakūṭa."
Having given it to five hundred bhikkhus, the Elder Dhammagutta of Pathavi-cālana consumed it.
Having given it to five hundred bhikkhus at the Kalyāṇī monastery,
the Elder Dhammagutta, resident of Talaṅgara, also gave it to twelve thousand bhikkhus on Piyaṅgudīpa and consumed it.
[The Elder] enjoyed [the meal]. The Elder Cūḷa-Tissa, resident of Maṅgaṇa, gave it to sixty thousand bhikkhus at the Kelāsakūṭa Monastery and enjoyed it.
The Elder Mahābhagga also gave it to seven hundred bhikkhus at the Ukkānagara Monastery and enjoyed it.
Furthermore, the Elder Saraka-Bhattagāhaka gave it to twelve thousand bhikkhus on Piyaṅgudīpa.
Having said, "He gave it and made use of it," he caused the king's mind to rejoice.
The king, having gained confidence in his heart, spoke thus: "Venerable sir, while exercising sovereignty for twenty-four years, I have been of great service to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus.
May my body also be of service to the Saṅgha; let my body, as a slave of the Saṅgha, [be placed] at the Mahācetiya."
"Have the work at the Saṅgha’s assembly hall burned in the crematorium. Then, addressing his younger brother, he said: "Dear Tissa!
You have successfully completed the unfinished work on the Great Thūpa. Morning and evening, perform flower offerings at the Great Thūpa and present oblations three times a day.
Do not let any part of the cycle of almsgiving established by me fall into neglect."
Having exhorted him, saying, "Always be diligent in the duties to be performed for the Saṅgha," he became silent.
At that moment, the monks began their communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*), but the deities took six chariots from the six directions, brought them along, and having placed them in a row, said:
"Great King, our heavenly world is delightful; our heavenly world..."
Saying, "It is delightful," they requested permission to return to their respective celestial realms.
Having heard their words, the king said, "Wait until I have finished listening to the Dhamma.
Thinking that the Saṅgha had stopped its communal recitation (sañjhāya) because the king had signaled with his hand to stop them, he ordered the recitation to cease.
The King asked, "Venerable sir, why have you suspended the communal recitation? "Great King, because you signaled with your hand to stop it.
"Venerable sir, I did not give you that signal. "The deities, having brought six chariots from the world of the Cātumahārājika gods, are requesting to return to their respective celestial realms.
Therefore, I gave the signal, saying: 'Please wait until I have finished listening to the Dhamma.'"
Hearing that he was not a slave, some thought, "This king is delirious with the fear of death;
there is no being indeed who does not fear death.
Then the Elder Abhaya said, "How can it be believed, O Great King, that six chariots have been brought from the six heavenly worlds?"
Having heard this, the king caused flower garlands to be thrown into the air. They went and hung separately from the front of the chariot.
When the great multitude saw the flower garlands hanging in the sky, they became free of doubt.
Then the king asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, which is the most delightful heavenly realm?"—"The Tusita abode," [he replied].
"Great King, it is delightful; Metteyya Bodhisatta also dwells right there, awaiting the time for his Buddhahood," he said.
Upon hearing this, the king fixed his heart upon that place. While gazing at the Great Thūpa, he passed away even as he lay down and was brought from the Tusita heaven like one awakening from sleep.
Having been reborn in a chariot, he became a dry land of merit for himself and for the great multitude.
To make it manifest, he stood upon his chariot, adorned with celestial ornaments, and while the great multitude looked on,
he circumambulated the Mahāthūpa three times, paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and departed for the Tusita realm. Thus,
the wise [perceive] that in this essence-less accumulation of wealth, sentient beings are impermanent.
Having practiced generosity and taken hold of the essence—the greatness of the Triple Gem—they go to a happy destination.

When the king’s dancing girls learned of his death, they released their flower buds at the very spot where they stood; the hall built at that location became known as the Makuḷamuttasālā (the Hall of the Released Flower Buds).
Once the king’s body had been placed upon the funeral pyre, at the place where the great multitude...

Having grasped [the earth] with his hand, he fashioned it. There, the hall that was built became known as the Viracitthasālā. The place where they cremated the king’s body became the Sīmāmālaka, known as the Rājamālaka.
Then the king’s younger brother, having become the great king named Saddhātissa, completed the remaining work and the plastering of the stupa, and thus constructed the Thūpa.
Thus ends the section on the Mahācetiya in the *Thūpavaṃsa* composed for the purpose of pleasing the minds of virtuous people. 26.
Now, King Kākavaṇṇatissa, the father of the Great King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, will become the father of the Blessed One Metteyya;
the Queen Mahādevī will become his mother; and Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya will be the chief disciple.
"He will come to be. His younger brother will become his second disciple. The King’s paternal aunt, Queen Anulā, will become the chief queen.
The King’s son, Prince Sāli, will become his son.
The treasurer Saṅghamitta will become the chief attendant to that minister, and the minister’s daughter will become the chief female attendant. Thus, all of them—
"Having performed their duties and being endowed with the necessary causes, having heard the Dhamma of that Blessed One and made an end of suffering,
they will attain final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
And up to this point—
Dwelling in the small cell named Mahiṇdasena, with his bowl and robes at his feet—
he who has mastered the Three Piṭakas, is endowed with the virtues of faith and morality,
and delights in the welfare of all beings.
Thus, having been well requested by him, I began this work;
now it has reached its conclusion, the history of the Thūpa,
unconfused, complete, and rightly praised by the wise.
Whatever wholesome deed we have performed with this alms-bowl,
by that merit may all beings go to Nibbāna,
and may they achieve success without obstacle.
The lineage of the excellent stupa has come to its conclusion;
likewise, may the heart's desires of people who are established in the true Dhamma swiftly attain fulfillment.
By him who desired the arising of the true Dhamma,
the *Līlātthadīpanī-Ṭīkā* was composed for the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*;
likewise, the *Atthadīpanā* was composed for the treatise *Saccasaṅkhepa*.
By that wise one, through whom the *Visuddhimagga* was well translated from the Sinhalese language,
and by whom this concise exposition of its meaning was made for the benefit of yogis,
it has been rendered from the Sinhalese tongue.
He who was appointed to the Dhamma-hall of King Parakkamabāhu,
the banner of all monarchs, who had mastered the Tipiṭaka,
and among whose disciples the Sasana was well-established—
Thus was it written by the venerable Vācissara Thera;
the *Thūpavaṃsa* is completed.
